title: Praying for a Reorganization

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You gave me a project that can't get funded because it's not in the strategic plan.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And you won't let me make waves by asking for a change to the strategic plan.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So I'll be in my cubicle creating "PowerPoint" slides and praying for a reorganization.

situation: Dilbert tells his boss that the project he was assigned cannot receive funding because it isn't part of the strategic plan. The boss also forbids him from asking to change the plan. With no options left, Dilbert says he will pass the time making slides and hoping a reorganization changes things.
punchline: Stuck in a catch-22 with no legitimate way to fix the problem, Dilbert's only hope is that a random corporate reorganization will make it disappear.
summary: Trapped between an unfundable assignment and a ban on rocking the boat, Dilbert resigns himself to busywork and wishful thinking.

file: 1999/1999-03-07_morale_family picture_picture of you_hard to look at_freaks_alice.gif
title: Boss Insults Family, Ignores Morale

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: ... So our morale is... umm...

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: What's that on your desk?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's a family picture.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I might be wrong, but I think it's only a picture of you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The rest of the family is hard to look at.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I see no reason I should suffer.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Now what was your question about morale?

transcript.speaker: Unseen voice
transcript.text: Alice?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're surrounded by freaks.

situation: Alice is in the Boss's office to discuss low morale when she notices the only family picture on his desk shows just him. The Boss casually explains that the rest of his family is too ugly to look at, then asks what her morale question was. After Alice leaves, he mutters that they are surrounded by freaks.
punchline: The Boss's shallow cruelty toward his own family shows how little empathy he has for employee morale, and he hypocritically calls everyone else freaks.
summary: A manager displays a framed photo of only himself because he finds his relatives too unpleasant to look at, then dismisses a subordinate's concern about workplace spirits.

file: 1999/1999-04-07_budget cycle_helipcopter_double rotor_respect_budget process_budget padding_albino tiger  cubs.gif
title: Absurd Budget Request Padding Escalates

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The budget cycle

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: And I'll need a helicopter, double rotor.

transcript.speaker: Budget Manager
transcript.text: If you have any respect for me or the budget process, you will not ask for such obvious budget padding.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: And I'll need that chopper filled with albino tiger cubs.

setting: Office desk during a budget meeting
situation: An employee sits across a desk from a budget manager and requests a double-rotor helicopter as part of his budget. The manager scolds him that such an obvious padding request shows disrespect for the budget process. The employee responds by adding that the helicopter must be filled with albino tiger cubs.
punchline: The employee ignores the warning about padding and escalates the absurdity, showing that the budget process rewards inflated requests that everyone expects to be negotiated down.
summary: A worker pads his budget with ridiculous demands, and when scolded for it, he simply makes the demands stranger.

title: Laziness Prevents Copycat Workplace Crimes

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Our company newsletter has reports of bizarre workplace crimes.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I've never thought of these crimes before, but now I have the urge to be a copycat.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Thank goodness my parents raised me to be lazy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: They were very wise.

situation: Wally reads the company newsletter and mentions its reports of bizarre workplace crimes. He admits the stories have given him the urge to copy them. He then says he is saved by his lazy upbringing, and Dilbert agrees his parents were wise.
punchline: Wally's notorious laziness is the only thing stopping him from committing workplace crimes, so his parents' bad parenting turns out to be protective.
summary: A newsletter's tales of strange office misdeeds tempt a coworker until his own idleness talks him out of it.

title: Budget Spreadsheet Error Futility Hum

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's a funny thing about budgets...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No matter how hard you try, there's always a spreadsheet error that makes it all an exercise in futility.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you mind if I hum?

situation: Dilbert stands holding a coffee mug beside a seated coworker and muses about budgets. He explains that a spreadsheet error always creeps in and makes the whole budgeting effort futile. He then casually asks if he can hum, as if resigned to the pointlessness.
punchline: After realizing that all budget work is doomed to futility by inevitable spreadsheet errors, Dilbert's resigned, deflated response is to ask politely whether he may hum, implying he has given up and will simply zone out.
summary: A weary engineer reflects that budget spreadsheets always hide a mistake that ruins the work, then calmly asks to hum to himself.

title: Fake Chinese Product Instructions Scribbles

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Tina, I want you to write the Chinese version of our product's instructions.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Can you tell the difference between Chinese words and random scribbles?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: I'll be done in five minutes.

situation: The Boss asks Tina, a technical writer, to produce a Chinese version of the product instructions. She asks whether he can tell real Chinese writing from random scribbles, and when he admits he can't, she says she'll be done in five minutes.
punchline: Because the Boss can't read Chinese and therefore can't check her work, Tina will simply hand in meaningless scribbles and he will never know.
summary: A writer realizes her clueless manager can't verify a translation, so she plans to fake it with nonsense in minutes.

file: 1999/1999-02-28_raises_young employees_few dollars_buy small motorcyel_crack cocaine_be your mentor_tickle my own fett_perfect sat.gif
title: Boss Denies Raises, Offers Mentoring

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Asok, I can't give raises to young employees.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Because as soon as you get a few dollars in your pocket...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You buy small motorcycles and disappear in the night.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I know that's a generalization.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Some of you prefer the crack cocaine.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The good news is that I'm willing to be your mentor.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Aaagh! I got double eight hundreds on my SAT!!! For what?!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Sometimes when I'm in a bad mood I tickle my own feet.

setting: The Boss's office, with Asok and the Boss seated on couch and armchair
situation: The Boss tells young intern Asok he can't give him a raise because young employees supposedly spend any extra money on motorcycles or drugs. He then offers to mentor Asok instead. Asok despairs over his perfect SAT score, and the Boss offers his own bizarre 'wisdom' about tickling his own feet.
punchline: The Boss denies a raise using absurd stereotypes about young people, then offers worthless 'mentoring' that consists of a bizarre personal confession, leaving the brilliant Asok bitterly asking what his perfect SAT score was for.
summary: A manager refuses to pay a gifted young employee more, insulting him with stereotypes, and substitutes useless life advice for actual compensation.

title: Teaching an Embryo to Drink Coffee

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I hear you're being replaced by a low-paid embryo. May I see it?

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: He is so-oo cute!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'm teaching him to drink coffee.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Is that healthy?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: It must be. I drink six quarts a day, and look at me.

situation: Carol hears that a bald, bespectacled coworker is being replaced by a cheap embryo and asks to see it. He shows her a jar holding the embryo and says he is teaching it to drink coffee through a tube into a mug. When she asks if that is healthy, he cites his own heavy coffee consumption as proof.
punchline: The coworker offers his own obviously unhealthy, caffeine-ravaged state as evidence that coffee must be healthy, which is sarcastically self-defeating.
summary: A man about to be replaced by a bargain-priced embryo in a jar trains it on caffeine and defends the habit by pointing to his own haggard appearance.

file: 1999/1999-05-28_million bucks_pay up_double or nothing_won't go to work_naked_exact words.gif
title: Double or Nothing Naked Bet

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You said you'd give me a million bucks if I went to work like this.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Pay up.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll bet you double or nothing that you won't go to work totally naked.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wait... What were his exact words?

setting: Dilbert's home, then his office cubicle
situation: Dilbert, dressed for work, demands that Dogbert pay the million bucks he promised for going to work as he is. Dogbert instead offers a double-or-nothing bet that Dilbert won't go to work totally naked. In the last panel Dilbert sits naked in his cubicle chair, belatedly wondering what the original deal actually said.
punchline: Dilbert took Dogbert's double-or-nothing bet and stripped for work, only to realize too late that he never confirmed the terms of the original wager, so he may have lost it all.
summary: A man who tries to collect on a bet gets talked into a riskier one and ends up sitting undressed at his desk, doubting the fine print.

title: Make the Website More Webbish

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The web site needs to be more webbish.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But not too webbish.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How long will that take?

situation: The Boss stands over Dilbert at his computer and gives him a vague order to make the company web site more 'webbish'. He then immediately qualifies it so it can't be too webbish, and asks for a time estimate. Dilbert says nothing throughout.
punchline: The Boss gives meaningless, self-contradictory requirements and still demands a schedule estimate for them.
summary: A manager issues a nonsensical, contradictory request about a web site and then wants to know how soon it can be done.

file: 1999/1999-08-23_putting you on team_intelligent_highly motivated_stubborn_dumb guy_v neck sweater.gif
title: Team Includes One Stubborn Dummy

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, I'm putting you on a team.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You'll be working with other intelligent, highly motivated people plus...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: A stubborn dumb guy with a V-neck sweater.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he is being assigned to a team. He first praises the other members as intelligent and highly motivated, then introduces one more teammate, a man in a blue V-neck sweater, whom he bluntly describes as stubborn and dumb.
punchline: The Boss's flattering team pitch collapses into an honest insult, showing that every team gets saddled with one obstinate, incompetent member that management knowingly assigns.
summary: A manager sells a new team assignment with glowing praise, then casually admits that one member is an obstinate fool.

title: Spying on the VP's Priorities

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Asok, I want you to observe our VP so we can figure out what our priorities are.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We've built a duck blind in his office using cubicle material.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: 10:28 a.m., the subject is flossing.

setting: Corporate office and the VP's office
situation: The Boss tells Asok to observe the VP so the company can work out what its priorities are. The Boss explains that a duck blind made of cubicle material has been built in the VP's office. Asok, hiding inside it with leaves on top, records in his notes that the VP is flossing his teeth at his desk.
punchline: Watching the VP to learn the company's priorities only reveals trivial personal habits like flossing, implying management has no real priorities and the VP does nothing of substance.
summary: An intern is sent to secretly stake out an executive from a camouflaged hide, and all he has to report is the man's dental hygiene.

file: 1999/1999-11-28_catbert_evil director_hr dept._views of management_exceeds expectations_renamed_drool_loser_die die die_category changes_performance review.gif
title: Catbert Renames Performance Review Ratings

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil Director of Human Resources

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I love my job.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Hello, hapless employee.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I've renamed the four levels of employee performance...

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: ...to accurately reflect the views of management.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: The category of "exceeds expectations" is renamed to...

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: ..."At least he or she doesn't drool on himself or herself."

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: "Meets expectations" will be called "loser". "Does not meet expectations" will now be called "Die! Die! Die!"

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I could send it out by e-mail but I enjoy seeing the looks on their faces.

situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, visits a bald, bespectacled employee at his desk to announce new names for the four performance review ratings. He reads out the renamed categories, which bluntly insult each level of performance. Afterward he reveals he delivers the news in person because he enjoys watching employees' reactions.
punchline: The renamed performance ratings honestly reflect management's real contempt for employees, and Catbert delivers the news in person purely for the sadistic pleasure of watching their faces.
summary: A gleefully cruel HR executive personally informs a worker that the performance rating labels now bluntly express what management really thinks of staff.

title: Catbert Reads Non-Compete, Dances Instead

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: So you think you're leaving for a better job?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Your agreement with us bans you from working in this industry if you quit. Ha!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Holy cripes! It does say you can dance on my head.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Hold still.

situation: Dilbert is packing up his cubicle to leave for a better job when Catbert, the evil H.R. director, appears over the cubicle wall. Catbert gleefully cites a non-compete clause in Dilbert's employment agreement that bars him from working in the industry. Dilbert reads the agreement and discovers it also gives Catbert the right to dance on his head, and Catbert promptly does so.
punchline: The employment contract is so one-sided that, besides the non-compete clause, it also gives H.R. the right to dance on an employee's head, and Catbert exercises that right out of pure malice.
summary: A departing employee learns that his contract traps him in the industry and also lets the cruel personnel chief use his skull as a stage.

title: Dogbert Drops His False Humility

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Do you think I have too much false humility?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Try going a week without using any false humility, so I can see the difference.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Wake up, you piece of fetid carp, and experience the joy of knowing Dogbert!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This could be a long week.

setting: Dilbert's living room and bedroom at home
situation: Dogbert asks Dilbert, who is eating chips on the couch, whether he has too much false humility. Dilbert challenges him to go a week without any so he can see the difference. The next morning Dogbert, wearing a crown and holding a gavel, wakes Dilbert by insulting him and boasting about the joy of knowing Dogbert.
punchline: Dogbert takes the challenge to drop false humility so literally that he becomes an arrogant, insulting tyrant, leaving Dilbert dreading the week ahead.
summary: A challenge to lose his modest act turns Dogbert into a crowned, boastful alarm clock for his weary owner.
themes: be careful what you wish for

title: Boss's Intuition Versus Dilbert's Analysis

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your analysis disagrees with my intuition.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your intuition also told you the Internet would be replaced by modems...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Whatever that means.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm misunderstood, just like... um... what's-his-face.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Satan?

situation: The Boss, seated at his desk, dismisses Dilbert's analysis because it conflicts with his own gut feeling. Dilbert points out that the Boss's intuition once predicted the Internet would be replaced by modems, which the Boss admits he doesn't even understand. The Boss then compares himself to a misunderstood figure he can't name, and Dilbert supplies Satan.
punchline: The Boss unwittingly compares himself to a misunderstood figure and Dilbert suggests Satan, implying the Boss is essentially evil as well as clueless.
summary: A manager waves away hard data in favor of his gut feeling, and his employee's reminder of past bad predictions ends with an unflattering comparison to the devil.

file: 1999/1999-09-07_everything went wrong_project wouldn't succeed_for managers_reverse amnesia_project.gif
title: Reverse Amnesia For Managers

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Everything went wrong in exactly the way I told you it would.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: In the next phase you will experience something I call "reverse amnesia for managers."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wait a minute; I'm the one who told you that the project wouldn't succeed.

setting: Office, during a project review meeting
situation: Dilbert stands beside a cost chart showing rising bars and tells the Boss that the project failed just as he predicted. He then warns that the Boss is about to develop "reverse amnesia," and the Boss immediately proves it by claiming he was the one who predicted the failure.
punchline: The Boss instantly rewrites history to claim credit for predicting the project's failure, confirming Dilbert's prediction that managers falsely remember being right.
summary: After a doomed project collapses, an engineer predicts his manager will rewrite history, and the manager obligingly does so on the spot.

file: 1999/1999-01-19_internet start up_engineer_interview_tv show_hot internet start up_engineering.gif
title: Wally Flirts With TV Interviewer

transcript.speaker: Interviewer
transcript.text: Wally, tell our viewers how your Internet start-up got so hot.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Beats me. I was wondering how YOU got so hot. I'm burning up over here!

transcript.speaker: Interviewer
transcript.text: It says here you were an engineer.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Is my ponytail doing anything for you?

setting: A television studio interview set with a camera and a rising-graph monitor
situation: A TV interviewer asks Wally why his Internet start-up has become so successful. Wally ignores the question and instead makes a clumsy pass at her, and when she notes that he used to be an engineer, he asks whether his ponytail is impressing her.
punchline: Wally, a classic socially awkward engineer, has suddenly become rich and trendy, and he assumes his new success and ponytail make him irresistible while having no idea why the company is doing well.
summary: A newly famous start-up founder uses his television interview to hit on the host with painfully dated pickup lines instead of explaining his success.

file: 1999/1999-08-15_pointy hired boss_phone_email_pager_electronic attempts_ruin productivity_send in ground trrops_return some calls.gif
title: Boss Sends Hiker to Summon Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Hiker
transcript.text: The Pointy-Haired Boss wants to see you.

transcript.speaker: Hiker
transcript.text: He tried to reach you by phone, e-mail and pager.

transcript.speaker: Hiker
transcript.text: But you resisted his electronic attempts to ruin your productivity.

transcript.speaker: Hiker
transcript.text: So he decided to send in the ground troops.

transcript.speaker: Hiker
transcript.text: Don't make me use this!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Could you wait outside while I return some phone calls?

transcript.speaker: Woman in line
transcript.text: Get to the back of the line.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Does anyone want to have a conversation?

transcript.speaker: Man in line
transcript.text: I have a magazine.

characters: Messenger with backpack and walking stick
situation: A messenger carrying a backpack and a walking stick arrives at Dilbert's cubicle because the boss could not reach him by phone, e-mail or pager. She threatens him with the stick, and Dilbert asks her to wait outside while he returns phone calls. He then finds a long line of people waiting to see him, so nobody is available for a conversation.
punchline: Dilbert avoids the boss's electronic messages, so the boss sends a person, and that person joins a long queue of people waiting for a face-to-face conversation with him.
summary: After dodging every electronic summons, Dilbert is tracked down by a trekking courier, only to discover an even longer line of people hoping to reach him.

file: 1999/1999-03-28_little experiment_stupid opinion_aggressively mock_passing fad_internet is fad_internet is everywhere_back up plan_attribute opinon.gif
title: Dogbert Practices Mocking Dilbert's Imaginary Opinion

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm trying a little experiment tonight.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll attribute a stupid opinion to you...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Then I'll aggressively mock you while you sit there saying nothing.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: So, according to you, the Internet is a passing fad.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You moron! Look around you! The Internet is everywhere!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And there's nothing you can do about it! Nothing!!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: How did that feel?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Quite satisfying.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I needed a back-up plan in case you ever get laryngitis.

setting: Dilbert's living room couch at home
situation: Dogbert announces an experiment in which he invents a stupid opinion for Dilbert, then loudly mocks him for it while Dilbert sits silently watching TV. Dogbert rants that the Internet is everywhere and Dilbert can do nothing about it. Afterward Dilbert admits it was satisfying and says he was rehearsing a backup in case Dogbert loses his voice.
punchline: Dogbert's elaborate experiment turns out to be Dilbert's idea of a convenient service: Dilbert wanted a spare ranting partner so he could enjoy the same satisfying argument if Dogbert ever loses his voice, implying the whole routine is a regular habit.
summary: A dog invents an opinion for his silent owner and berates him for it, only to learn the owner enjoys these tirades and wants a substitute in case the dog's voice gives out.

title: Dilbert Pays for Her Ex

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: I never told my last boyfriend what a despicable creep he was.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: But you'll pay for his crimes, and pay dearly!!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why don't you call him and tell him how you feel?

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: I have a date with him at ten o'clock tonight.

setting: Neutral pink background, apparently on a date
situation: Dilbert's date admits she never confronted her previous boyfriend about what a creep he was. She then grabs Dilbert by the shirt and threatens to make him pay for her ex's crimes. Dilbert suggests she simply call the ex and tell him, only to learn she has a date with that same ex later that night.
punchline: Dilbert is being cast as the stand-in for her ex's misdeeds, and she is dating Dilbert while also planning to go out with the creepy ex that very night.
summary: A woman takes out her old grievances on her current date instead of the ex who earned them, and she's still seeing that ex.

title: Meeting Moth Eats Employees' Clothes

transcript.speaker: Meeting Moth
transcript.text: A "meeting moth" should never go to a meeting on an empty stomach.

situation: Dilbert walks along with his shirt and trousers chewed into tatters, silently cursing. Alice does the same, her pink dress shredded and her hair a mess. In the last panel a man in moth wings and antennae, the meeting moth, appears to be the culprit, holding a bit of fabric and thinking about eating before meetings.
punchline: The meeting attendees' clothes were ravaged by a moth-like person who ate them because he went to the meeting hungry, a pun on clothes moths eating fabric.
summary: Two colleagues stagger out of a meeting with their clothes in ruins, and the culprit turns out to be a hungry man dressed as a moth.

file: 1999/1999-10-10_positive attitude alice_coworker_paper weight_throws at head_clocks head_positive attitude.gif
title: Positive Attitude Paperweight Thrown at Head

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's "Positive Attitude Week," Alice.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If you see a co-worker with a positive attitude ...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: ... give him the positive attitude paperweight.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: There's one!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: (No dialogue: the paperweight flies through the air and hits the humming co-worker on the head.)

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: It worked. He's back to normal.

transcript.speaker: Co-worker
transcript.text:
#
ing!!

transcript.speaker: Coworker with glasses
transcript.text: Ha ha ha!!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Uh-oh.

transcript.speaker: Co-worker
transcript.text:
#
ing!!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: One more! Quick!!

situation: The Boss announces Positive Attitude Week and instructs Alice to hand a paperweight to any co-worker who shows a positive attitude. Alice spots a happy, humming co-worker and throws the paperweight at his head, which knocks the cheer out of him. When another co-worker laughs, she calls for another paperweight.
punchline: Alice treats the "reward" paperweight as a projectile, using violence to cure anyone's cheerfulness and restore the normal office misery.
summary: A mandatory cheerfulness campaign turns into a game of bonking happy colleagues with a rock.

title: Management: Unskilled Labor Without Labor

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: It takes years of training to be an engineer.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: But you don't need any training whatsoever to be an engineer's boss.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: It's unskilled labor without the labor.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: I could do that.

situation: Carol, the boss's assistant with big curly hair, explains to Tina, a black-haired woman taking notes, that engineering requires years of training while managing engineers requires none. She sums up management as unskilled labor with no actual labor involved. Tina, intrigued, says she could do that job.
punchline: Management is portrayed as a job that needs no skills and no effort, so the listener immediately concludes she could do it.
summary: Two coworkers discuss how becoming a manager of engineers demands no qualifications or work, and one decides she is up to the task.

file: 1999/1999-03-30_bill gates_dogbert_incoming missles_anti microsoft weapons_press conference_huge catapult.gif
title: Anti-Microsoft Missiles Hit Press Conference

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Dogbert, Mom told Bill Gates she uses the "Linux" operating system!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm tracking four incoming missiles. I'll launch our anti-Microsoft weapons to intercept.

transcript.speaker: Reporter
transcript.text: I wondered why a press conference was being held on a huge catapult.

setting: Dilbert's living room, then Dogbert's missile control room, then in mid-air
situation: Dilbert's mother is on the phone and has told Bill Gates that she uses Linux, and Dilbert alerts Dogbert to the news. Dogbert, at a missile control console, detects four incoming missiles and prepares to intercept them with his anti-Microsoft weapons. The final panel shows reporters flying through the air alongside a missile marked MS, revealing that Microsoft launched its press conference on a giant catapult.
punchline: Microsoft's response to a customer switching to Linux is an absurd military-style strike, with its press conference literally catapulted at its enemies, mocking the company's aggressive tactics against competitors.
summary: A phone call about Linux triggers a missile defense, and Microsoft's press conference turns out to be hurtling through the sky on a catapult.

title: Mordac Rethinks Damaged Equipment Policy

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Mordac denies your request to add memory to your laptop!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But you would replace it if it were damaged, right?

transcript.speaker: Mordac
transcript.text: That is my policy.

transcript.speaker: Mordac
transcript.text: Maybe I should rethink that policy.

setting: Office, with a computer-filled window view in the last panel
situation: An employee tells a man that Mordac, head of IT security, has refused his request for more laptop memory. The employee then asks whether the laptop would be replaced if it were damaged, and Mordac confirms that is the policy. In the last panel Mordac sits at his desk, imagining computers and a laptop falling past his window.
punchline: Mordac realizes his replace-if-damaged policy gives people an incentive to destroy their equipment, hinting that he is being threatened with sabotage if he keeps refusing upgrades.
summary: An IT gatekeeper who turns down a hardware upgrade is reminded that his own damage-replacement rule rewards anyone willing to wreck their machine.

title: Hidden Camera Catches The Boss

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I used a hidden camera to capture the thief who's been raiding our cubicles.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The picture is grainy but I can almost make out a human form... or maybe a cat...

setting: Office, in front of a TV monitor
situation: Dilbert proudly announces that he used a hidden camera to catch the thief raiding the cubicles and plays the footage on a TV. The footage shows the Pointy-Haired Boss himself, but the Boss studies the grainy image and fails to recognise himself, guessing it might be a human or a cat.
punchline: The Boss is the thief on the video but is too clueless to recognise himself, even speculating that he might be a cat.
summary: A surveillance tape exposes the culprit behind the office thefts, yet the culprit is the one squinting at the screen without realising it is him.

title: Candidate Judged Disloyal for Applying Elsewhere

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I just got this résumé from a headhunter.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Evaluate her engineering skills and let me know if I should interview her.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well, Alice, you're almost qualified to work here, but I'm concerned about your loyalty.

situation: The Boss hands Dilbert a résumé from a headhunter and asks him to evaluate the candidate's engineering skills before deciding on an interview. Dilbert reads it and tells the candidate, who turns out to be Alice, that she is nearly qualified but that her loyalty is in question.
punchline: Alice is faulted for disloyalty because she is seeking a job elsewhere, even though the company is the one considering hiring her through a headhunter, which makes the loyalty concern absurd.
summary: A résumé arrives through a headhunter, and the candidate turns out to be a coworker who is suddenly questioned about her allegiance.

file: 1999/1999-09-27_found no problem_our drinking water_drink bottled water.gif
title: Safety Department Drinks Bottled Water

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our safety department has tested our drinking water and found no problem.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then why do you only drink bottled water?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Because that's what the safety department drinks.

situation: At a meeting, the Boss assures everyone that the safety department tested the office tap water and found it fine. Dilbert points out that the Boss himself only drinks bottled water. The Boss explains he does so because the safety department drinks bottled water too.
punchline: The safety department's own choice to drink bottled water reveals it doesn't trust the tap water it officially declared safe.
summary: A manager vouches for the tested tap water while quietly copying the safety experts in sipping from a bottle instead.
keywords: do as I say not as I do

file: 1999/1999-05-16_proactive_boring meeting_fake death_coffee is posioned_stiffen_easier to drag_pose_obscene_spread eagle_casket_dispose of body_wally.gif
title: Faking Death to Escape Meeting

transcript.speaker: Unseen speaker
transcript.text: Blah blah blah

transcript.speaker: Wally (thought)
transcript.text: I'll have to be proactive to escape this boring meeting.

transcript.speaker: Wally (thought)
transcript.text: I'll fake my own death and hope someone drags me into the hallway.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Aack!! My coffee is poisoned!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe we should drag him into the hallway.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Let's wait for him to stiffen. Then he'll be easier to drag.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: We should pose him before he stiffens.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Something obscene?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Or spread eagle, so he won't fit in a casket.

transcript.speaker: Wally (thought)
transcript.text: It never pays to be the proactive one.

setting: Conference room during a boring meeting
situation: Wally, bored in a meeting, decides to fake his own death by pretending his coffee is poisoned, hoping someone will drag him out into the hallway. Instead, Dilbert and Alice and a coworker coldly discuss waiting for rigor mortis or posing his body in an obscene position. Wally ends up lying on the floor with the cup on his head, stuck playing dead.
punchline: Wally's plan to escape the meeting backfires because his colleagues callously plan to leave and mock his 'corpse' rather than help, proving that taking initiative doesn't pay.
summary: A bored employee stages a dramatic fake poisoning to get out of a meeting, only to have his indifferent coworkers casually plot how to arrange his body.

title: Replacing Wally With an Embryo

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, technology is a young man's game.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's why I'm replacing you with this low-paid embryo.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Teach him to do what you do.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: He's already doing it.

situation: The Boss tells Wally that technology favors the young, then announces he is replacing Wally with a cheap embryo he holds in a jar. He orders Wally to train the embryo to do his job. Wally replies that the embryo is already doing it.
punchline: Wally's job requires so little effort or activity that an inert embryo in a jar is already performing it, implying Wally does essentially nothing.
summary: A boss tries to swap an aging employee for a jarred embryo, only to be told the embryo is already matching the employee's output.

title: Hacker Leaked Strategy, Please Share

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: A hacker broke into our system and found out our corporate strategy.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Did he post it on the Internet? I'd like to read it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm also curious about my objectives for this year. Do you have the guy's e-mail address?

situation: At a meeting, the Boss announces that a hacker broke into the company system and learned the corporate strategy. Alice hopes the hacker posted it online so she can read it, and Dilbert asks for the hacker's e-mail address so he can find out what his own objectives are for the year.
punchline: Employees are so poorly informed about their company's strategy and their own objectives that they would rather get the information from a hacker than from management.
summary: Staff react to a security breach by wishing the intruder would share the strategy that management never bothered to tell them.

title: Boss Uses Alice as Ventriloquist Dummy

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, I need you to attend a meeting with me to handle the technical questions.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If they ask me a question, I'll move my lips while you do ventriloquism.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: ... And that's why I suggest putting your I.P. router in a suppository configuration.

setting: Office cubicle area, then a conference room
situation: The Boss asks Alice to accompany him to a meeting to answer technical questions. He proposes that he simply move his lips while she throws her voice like a ventriloquist. In the meeting, Alice, reading from a folder, delivers an absurd and insulting technical recommendation through the Boss's mouth.
punchline: Alice, forced to be the Boss's voice, gets her revenge by having him 'say' something ridiculous and crude about the client's router, making the Boss look foolish.
summary: A clueless manager recruits his engineer to secretly speak for him in a client meeting, and she makes him sound ridiculous.

title: Dilbert Declines the Motivational Mug

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Every employee gets a lovely mug with our new motto, "I made a difference."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Question: May I have the cash equivalent of the mug instead?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: May I have a mug that says, "I didn't make a difference"?

setting: Conference room during a staff meeting
situation: The Boss announces that every employee will receive a mug bearing the company's new motto, "I made a difference." Dilbert, seated at the meeting table with coworkers, asks whether he can take the cash value of the mug instead, and the Boss refuses. Dilbert then asks for a mug with the opposite slogan.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically implies that the motto is hollow and that his work has made no real difference, so he would rather have the money or a mug with the honest message.
summary: When management hands out slogan mugs as a reward, one employee cheekily asks for money or a mug admitting his efforts changed nothing.

file: 1999/1999-12-09_website_various sponcers_pay for eyeballs_link to us_owe ourselves_billion dollars_technology.gif
title: Circular Links Worth a Billion

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I linked our web site to various sponsors who pay us for eyeballs.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Those sponsors link to other web sites who link to us.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: The net-net at the end of the day is we owe ourselves a billion dollars.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Eyeballs?

situation: Alice presents her plan to a meeting with Dilbert and the Boss, explaining that she linked the company web site to sponsors who pay for eyeballs. She reveals that those sponsors link to other sites that link back to the company, forming a loop. She concludes that the company is owed a billion dollars, while the Boss can only think about the word 'eyeballs'.
punchline: Alice's circular linking scheme means the company is essentially paying itself, a satirical take on dot-com-era business models that invented value out of nothing, while the Boss is fixated on the buzzword 'eyeballs'.
summary: A tech-savvy employee explains a loop of paid web links that supposedly generates a fortune, leaving her baffled boss stuck on one piece of jargon.

title: Security Guard Tricked Into Signing

transcript.speaker: Security Guard
transcript.text: Stop.

transcript.speaker: Security Guard
transcript.text: Show me your "Equipment Removal Authorization Form."

transcript.speaker: Security Guard
transcript.text: This requires the signature of TWO employees.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Good catch. You'd better sign it so it's legal.

transcript.speaker: Security Guard
transcript.text: This seems wrong... but I don't know why.

transcript.speaker: Security Guard
transcript.text: And I'll need to see your birth certificate.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't have one.

transcript.speaker: Security Guard
transcript.text: Then how do you know you were born?

transcript.speaker: Security Guard
transcript.text: I have baby pictures, but they could have been doctored by my alleged mom.

setting: Security desk in a office building lobby
situation: A security guard stops Dilbert, who is carrying a piece of equipment out of the building, and demands an equipment removal authorization form. When told it needs two signatures, Dilbert hands the guard his pen and has him sign it himself. The guard senses something is off, then turns to demanding a birth certificate and spirals into paranoia about his own origins.
punchline: Dilbert gets the guard to authorize the removal himself by flattering his diligence, leaving the confused guard so rattled that he doubts his own existence and even his mother.
summary: A bureaucratic guard ends up signing off on the very theft he was meant to prevent, then falls into absurd doubt about whether he was ever born.

title: One-Hour Executive MBA Degree

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I signed up for an executive MBA program.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's one-hour long and I get a degree from a prestigious university.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'd better run. I'm already a half-hour late.

situation: The Boss announces to his colleagues at a meeting table that he has enrolled in an executive MBA program. He explains that it lasts only one hour and awards a degree from a prestigious university. He then rushes off, noting he is already half an hour late for it.
punchline: The Boss proudly touts a degree that takes just one hour, a laughably shallow credential, and he is already late for it, underscoring his incompetence and love of shortcuts.
summary: A clueless manager brags about a lightning-fast MBA he can earn in a single lunch-length session, then dashes off because he is already behind.

file: 1999/1999-10-08_leader_listen to customers_hearing from customers_customers are defective.gif
title: Customers Are Defective, Not Silent

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: As a leader, I must listen to my customers.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What are you hearing from our customers?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Not a peep.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our customers are defective.

situation: The Boss thinks to himself that a good leader must listen to customers, then asks Dilbert what customers are saying. Dilbert replies that he hears nothing from them. Instead of questioning the company's own failings, the Boss concludes in his thoughts that the customers themselves are at fault.
punchline: When customers say nothing, the Boss blames the customers for being defective rather than considering that he or the company might be failing to engage them.
summary: A manager who prides himself on listening to customers hears only silence and decides the fault must lie with the customers.

file: 1999/1999-10-24_dogberts ad agency_research_don't use prodcut_outdoors_indoors_intensive ad campaign_outdoors for losers_humming birds_man in garden_happiness of gullible people_science.gif
title: Ad Campaign Keeps People Indoors

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert's Ad Agency

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: According to my research...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: ...people don't use your products when they are outdoors.

transcript.speaker: Client
transcript.text: Somehow we must keep people indoors.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I recommend an intensive ad campaign...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Featuring this slogan... 'Outdoors is for losers'

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The TV spot will show hummingbirds attacking a man in his garden.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Question: Wouldn't that destroy the happiness of gullible people?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: We'll tell them it doesn't.

setting: Conference room at Dogbert's Ad Agency
situation: Dogbert pitches an ad campaign to a client, explaining that people don't use the client's products outdoors, so the solution is to keep people indoors. He proposes a slogan calling the outdoors for losers and a TV spot of hummingbirds attacking a gardener. Dilbert asks whether this would ruin the happiness of gullible people.
punchline: Dogbert's answer to the ethical concern is that the agency will simply lie and tell the gullible people the campaign doesn't harm them, showing advertising as cynical manipulation.
summary: A canine ad executive proposes scaring consumers into staying inside with fearmongering commercials, then brushes off an ethical objection with a promise to simply deceive people further.

file: 1999/1999-07-31_good product design_gave three_leadership_product is bad_stock willplunge_totally meaningless_signed card_happy birthday.gif
title: Bleak Birthday Card From Engineers

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We need six weeks to make a good product design.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You gave us three.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Thanks to your leadership, the product is bad, our stock will plunge, and our lives are totally meaningless.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Oh, and happy birthday.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We all signed a card.

situation: Dilbert tells the boss his team needs six weeks for a good product design, but the boss reminds him that only three were allotted. Dilbert then bluntly lists the consequences of the boss's leadership: a bad product, a plunging stock price and meaningless lives. He finishes by wishing the boss a happy birthday, and the team hands over a signed card.
punchline: The team delivers a scathing condemnation of the boss's leadership and then politely follows it with a birthday card, showing the cold courtesy of employees who have given up.
summary: After bitterly blaming their manager for an inevitable product failure, an employee cheerfully adds birthday wishes and a group card.

file: 1999/1999-06-01_assertive men_woman_b word_boxer_bitch_fist of death_fist in face.gif
title: The B Word Misunderstood

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, it's okay for men to be assertive, but when a woman acts that way...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Well, it's the "B" word.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Boxer?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: O-o-okay.

situation: The Boss lectures Alice about how assertive behavior is acceptable in men but gets a woman labeled with a certain 'B' word. Alice has already knocked out a male coworker, whose limp body is slumped at her feet. When the Boss hesitates to say the word, Alice deliberately guesses 'Boxer?' while brandishing her fist, intimidating him into backing down.
punchline: Alice pretends the 'B' word could be innocuous, using her fist and a knocked-out coworker as a threat, so the Boss nervously agrees and abandons his sexist criticism.
summary: Faced with a sexist lecture about assertive women, Alice answers with a menacing fist and a pointed guess that makes her boss retreat.

file: 1999/1999-10-06_new guy doing_embryo in jar_got fertiziled_cute one.gif
title: Embryo In A Jar Outperforms Wally

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How's the new guy doing?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Not bad for an embryo in a jar.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I hate the fact that he only got fertilized a week ago and he gets paid more than I do.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: In all fairness, he does obstruct progress less than you do.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Everyone sides with the cute one.

situation: Dilbert asks Wally, who is sitting at his desk with a coffee mug, how the new hire is doing. Wally says the new guy is an embryo in a jar sitting on his desk, and he resents that the week-old embryo earns more than he does. Dilbert points out the embryo gets in the way of progress less than Wally does.
punchline: Wally, famous for doing as little as possible, is outperformed and outpaid by a literal embryo in a jar, and he complains that favoritism for the cute one is the only reason.
summary: A lazy employee grumbles that a week-old embryo in a jar has been hired at a higher salary than his own, and a coworker notes the embryo is less of a roadblock.

file: 1999/1999-09-04_catbert_evil director_reduce airline  expense_weed out dumb ones_sprint across runway_cling to plane_takeoff.gif
title: Catbert's Deadly Travel Savings Plan

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: "To reduce airline travel expenses..."

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: "Sprint across the runway and cling to the plane during takeoff."

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: That'll weed out the dumb ones.

setting: Office, at computer desks (an email from H.R. is read on screen)
situation: Catbert, the evil H.R. director, types out a company-wide message with a new policy for cutting airline travel costs. Dilbert reads the email on his computer and sees that employees are instructed to run onto the runway and cling to the plane as it takes off. Catbert privately gloats that the policy will eliminate the foolish employees who obey it.
punchline: Catbert's absurd and lethal cost-cutting travel policy is really a scheme to get rid of employees dumb enough to follow it.
summary: A malicious H.R. cat disguises a deadly stunt as a money-saving travel tip, calculating that only the gullible will try it.

title: Synergistic Realignment Triggers Conference Room Wave

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Reorganizing didn't work. We're going to try something new.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Synergistic realignment!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: What did I tell you about doing "the wave"?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I got swept up in the emotion.

situation: The Boss announces that the last reorganization failed and that the company will try something new, which he then names with a buzzword. A cheerful employee, Asok, throws his arms up in the air as if at a sporting event. Wally scolds him for doing "the wave" again, and Asok explains he was caught up in the emotion.
punchline: The boss's meaningless buzzword is treated like a rousing rallying cry, so the earnest young employee cheers as if it were a sports event, mocking how empty corporate jargon is greeted with forced enthusiasm.
summary: After announcing yet another vague management initiative, the boss gets an overenthusiastic cheer from a young employee who treats the meeting like a stadium.

file: 1999/1999-09-11_words have squiggles_bad grammar_every sentence_third grade_enrollment form.gif
title: Boss's Third Grade Grammar Squiggles

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carol, come here! All of my words have squiggles under them!

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: The software is telling you that every sentence you wrote has bad grammar.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Press F1 for help and ... it's a third grade enrollment form.

setting: Boss's office, at his desk with a computer
situation: The Boss summons his assistant Carol because his word processor has put squiggly lines under all his words. Carol explains the software is flagging every sentence for bad grammar. When she presses F1 for help, the document turns out to be a third grade enrollment form.
punchline: The Boss's writing is so poor that his grammar-checked document is actually a form to enroll him in third grade, implying his skills are at an elementary school level.
summary: A baffled manager asks his assistant why his computer is marking up his writing, and the answer is a gentle insult about his literacy.

title: Bathrobe Mistaken for Market Power

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: A bathrobe! This can only mean he found out how much market power an engineer has.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll give you a 30% raise if you don't quit!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Um... okay.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Take me, you terry-cloth rebel.

situation: Dilbert arrives at work wearing a bathrobe, and the Boss assumes it is a protest signalling that Dilbert knows how valuable engineers are in the job market. In a panic he offers Dilbert a 30% raise not to quit. Dilbert accepts, bewildered, while Alice, seeing the payoff, eagerly asks to be 'taken' as well.
punchline: The Boss misreads a bathrobe as a bold negotiating tactic and rewards it with a big raise, prompting Alice to seize the same opportunity.
summary: A manager misinterprets an employee's casual robe as a bargaining ploy and hastily buys his loyalty with extra pay.

file: 1999/1999-02-04_immense ego_seems normal_decided_doctor_determine lives_dies_die from ulcer_enjoy challenge_medical.gif
title: Dogbert's Ego Leads Him to Medicine

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I need a job where my immense ego seems normal.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I've decided to be a doctor. I will determine who lives and who dies!

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: What? I can't die from an ulcer!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Maybe not, but I enjoy the challenge.

setting: Dilbert's cubicle, then a doctor's examination room
situation: Dogbert, wearing a crown and holding a scepter, tells Dilbert he wants a career where his huge ego looks normal. He settles on being a doctor who decides who lives and dies. In the exam room, a shirtless patient with stomach pain is told by Dogbert, who is holding a stethoscope, that he enjoys the challenge of trying to kill him.
punchline: Dogbert regards medicine as a chance to indulge his god complex, so he cheerfully treats a harmless ulcer as an opportunity to make the patient die.
summary: A self-important Dogbert picks medicine as the profession that best suits his god complex, then threatens a patient with a minor ailment.

title: Hostile Takeover of Dilbert's Presentation

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then if you...

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: ...analyze the data...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's a hostile takeover of my presentation!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: ...you'll see a pattern...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And you let him do it?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He had a laser pointer the size of your head.

setting: A conference room during a presentation, then Dilbert's living room at home
situation: Dilbert is giving a presentation on a flowchart when a coworker steps in, finishes his sentences, and takes over with his own laser pointer. Dilbert fumes silently in a thought bubble. At home, in his robe on the couch, he tells Dogbert what happened and Dogbert asks why he let it happen.
punchline: Dilbert excuses his passivity by claiming the coworker's laser pointer was absurdly huge, treating a harmless presentation tool as an intimidating weapon.
summary: A pushy colleague hijacks Dilbert's talk, and Dilbert later justifies his meekness with an exaggerated claim about the intruder's oversized pointer.

title: Sick Telecommuter Shows Up in Pajamas

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I thought you were telecommuting today.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm sick.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: So I came into the office to get some rest and be pampered.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Fortunately, my pajamas look exactly like work clothes.

situation: Dilbert, holding a coffee mug, notices Wally sitting at his desk even though he was supposed to be telecommuting. Wally explains he is sick and has come into the office to rest and be pampered, then remarks that his pajamas conveniently resemble ordinary work clothes.
punchline: Wally's reasoning is absurd: being sick, he comes to the office to be taken care of, and he's dressed in pajamas that nobody can tell from work attire, which pokes fun at how little effort his normal workwear shows.
summary: A employee who should be working from home shows up at the office to be looked after while ill, secretly wearing his sleepwear.

title: Salesman Tricked By Own Tactics

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: You're a tough negotiator, but I think we have a deal.

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: Just sign the contract and we'll deliver the equipment.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This contract is totally different from what we agreed.

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: Must act surprised.

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: Really?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why are you springing all these conditions on me at the last minute?

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: No one has ever complained before.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: May I borrow your briefcase for a minute?

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: Um... okay.

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: That wasn't nice.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No one has complained before.

setting: Office meeting table, then a high rooftop ledge
situation: A salesman claims a deal is done and slides over a contract that differs from what was agreed. Dilbert calls him out, and the salesman brushes it off by saying no one has ever complained. Dilbert borrows the salesman's briefcase, and in the last panel the salesman is shown plummeting past a ledge, having been pushed off by Dilbert.
punchline: Dilbert turns the salesman's own excuse, that no one has ever complained, against him by using it to justify pushing him off a building.
summary: A buyer answers a vendor's sneaky last-minute contract changes with a taste of his own dismissive logic, delivered with fatal consequences.

file: 1999/1999-04-21_dogbert consults_eliminate phone support_via internet_discourage people_ominous list_personal questions.gif
title: Discouraging Support Requests With Creepy Questions

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert consults

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Eliminate phone support for your product. Provide help only via the Internet.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Then discourage people by making them answer an ominous list of personal questions.

transcript.speaker: Computer screen
transcript.text: 1. What is your home address? 2. When do you shower?

setting: The Boss's office, then a customer's computer desk
situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, advises the Boss to cut phone support and offer help only online. He then suggests deterring users by forcing them to answer an ominous list of personal questions first. A customer is shown staring nervously at his computer, which asks for his home address and when he showers.
punchline: The online support form is deliberately creepy and invasive so that customers give up and stop asking for help, cutting support costs.
summary: A canine consultant shows how to shrink support costs by scaring customers off with intrusive personal questions before they can get help.

file: 1999/1999-09-25_evil director_catbert_sick days_unusual reasons_imagined to be fly_hair_crazy reasons_made up reason_fake excuses.gif
title: Wally's Absurd Sick Day Excuses

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Wally, you've taken sick days for unusual reasons.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: For example, one day you got sick because you "...accidentally imagined what it would be like if you were a fly."

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: And today it's your hair?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I lathered and rinsed but I don't remember repeating.

situation: Catbert, the evil H.R. director, confronts Wally about his record of taking sick days for strange reasons. He reads out an earlier excuse about imagining being a fly, then asks about today's excuse involving his hair. Wally answers with a deadpan explanation about the shampoo instructions.
punchline: Wally's sick-day excuse is that he followed the shampoo instructions (lather, rinse, repeat) but cannot remember repeating, treating a trivial lapse as a legitimate reason to miss work.
summary: A scheming personnel chief grills a lazy engineer over his ridiculous absence excuses, and the engineer's latest one is just as silly as the last.

file: 1999/1999-12-05_carol got mba_hard wirk_rewarded_pompous baboon_sensitive way_secretarial stigma_wet caroets_coffee_fetch me one.gif
title: Carol's MBA Earns Her Coffee Duty

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Congratulations to my secretary Carol for getting her MBA.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: At this company we believe hard work should be rewarded.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The next time you fetch my coffee, get some coffee for yourself too!

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: You should be promoting me, you pompous baboon!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How can I explain this in the most sensitive way?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The secretarial stigma will cover you like a mountain of wet carpets until the day you die.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm glad we had this talk. I think it helped.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: The next time you ask for coffee, we'd like to watch.

setting: Office, during a staff gathering and a private talk
situation: The Boss publicly congratulates his secretary Carol for earning her MBA and claims the company rewards hard work, but his only reward is letting her fetch herself a coffee. When Carol demands a promotion, he cheerfully tells her she'll be stuck with the secretarial stigma forever. Coworkers then say they'd like to watch the next time she asks him for coffee.
punchline: The Boss's idea of rewarding a newly minted MBA is a free coffee, and he brushes off her promotion request by insisting she will always be seen as just a secretary.
summary: A manager praises his secretary's new degree, then shuts down her bid for advancement with an insultingly cheerful explanation that her job label will never change.

title: The Anti-Crust Manager

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Before I eat a sandwich, I always remove the useless edges of the bread.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That tells you what kind of manager I am.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: You're the anti-crust?

situation: The Boss sits at a conference table and announces to his team that he always cuts the crusts off his sandwiches. He insists this reveals something profound about his management style. A young employee deadpans back by calling him the anti-crust.
punchline: The Boss presents a trivial lunch habit as deep evidence of his leadership philosophy, and the employee's 'anti-crust' label mocks the idea that this means anything at all.
summary: A boss tries to turn his habit of trimming sandwich bread into a statement about his management approach, only to be met with a bemused one-liner.

title: Punished By Watching Boss Eat

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, your performance is slipping again.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This calls for my most severe disciplinary action.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: He made you watch him eat?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Monster!

setting: The Boss's office, then a hallway or cubicle area
situation: The Boss tells Wally his performance is slipping and announces his most severe disciplinary action. In the final panel Wally, shaken and trembling, is questioned by Asok and Dilbert, who are horrified that the punishment was being forced to watch the Boss eat.
punchline: The Boss's ultimate punishment is not firing or demotion but making an employee watch him eat, which his coworkers treat as an act of monstrous cruelty.
summary: A manager's dreaded punishment for a slacking employee turns out to be the revolting ordeal of sitting through his meal.

file: 1999/1999-03-27_use art_find self_over there_ratbert_bad painting_without using art_bob_dinosaur.gif
title: Finding Yourself Without Art

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I use art as a way of finding myself.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: You're over there, Ratbert, in front of a bad painting!

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: And I did it without using any art.

setting: A living room or home studio with an easel and a couch
situation: Ratbert, wearing a beret and holding a paint palette, says he paints in order to find himself. Bob the dinosaur literally points out where Ratbert is, standing in front of a bad painting. Bob then walks off thinking he found himself without any art.
punchline: Bob takes 'finding yourself' literally and shows that self-discovery is trivially easy, undercutting Ratbert's pretentious claim about art.
summary: A pretentious little rat artist claims painting helps him find himself, and his dinosaur friend deflates him by literally locating him.

file: 1999/1999-08-29_last bullet point_bullet point_admit wrong_alice heard wrong_boss has to admit wrong.gif
title: Boss Admits Alice Was Wrong

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Remove that last bullet point. It's stupid.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Gasp.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Yesterday you told me to add that bullet point.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: So either you were wrong today or you were wrong yesterday.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Everyone come quickly! He has to admit he's wrong!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Say it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice heard me wrong yesterday.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It takes a big man to admit Alice is wrong.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Can you hear us, Alice?

situation: The Boss orders Alice to delete a bullet point from her document, calling it stupid, even though he told her to add it the day before. Alice triumphantly gathers her coworkers to witness him admit he was wrong. Instead, the Boss claims Alice misheard him, and the coworkers praise his bigness for admitting Alice's error while she fumes.
punchline: The Boss dodges accountability by twisting an admission of his own mistake into blaming Alice, and the sycophantic coworkers praise him for it.
summary: Alice catches her boss contradicting himself and rounds up an audience for his confession, but he pins the blame on her instead.

file: 1999/1999-04-10_ease of use_lab_budget for staff_two sided_photocopies_live by sword_die by sword.gif
title: Budget Hidden on Photocopy Backs

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I downsized the "Ease of Use" lab because there's no budget for a staff.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: They HAVE a budget. I put it on the back of these two-sided photocopies!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Well, they lived by the sword, and they died by the sword.

situation: At a meeting, the Boss announces he downsized the Ease of Use lab because there was supposedly no budget for staff. A coworker holds up a sheet and points out the lab did have a budget, printed on the back of the photocopies. The Boss, reading the page, shrugs it off with a cliché about living and dying by the sword.
punchline: The Boss brushes aside evidence that his justification was false by misapplying a cliché, showing he never intended to let facts change a decision already made.
summary: A manager's excuse for cutting a team collapses when a colleague shows the funding existed all along, yet the manager just shrugs with a tired proverb.

title: Dot-Com Tuna Sandwich Startup

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How's your Internet start-up company coming?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Good.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: My plan is to be the dominant Internet source for tuna sandwiches.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So, if I buy one, you ship it overnight?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: No, you have to come pick it up.

situation: Dilbert asks Wally, who is sitting at his computer, how his Internet start-up is going. Wally says he plans to be the dominant online source for tuna sandwiches. When Dilbert asks if he ships overnight, Wally admits customers must pick up their sandwiches in person.
punchline: Wally's supposedly internet-based business has no actual online delivery, mocking dot-com startups that slapped 'internet' onto ordinary, unscalable businesses.
summary: A coworker's grand web venture turns out to be a sandwich shop where customers must collect their own orders.

file: 1999/1999-05-17_alpha numeric pager_clips to ear_belt_going to hell.gif
title: Pager Clips to Ear, Not Belt

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Look at this great alpha-numeric pager I bought.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wow! It's the kind that clips to your ear instead of your belt.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Is it?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're going to hell.

transcript.speaker: Off-panel voice
transcript.text: Ow! Ow!

setting: Office break area where coworkers hold coffee mugs
situation: The Boss proudly shows off a new alpha-numeric pager he bought. Dilbert sarcastically praises it as the kind that clips to your ear instead of your belt, and the Boss, unaware, asks if it is. In the last panel Dilbert tells him he's going to hell while a voice cries out in pain off-panel.
punchline: Dilbert tricks the clueless Boss into believing the pager clips to the ear, so the Boss pins it painfully to his own ear, which Dilbert deems worthy of damnation for his cruel prank.
summary: A gullible manager is fooled by a sarcastic remark about his gadget and ends up hurting himself while the instigator admits his own wickedness.

title: Farmer Culls Cubicle Worker

transcript.speaker: Farmer
transcript.text: My cube farm has an excellent yield this year.

transcript.speaker: Farmer
transcript.text: I reckon I'll have to put this one down so he won't reproduce.

transcript.speaker: Farmer
transcript.text: Sorry.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: No problem; I hear that a lot.

situation: A farmer in green overalls carries a pitchfork through an office of cubicles, treating it like a crop field and thinking about his harvest. He stands over a bald, bespectacled office worker at his computer and says he must put him down so he won't reproduce. The worker, unfazed, replies that he hears an apology like that a lot.
punchline: The employee is so socially awkward and unappealing that being told he's unfit to reproduce is nothing new to him, so he calmly accepts the farmer's apology.
summary: A pitchfork-wielding farmer tends a field of cubicles and decides to cull one lonely worker, who responds with weary resignation about his dating life.

title: Catbert Praises Sadistic Employee, Invites Him

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Your co-workers say you're a sadistic nut.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Gimme five, you big nut! And keep up the good work!

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Hey, I'm having a party on Saturday. Can you make it?

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Sure! I'll bring my spinach dip.

situation: Catbert, the H.R. director, tells an employee that his co-workers consider him a sadistic nut. Instead of reprimanding him, Catbert congratulates him with a high five and tells him to keep it up. Catbert then invites the employee to his Saturday party, and the employee agrees to bring spinach dip.
punchline: The H.R. director, whose job is to discipline employees, treats sadism as a virtue and befriends the cruel employee, since Catbert is himself sadistic.
summary: A cruel employee expects discipline from the evil H.R. director but instead gets applause and a party invitation.

file: 1999/1999-09-05_few changes_vinery idea_unimaginative retread_idea_discredited_energizing force_chat_manage someone else.gif
title: Boss Ruins Dilbert's Visionary Idea

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Good idea, Dilbert. I made a few changes and sent it out.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Gaaa!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You removed the parts that made it a visionary idea!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now it's just an unimaginative retread of an idea that has been widely discredited.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Gaaa! And it has my name on it!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That idea was the energizing force that gave me strength to work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now it's dead! You killed it!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'd love to chat but I have to manage someone else now.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Gurgle

situation: The Boss praises Dilbert's idea but reveals he edited it before sending it out. Dilbert reads the altered version, realizes the visionary elements were removed and his name is still attached, and collapses in despair. The Boss cheerfully leaves to go manage someone else while Dilbert lies limp on his desk.
punchline: The Boss ruins an employee's best idea through careless edits, leaves the employee's name on the botched result, and shows no concern for the emotional damage he caused.
summary: A manager mangles an employee's brilliant proposal, then brushes off the resulting breakdown to go bother someone else.

file: 1999/1999-05-04_quick call_continue_presentation_ignore_vice presidentail_pile of money_capital spending_small phone.gif
title: Vice President's Rude Phone Call

transcript.speaker: Vice President
transcript.text: Continue with your presentation while I take this quick call.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Ring ring

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Go ahead and ignore me, you vice presidential pile of stinkin' monkey...

transcript.speaker: Vice President
transcript.text: Okay, bye.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Crapital spending.

transcript.speaker: Vice President
transcript.text: Look how small my phone is.

situation: A vice president tells Dilbert to carry on with his presentation while he takes a phone call. Dilbert sarcastically insults him under his breath, assuming he is being ignored. The call ends, and the vice president has heard nothing, but instead shows off his tiny new phone.
punchline: Dilbert's insult is lost on the vice president, who is too preoccupied with showing off his expensive, tiny phone to notice, which exposes the pointless gadget spending ('crapital spending') that executives indulge in.
summary: A boss who ignores a presenter for a phone call is insulted to no effect, then proudly displays his miniature gadget.

title: Critical Paper Returned To Pile

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This one has been on my desk for a month. It's critical.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll stick it back in the pile and see if that helps.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Yes, I feel better already.

setting: The Boss's office, at his desk
situation: The Boss sits at his desk beside a tall stack of papers, thinking about a document that has sat there for a month and is critical. Instead of acting on it, he puts it back on the pile. He then feels satisfied, as if that solved the problem.
punchline: The Boss treats moving an urgent document back into the pile as a solution, feeling relief without doing any actual work.
summary: A manager responds to an overdue urgent document by burying it in his paper pile and congratulating himself.

file: 1999/1999-07-23_catbert_evil director_shooting credenza_tina was bad_card board_special hat_suspended_sentence.gif
title: Suspended Sentence Hat Punishment

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Tina, you are accused of shooting the CIO's credenza five times.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I'm writing "Tina was bad" on this cardboard. I order you to attach it to a special hat for two weeks.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
