transcript.text: How did it go?

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: I got a suspended sentence.

setting: Catbert's H.R. office and a hallway or cubicle area
situation: Catbert, as evil H.R. director, tells Tina she is accused of shooting the CIO's credenza five times. His punishment is to write "Tina was bad" on a piece of cardboard and make her attach it to a hat for two weeks. Afterward Dilbert asks how it went, and Tina is wearing the hat with the cardboard sign dangling from it.
punchline: The 'suspended sentence' is taken literally: the cardboard sign with her sentence is hanging (suspended) from her hat.
summary: After being disciplined by H.R. for gunning down an executive's furniture, a worker wears a dangling placard that turns a legal phrase into a visual pun.

title: Boss Discovers Internet, Wants Credit

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Webmistress Ming

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ming, I think the Internet might catch on.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I rushed over here so I could be the first to say it's a new paradigm.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Did anyone beat me?

transcript.speaker: Ming
transcript.text: I wish someone would.

setting: Ming's office, at her computer desk
situation: The Boss walks up to Ming, the webmistress, and solemnly announces that the Internet might catch on. He explains he hurried over to be the first person to call it a new paradigm, then asks whether anyone beat him to it. Ming, seated at her computer, deadpans that she wishes someone had.
punchline: The Boss is years behind on the Internet but still wants credit for being first, and Ming's wish that someone had beaten him is a dry jab at his cluelessness.
summary: Late to the web revolution, a manager rushes to claim the honor of announcing a paradigm shift, only to have his own web specialist wish he'd been upstaged.

file: 1999/1999-09-20_boss in office_thank me_all hard work_measure torso_knitting sweater.gif
title: Asok Expects Thanks, Gets Measured

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Asok, the Boss wants to see you in his office.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: He must want to thank me for all of my hard work. Am I right?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm supposed to measure your torso.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Is he knitting me a sweater?

situation: Alice tells Asok that the Boss wants to see him in his office. Asok cheerfully assumes he is about to be thanked for his hard work. Alice instead says she has to measure his torso, and Asok naively guesses the Boss is knitting him a sweater.
punchline: Asok's relentless optimism leads him to imagine a kindly gift, while the real reason for the torso measurement is clearly something far more sinister, which he fails to grasp.
summary: A cheerful young intern assumes a summons to the boss means praise, then misreads a tape measure as a gesture of warmth.

title: Dilbert Testifies: Jargon Is Perjury

transcript.speaker: Lawyer
transcript.text: Can you explain the meaning of this internal e-mail message?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It says we'll "use integration tools to leverage the utility of our enterprise-wide processes."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It appears to be something we call communication.

transcript.speaker: Lawyer
transcript.text: Perjury!

setting: A courtroom, with Dilbert on the witness stand
situation: Dilbert is a witness in court, and a lawyer asks him to explain an internal company e-mail. Dilbert reads out a passage full of corporate buzzwords and then says it is a form of communication. The lawyer immediately accuses him of perjury while a judge looks on.
punchline: Corporate jargon is so meaningless that calling it 'communication' is such an obvious lie that the lawyer treats it as perjury.
summary: A witness reads a buzzword-laden company e-mail aloud and claims it counts as communication, prompting an accusation of lying under oath.

title: Reorg Already Happened By Neglect

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carol, give everyone a copy of my reorg announcement.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: They're already organized this way because I never distributed your last reorg announcement.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let's see your "Employee of the Week" do that!

situation: The Boss hands Carol a paper showing a new org chart and asks her to distribute it to everyone. Carol calmly explains the staff is already organized that way, because she never handed out his previous reorg announcement. The Boss, impressed, boasts that the 'Employee of the Week' couldn't do that, apparently unaware her inaction is what made it work.
punchline: The Boss mistakes Carol's failure to follow his instructions for brilliant efficiency, and praises her by comparison to the officially recognized top employee.
summary: A secretary's neglected paperwork turns out to have anticipated her boss's latest restructuring, and he is thrilled by her unintended foresight.

file: 1999/1999-01-11_wally report_hair grow long_ponytail_artistic side_collect coffee mugs_meeting_business.gif
title: Wally's Artistic Side: Coffee Mugs

transcript.speaker: Wally

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Eventually, I'll put it in a ponytail to show I have an artistic side.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What's your artistic side?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I collect coffee mugs.

setting: Conference room during a team meeting
situation: At a meeting, Wally gives his weekly 'Wally Report' and announces he is growing his hair long in the back so he can wear a ponytail. He says this will show he has an artistic side. When the Boss asks what his artistic side actually is, Wally says he collects coffee mugs.
punchline: Wally's claim to artistic creativity amounts to collecting coffee mugs, which is neither art nor creative, exposing how thin his 'artistic side' really is.
summary: A coworker plans a ponytail to signal his creative nature, but his only artistic credential turns out to be a mug collection.

title: Meeting About Project Without Dilbert

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm off to a meeting about your project. Is there anything I should know?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes. You should know how dumb it is to have a meeting about my project without inviting me.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Every time I learn something it makes me unhappy.

situation: The Boss stops by Dilbert's desk on his way to a meeting about Dilbert's project and asks if there is anything he should know. Dilbert points out that it is foolish to hold a meeting about his project without inviting him. The Boss, in a thought bubble, complains that learning anything makes him unhappy.
punchline: The Boss prefers staying ignorant, since learning facts, even useful ones, only makes him unhappy.
summary: A manager heading to a discussion of an employee's work is told the discussion is pointless without that employee, and he privately resents being informed.

title: No Risk of Any Management

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: As requested, I did a "risk management" assessment.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I concluded that there was no risk of any management.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do you have anything to add?

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I'll get back to you.

situation: Carol presents a risk management assessment to the Boss, pointing at a flip chart showing a drawing of his head. She says she concluded there was no risk of any management, and when he asks if she has anything to add, she says she'll get back to him.
punchline: Carol turns the phrase 'risk management' into an insult, saying the company is at no risk of having any actual management, and the Boss is too oblivious to notice the dig.
summary: A subordinate uses a requested assessment to slyly announce that her manager's department is in no danger of being managed at all.

title: Dogbert's Infomercial Couch Potato Dilbert

transcript.speaker: TV
transcript.text: In tape one, I'll teach you how to conquer a small island for no money down.

transcript.speaker: TV
transcript.text: First, you must travel to the place you plan to conquer.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm designed for sitting. That's why my butt is covered with soft fur.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think that's happening to me too.

situation: Dogbert sits on a stool watching a get-rich-quick infomercial on TV about conquering a small island with no money down, holding the remote. The tape's first step is to travel to the island, which prompts Dogbert to explain that he is built for sitting. Dilbert, sitting on the couch eating a sandwich, remarks that he seems to be growing soft fur on his rear too.
punchline: Dilbert's remark implies that years of sitting around and watching TV are changing his body, and he is turning into a lazy, furry-bottomed couch potato like Dogbert.
summary: While a TV seminar promises easy world domination, a lazy dog and his owner admit they are better suited to lounging than to any real effort.

title: Hired Only to Placate Talented Spouse

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, come meet the two new employees.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This is Sophie, one of the best engineers in the business.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The other one is her incompetent husband.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We had to hire him so Sophie would agree to relocate.

transcript.speaker: Husband
transcript.text: Are you saying I didn't get hired for my talent?

transcript.speaker: Sophie
transcript.text: You don't have any talent, honey.

transcript.speaker: Husband
transcript.text: Oh, that's right.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, your job is to do his job in addition to your own.

transcript.speaker: Husband
transcript.text: Do you want to see my collection of squirrel heads?

situation: The Boss introduces Dilbert to two new hires: Sophie, a top engineer, and her husband, whom he openly calls incompetent and says was hired only to get Sophie to relocate. The husband is briefly offended but is reminded by his wife that he has no talent. The Boss then assigns Dilbert to do the husband's work on top of his own, and the husband cheerfully offers to show off his squirrel head collection.
punchline: Dilbert gets stuck doing double work for a useless hire, who obliviously offers a creepy hobby as his only contribution.
summary: A manager reveals he hired a gifted engineer's hopeless spouse as a relocation bribe, then dumps the spouse's workload on Dilbert while the spouse proudly mentions his odd taxidermy hobby.

situation: A presenter dressed in a blimp costume opens the annual employee meeting with a Hindenburg theme, showing he knows almost nothing about the disaster. He publicly credits Alice with choosing the theme and planning the event. During the film clip he panics in costume, and Alice, apparently holding a detonator, counts down to blow up his costume while Wally eggs her on.
punchline: Alice, who was blamed for the ill-conceived Hindenburg theme, takes revenge by re-enacting the disaster and blowing up the clueless presenter in his blimp costume.
summary: A hapless emcee in a zeppelin outfit pins the tasteless disaster-themed party on a coworker, who responds by preparing to blow him up.

title: Life Is Like This Dumpster

transcript.speaker: Devil Dogbert
transcript.text: Asok, life is like this dumpster.

transcript.speaker: Devil Dogbert
transcript.text: On one hand, it stinks...

transcript.speaker: Asok

transcript.text: And then you reincarnate.

Dogbert offers a philosophical comparison of life to the dumpster, and Asok literally tests the 'on one hand' idea by getting his hands dirty. Dogbert then adds that you reincarnate afterward.
punchline: Asok takes the 'on one hand' metaphor literally and ends up with two stinking hands, while Dogbert's grim reply implies that life's stench is followed only by being reborn into the same mess.
summary: A devilish Dogbert offers a bleak life lesson from inside a dumpster, and his young colleague's literal-minded reaction only leaves him smellier and doomed to repeat it all.

title: Spring-Loaded Butt Joins Conversations

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: My spring-loaded butt will help me join nearby conversations faster.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: So then I...

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Sproing

transcript.speaker: Man in cubicle
transcript.text: Did you know I'm an authority on whatever you're discussing?

situation: A man in a cubicle imagines that a spring attached to his rear end will launch him into nearby conversations. Two coworkers chat over coffee when he springs over the cubicle wall and lands upside down. He then announces that he is an authority on whatever they are discussing.
punchline: Someone desperate to insert himself into every conversation will literally throw himself into the discussion and claim expertise on a topic he knows nothing about.
summary: An eager coworker rigs himself with a spring so he can bounce into other people's chats and pose as an expert.

title: Alice Lost in Org-Limbo

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, your name was accidentally omitted from the reorganization paperwork.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're in a place known only as Org-Limbo.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Stop making it sound scary!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Where did Alice go?

situation: The Boss reads from a sheet of paper and tells Alice that her name was left off the reorganization paperwork, which he dramatically calls Org-Limbo. Alice, sitting right in front of him, angrily tells him to stop making it sound scary. The Boss then wonders where Alice went, as if she no longer exists.
punchline: Because Alice has been left off the reorg paperwork, the Boss behaves as though she has literally vanished from the organization, even though she is standing right in front of him.
summary: A clerical omission leaves an employee officially nonexistent, and her boss can no longer even perceive her.

title: Alice's Disguise Exposed by Catbert

transcript.speaker: Interviewer
transcript.text: I'm prepared to offer you $120,000 per year plus a parking space for your gigantic hat.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Ha ha! It is I, Alice! I accept your offer for a higher-paying job!

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Ha ha! It is I, Catbert! I'm not authorized to hire anyone!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: #!*@ing cat!

situation: A horned interviewer offers a candidate wearing a gigantic pink hat a $120,000 salary and a parking space for the hat. The candidate throws off the hat and reveals herself as Alice, accepting the offer for a higher-paying job. The interviewer turns out to be Catbert in disguise, who gleefully says he has no authority to hire anyone.
punchline: Alice's elaborate disguise to land a better job is a waste, because the interviewer is Catbert, who tricked her and can't actually hire anyone.
summary: A disguised job seeker springs her identity on an interviewer, only to find that he too is a prankster in disguise with no power to hire.

title: Secretary's Assistant Yells At Kids

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Asok! Did you escape your job at quality assurance?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Yes. I had to take a job as a secretary's assistant. I'll work my way back up to intern.

transcript.speaker: Secretary
transcript.text: It's four o'clock. Call my kids and yell at them.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Cursing or no cursing?

situation: Dilbert asks Asok whether he got out of his quality assurance job. Asok explains he is now a secretary's assistant and hopes to work his way back up to intern. The secretary then orders him to phone her kids and yell at them, and Asok asks whether she wants cursing included.
punchline: Asok's new job is so degrading that he has to scold his boss's children by phone on command, and he treats it as a routine task with options, which shows how low his career has sunk.
summary: An escapee from quality assurance reveals his demotion to personal assistant duties, including shouting at his superior's children on schedule.

title: Pierced Bellybutton Causes Dilbert's Dry Heaves

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: Would you like to see my pierced bellybutton?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Um...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Aaah! Aaah! Ow! Ow! Ow!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I still have a chance of a kiss if I keep this to dry heaves.

setting: Outdoor path on a grassy hillside during a walk
situation: Dilbert is out walking with a blonde woman on a date when she offers to show him her pierced bellybutton. He reacts with squeamish pain and flinching, then privately resolves to keep his reaction down to dry heaves so he can still get a kiss.
punchline: Dilbert is so squeamish that the mere mention of a body piercing makes him retch, but he is so desperate for a kiss that he tries to contain the damage to dry heaves.
summary: A date's offer to reveal her body piercing leaves a queasy Dilbert gagging while he tries to salvage his romantic prospects.

file: 1999/1999-05-10_volume tcalls_tech support calls_on hold music_ballon rub_driving getaway car.gif
title: Balloon Squeak Hold Music Reduces Calls

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We've reduced the volume of technical support calls...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: By replacing our "on hold" music with the sound that balloons make when you rub them.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Do you ever feel like we're driving the getaway car?

setting: Conference room during a management presentation
situation: The Boss proudly announces to the team that technical support call volume has dropped. He reveals the cause: he replaced the on-hold music with the irritating squeak of rubbed balloons, so customers hang up. Wally, seated next to Dilbert and Alice, remarks that they feel like they are driving the getaway car.
punchline: The Boss's 'success' comes from driving customers away with an unbearable sound rather than helping them, making the employees feel like accomplices to a crime.
summary: A manager takes credit for fewer support calls after making customers flee with an awful hold sound, and a coworker likens the staff to getaway drivers.

title: Guessing Requirements From Document Weight

transcript.speaker: Man with glasses
transcript.text: Your requirements document is the biggest I've ever seen.

transcript.speaker: Man with glasses
transcript.text: It's too big to read, but I can guess from its weight what must be in there.

transcript.speaker: Man with glasses
transcript.text: You know it's a multi-user, global system, right?

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: No, I'm not getting that.

characters: Software developer (man with glasses and green tie)
situation: A man holding a huge purple requirements document tells the woman who wrote it that it is too big to read. He claims he can deduce its contents just by feeling its weight, then guesses it is a multi-user, global system. The woman, who authored it, says he is wrong.
punchline: The man's claim to infer the requirements from the weight of the document is absurd, and his guess is wrong, which highlights how nobody actually reads oversized requirements documents.
summary: A man who refuses to read a gigantic specification tries to divine its contents by hefting it, and gets it wrong.

file: 1999/1999-07-13_all the copies_bestseller_house as colleral_dump_pay back_dogbert gets loan.gif
title: Dogbert's Bestseller Loan Scheme

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert gets a loan

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I plan to buy all the copies of a book I authored, thus making it a bestseller.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And I'd like to use your house as collateral.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Unless it's a dump.

transcript.speaker: Loan Officer
transcript.text: How are you planning to pay us back?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Do you take books?

situation: Dogbert sits across the desk from a bank loan officer and applies for a loan. He explains that he will use the money to buy every copy of his own book to force it onto the bestseller list, and offers the loan officer's house as collateral. When asked how he will repay the loan, he asks if the bank accepts books.
punchline: Dogbert's scheme leaves him holding a pile of unsold books as his only asset, so his repayment plan is to hand the bank worthless copies of the very book he bought.
summary: A scheming dog asks a banker to fund a plan to inflate his own book sales, then proposes paying the bank back in the unsold books themselves.

file: 1999/1999-09-15_ceiling_hear strange sounds_leap out window_roof collapse_water damage.gif
title: Dilbert's Alarming Home Repair Advice

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I see some water damage on your ceiling, Mom.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's usually the first sign that the roof will collapse.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mom
transcript.text: What should I do?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well, if you hear any strange sounds, you might want to leap out a window.

situation: Dilbert visits his mother at home and notices water damage on her ceiling. He warns her that it is a sign the roof could collapse. When she asks what to do, he offers only the advice to jump out a window if she hears strange noises.
punchline: Dilbert's engineering-minded advice is no real solution at all: he just tells his worried mother to flee out a window when the collapse begins, rather than offering to fix anything.
summary: A son diagnoses a looming roof collapse at his mother's house and responds to her plea for help with a hopelessly useless escape plan.

title: Boss Zaps Computer Board With Static

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do you want to see a technical trick I taught myself?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If I shuffle my feet, I can make a tiny spark with my finger.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: She's right; this thing does make an excellent doorstop.

setting: Office or computer repair area with a workbench
situation: The Boss proudly offers to demonstrate a 'technical trick' to a woman holding a circuit board from a parts box. He shuffles his feet and zaps the board with a static spark, and a 'zzzt' sound appears. In the last panel the board lies ruined on the floor, propping open a door.
punchline: The Boss's static shock fried the circuit board, leaving it useful only as a doorstop, which proves his technical ignorance and carelessness.
summary: A clueless manager shows off a static spark trick and destroys an electronic component, which ends up wedging a door open.

title: Secret Strategic Plan, Glance Only

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Make your report consistent with our strategic plan.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What's our strategic plan?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's a secret.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you saying you don't trust me?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't think it's a coincidence that most employee sabotage is done by employees.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How can I do my report if I don't know the strategy?!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay, okay. I'll let you glance at it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Time's up! That's long enough!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's the warranty for your chair.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Really? I've been managing to this for years.

situation: The Boss orders Dilbert to make his report consistent with a strategic plan, but refuses to share it because he fears employee sabotage. He finally lets Dilbert glance at the document for a split second, then snatches it back. The document turns out to be just the warranty for his chair, which the Boss admits he has been using as his management strategy for years.
punchline: The supposedly secret strategic plan is nothing more than a chair warranty, revealing that the Boss has no real strategy and has been managing by it for years.
summary: A paranoid manager guards his top-secret company strategy so closely that it turns out to be a piece of furniture paperwork.

title: New Budget Code for Bald Engineers

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Wally, what's your project budget code?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm switching you to E947, effective immediately.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Why?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: That's my new code for bald engineers.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It will grow back!

situation: Alice asks Wally for his project budget code, then announces she is reassigning him to a different code effective immediately. When Wally asks why, she explains the new code is for bald engineers, and Wally indignantly protests that his baldness is temporary.
punchline: Wally's budget code is being changed simply because he is bald, and his absurd reaction is to insist his hair will grow back, as if that were the only thing wrong with the arbitrary categorization.
summary: Alice casually reclassifies Wally under an accounting code created purely to lump together hairless engineers, and he defensively insists his baldness is only temporary.

file: 1999/1999-11-05_call center_hire you_challenge_inhumane working conditions_without break_four hours.gif
title: Ratbert Thrives on Inhumane Conditions

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So, Mister Ratbert, why should I hire you to work in my call center?

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I thrive on the challenge of inhumane working conditions.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Watch me go without a restroom break for four hours!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're hired.

setting: The Boss's office, during a job interview
situation: The Boss interviews Ratbert for a job in his call center and asks why he should be hired. Ratbert answers that he thrives on inhumane working conditions and offers to demonstrate by going four hours without a restroom break, squirming as he does so. The Boss hires him on the spot.
punchline: The Boss treats a candidate's willingness to endure abusive conditions, like being denied restroom breaks, as the ideal qualification for a call center job.
summary: A job candidate impresses a call center manager by boasting he can endure miserable treatment and bodily discomfort.

file: 1999/1999-10-12_after 5 club_select group_employees_creative ideas_club for people_during business hours_business.gif
title: Creative Thinking Only After Hours

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, you're invited to my new "After-5 Club."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: A select group of employees will meet after work to think of creative ideas.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Is there a club for people who know how to think during business hours?

situation: The Boss invites Wally to join his new "After-5 Club," a select group that meets after work to brainstorm creative ideas. Wally responds by asking whether there is a club for people who can think during regular business hours.
punchline: Wally sarcastically implies that the Boss expects creativity only on employees' unpaid personal time, and that thinking during the workday is apparently not valued or expected.
summary: A manager's exclusive evening brainstorming group draws a deadpan jab from an employee who wonders about daytime thinking.

title: Ignoring Employees To Avoid Paying

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Good morning!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I said, good morning.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If I convince them they don't exist, I won't have to pay them.

situation: Dilbert cheerfully greets The Boss as they pass in the hallway, and The Boss walks by without responding. Dilbert repeats the greeting and is ignored again. As The Boss opens a door, his thought bubble reveals he is deliberately ignoring Dilbert as a scheme to avoid paying employees.
punchline: The Boss isn't merely rude: he is ignoring employees on purpose, reasoning that if they don't exist to him, he won't owe them any salary.
summary: A manager snubs an employee's greeting twice, secretly hoping that pretending staff are invisible will get him out of paying them.

file: 1999/1999-02-05_doctor dogbert_herbal therapy_eat lawn_storm gutters_hair grow back_perscription.gif
title: Dogbert Prescribes Eating His Lawn

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Doctor Dogbert

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm putting you on an extreme herbal therapy.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Come to my house once a week and eat my lawn down to one inch.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: After six months, if your hair doesn't grow back, I have more herbs in my storm gutters.

situation: Dogbert, wearing a crown and playing doctor, examines a bald patient sitting shirtless on an exam table. He prescribes an 'extreme herbal therapy' that consists of the patient eating his lawn weekly. When the patient gets dressed, Dogbert hands over a note and adds that if the hair doesn't grow back in six months, he has more herbs in his storm gutters.
punchline: Dogbert's 'herbal therapy' is just making a gullible patient eat his grass and gutter weeds, exploiting him for free lawn care while offering a worthless cure for baldness.
summary: A fake doctor dog sends his balding patient to mow his yard with his mouth as a miracle hair-regrowth treatment.

title: Police Join Computer Manufacturer Vendetta

transcript.speaker: Police Officer
transcript.text: We have a report that you threatened to kill a computer manufacturer.

transcript.speaker: Old Woman
transcript.text: It freezes up five times a day. I have to unplug it to turn it off.

transcript.speaker: Police Officer
transcript.text: Okay, we're with you. When's it going down?

transcript.speaker: Old Woman
transcript.text: Is Tuesday good?

situation: Two armed police officers show up at an elderly woman's door after a report that she threatened to kill a computer manufacturer. She explains that her computer freezes five times a day and must be unplugged to turn off. The officers sympathize and ask when the hit is happening, and she cheerfully proposes Tuesday.
punchline: Anyone who has suffered through a constantly crashing computer is so sympathetic that even the police will cheerfully join a plot to kill the manufacturer.
summary: Cops responding to a murder threat against a computer company side with the frustrated customer once they hear how badly her machine crashes.

file: 1999/1999-02-14_catbert_director_ceiling collapsed_complained_steel beam_hit head_happen in home_losing consciousness_suicide note_doubting story_questioning reality.gif
title: Catbert Blames Injured Employee's Home

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: The ceiling in my work area collapsed.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: No one else has complained.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: A steel beam hit me in the head!

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: How can I be sure it didn't happen in your home?

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: There aren't any steel beams in my house!!

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Maybe you removed them with your head.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Uh-oh... losing consciousness.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: If you can hear me, don't worry! I'll write your suicide note!!

situation: An employee with a steel beam resting on his head reports to Catbert, the H.R. director, that the ceiling in his work area collapsed. Catbert refuses to accept responsibility and suggests the injury happened at the employee's home. As the employee passes out, Catbert cheerfully offers to write his suicide note.
punchline: Catbert not only denies the company's liability for a workplace injury but callously plans to cover it up by framing the employee's collapse as a suicide.
summary: A hurt worker pinned under a fallen steel beam gets only blame and a macabre offer of paperwork from his heartless human resources chief.

file: 1999/1999-10-02_do for living_slavishly obey_insane commands_pointy haired baboon_best catch_big box.gif
title: Dilbert's Honest Answer at Party

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: So, what do you do for a living?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I slavishly obey the insane commands of a pointy-haired baboon.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: The sad thing is that you're the best catch at this party.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I work in a big box.

setting: A social party, with both holding wine glasses
situation: At a party, a woman asks Dilbert what he does for a living. He bluntly says he slavishly obeys the insane commands of a pointy-haired baboon, meaning his boss. She responds that he is the best catch at the party, and Dilbert adds that he works in a big box (his cubicle).
punchline: Dilbert's brutally honest, self-deprecating job description is still considered the best offer at a dismal party, and he makes it worse by admitting he works in a big box, meaning a cubicle.
summary: Asked about his career at a social gathering, a bleak engineer admits to servitude under a baboon-like boss and a boxy workspace, and still tops the list of eligible singles.
keywords: what do you do for a living

title: Spying on a Decision-Avoiding VP

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: 2:19 P.M., the VP reads a document.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The subject tries to lose the document to avoid making a decision.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: 2:21 P.M., the subject learns to use tools.

setting: A vice president's office with a large desk and a tall potted plant
situation: A hidden observer peers through a plant and narrates the behavior of a VP like a nature documentary. The VP reads a document, then tries to get rid of it by tossing it behind his chair so he won't have to decide anything. Two minutes later he is using a pen to scratch inside his ear.
punchline: The VP's idea of using tools is scratching his ear with a pen, which shows how little useful work he does, and he even tries to dodge decisions by losing the paperwork.
summary: A secret watcher in a potted plant studies a vice president as if he were a wild animal, noting his document-dodging and his clumsy tool use.

title: Don't Mix Enthusiasm With Stupidity

transcript.speaker: Presenter
transcript.text: I'd like to spend the first hour defining what "information technology" means.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Ooh ooh! Can I help pass out the materials?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It's not a good idea to mix enthusiasm with stupidity, Asok.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Oh. Sorry.

setting: Conference room during a training meeting
situation: A presenter opens a session by announcing that the first hour will be spent defining what information technology means. Asok, eager as ever, excitedly volunteers to hand out the materials. Wally, seated at the table, tells him that enthusiasm and stupidity make a bad combination, and Asok apologizes.
punchline: Wally bluntly points out that Asok's eagerness to help with a pointless, drawn-out meeting reveals his stupidity, implying that anyone enthusiastic about such a session is foolish.
summary: A coworker's keen offer to help at a painfully basic training session earns him a blunt put-down from a jaded colleague.

title: Sociopath Boss Schedules Dawn Meeting

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I scheduled the meeting for 6:00 a.m. so everyone can make it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I assume you'll show up at eight o'clock and blame traffic.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The great thing about being a sociopath is that I always get enough sleep.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he has scheduled a meeting for 6:00 a.m. so that everyone can attend. He then predicts that Dilbert will turn up two hours late and blame traffic. In the last panel, the Boss reveals in a thought bubble that being a sociopath lets him sleep well despite his behavior.
punchline: The Boss knowingly sets an unreasonable meeting time, expects people to cope by lying about traffic, and admits privately that his lack of conscience is why he feels no stress or lost sleep over it.
summary: A manager sets an absurdly early meeting, cynically expects his employee to arrive late with an excuse, and smugly credits his lack of conscience for his good night's rest.

title: Merger Layoffs Exclude Everyone Except Tech Writers

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We'll be destroying another healthy company via a process we call merging.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No engineers will be downsized after the merger.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And tech writers...

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Yes?!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Should write that down.

situation: The Boss addresses a meeting about an upcoming corporate merger, openly admitting it will destroy a healthy company. He reassures the engineers they won't be laid off, then pauses on the tech writers. Tina hopefully asks 'Yes?!' and he merely tells them to write it down.
punchline: The tech writer hopes the Boss is about to say she is safe from layoffs, but he only wants her to document the announcement, implying her job is not secure.
summary: At a merger briefing, a manager promises job security for engineers, then gives the hopeful tech writers nothing but a transcription task.

title: Wally Blames the Carpet, Goes Home

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: The wavy pattern on the carpet is making me dizzy.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'd better go home and sleep it off.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'll be back tomorrow unless all the sleep makes me groggy.

situation: Wally stands in front of the Boss's desk and claims the wavy carpet pattern is making him dizzy. He announces he is going home to sleep it off, then says he will return tomorrow unless the sleep makes him groggy. The Boss sits silently in his chair throughout.
punchline: Wally invents an absurd, ever-expanding chain of excuses so that he can skip work, with the possible side effects of his own cure serving as a built-in reason not to come back.
summary: A workshy employee comes up with a ridiculous ailment as his ticket out of the office and leaves himself an escape hatch for the following day too.

title: Exiled Engineer Haunts Old Department

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I'm exiled to the Quality Assurance department. My career is doomed.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I can't let my old department forget me. They're my only hope of returning to Engineering.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It must be break time in the Q.A. department.

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: I'll get the fire hose.

setting: Office hallway and the engineering department cubicles
situation: Asok, reassigned to Quality Assurance, worries his career is over and decides to stay visible to his old engineering colleagues. He goes back and stands at their door waving his arms. The engineers, huddled together in alarm, mistake him for a pest and one offers to fetch a fire hose.
punchline: Asok's desperate attempt to be remembered by his old department only makes the engineers treat him like a nuisance to be driven off, probably because they consider QA people a pain.
summary: A demoted employee keeps showing up at his former team's door to be remembered, and they respond by reaching for a fire hose to chase him away.

title: Counseling Alice By Changing DNA

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, I've been asked to counsel you about your abuse of co-workers.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The theory is that I can alter your personality by talking to you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If you feel a tingle, that's probably your DNA changing.

situation: The Boss has been told to counsel Alice about her abusive behavior toward co-workers. He explains that his talking is supposed to change her personality, then claims any tingle she feels is her DNA changing. Alice sits silently, increasingly irritated.
punchline: The Boss's absurd, pseudo-scientific claim that a chat can rewrite her DNA shows how ineffective and clueless his counseling is, and Alice's clenched-fist silence suggests she is about to prove her reputation right.
summary: A clueless manager tries to talk a hot-tempered engineer out of her personality, promising her genes will rewrite themselves.

file: 1999/1999-04-28_pick up phone_calling and calling_fist of death_gnawed_wall to escape.gif
title: Alice's Fist of Death Strikes Asok

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Asok, I've been calling and calling, but you don't pick up your phone.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'd like you to meet a little something I call the "Fist of Death."

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It looks like he gnawed through the wall to escape.

situation: Alice complains to Asok that he never answers his phone, then threatens him with her "Fist of Death" while he looks up at her nervously. In the last panel, Wally and Dilbert stand holding coffee mugs beside a ragged hole punched through the cubicle wall, and Wally suggests Asok chewed his way out.
punchline: Asok's disappearance is blamed on him gnawing through the wall, when the jagged hole was obviously made by Alice's violent fist, and the coworkers casually accept it.
summary: After an angry coworker threatens a junior employee with a violent signature move, the others calmly puzzle over the hole in the wall he vanished through.

file: 1999/1999-12-02_no class_need in offcie_someplace else_use you_coffee cup_walk around.gif
title: Obsolete Skills, Just Carry Coffee

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I can't send you to this class, Alice. We need you here.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And after we use you up, we'll need you to be someplace else.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: What will I do when my skills are obsolete?

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Try walking around with a coffee cup.

setting: The Boss's office, then the cubicle area
situation: Alice asks to attend a training class, but the Boss refuses because the company needs her working. He adds that once they have used her up they will need her elsewhere. Alice asks what she will do when her skills are obsolete, and Phil, holding a coffee cup, suggests she walk around with one.
punchline: Phil's advice implies that employees with outdated skills survive by simply looking busy, since carrying a coffee cup around the office makes you appear to be doing something useful.
summary: A manager denies an employee training because she is too useful, so a coworker offers a cynical survival tip for when her skills go stale.

file: 1999/1999-01-03_human resources_job interview_name_tubby_human resources dept_sent resume_entrepreneur_toby_made up name_business.gif
title: Catbert Mauls Job Applicant Toby

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert the Director of Human Resources

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: So, you want a job here, Tubby?

transcript.speaker: Applicant
transcript.text: It's "Toby."

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Did you just correct me?

transcript.speaker: Applicant
transcript.text: Um...

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I alone will determine your name!!

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Now, what is your name?

transcript.speaker: Applicant
transcript.text: Tubby.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Tubby, is it true that you're so dumb that you...

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: ...sent your résumé to the Human Resources department?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Do you think that's what this department does? Let me show you what I do.

transcript.speaker: Applicant
transcript.text: I think I just became an entrepreneur.

situation: Catbert, the HR director, interviews a job applicant and calls him Tubby. When the man corrects him that his name is Toby, Catbert angrily insists he alone decides names, then mocks him for sending his résumé to HR. In the last panel the applicant is shown outside, clothes shredded and carrying a briefcase.
punchline: After being mauled by Catbert, the applicant is left jobless and in tatters, so he sarcastically declares himself an entrepreneur, a euphemism for being unemployed.
summary: A job seeker who dares to correct an HR cat's mistake gets savaged and walks out ragged, jokingly rebranding his unemployment.

title: Engineer Fakes Heart Attack for CPR

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: Chest pains... my heart...

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: I invented an antigravity belt, but it's hidden!!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Do you think it's true?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's what engineers say to increase the odds of getting CPR.

situation: During a meeting, a coworker clutches his chest and claims to be having heart trouble, then blurts out that he invented an antigravity belt but it's hidden. His feet are shown floating off the floor as a colleague wonders if the claim is true. Dilbert explains it's a line engineers use to make sure people give them CPR.
punchline: Engineers are so socially undervalued that they must make outlandish claims about their inventions to get anyone to bother saving their lives.
summary: A collapsing engineer tries a desperate boast about a secret invention so that his colleagues will rush to revive him.

title: Ratbert's Call Center Is Slippers

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Here's where you'll be working, Ratbert.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: This must be where people leave their shoes.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Is it okay if I hang things on my wall?

setting: Outside and inside the company call center
situation: Dilbert shows Ratbert to his new workplace, a door labeled Call Center. Inside is a floor packed with rows of identical slippers, and Ratbert assumes it is a shoe-storage room. In the last panel he is shown working from a tiny cubicle-like hole in the floor among the shoes, and asks if he can decorate his wall.
punchline: Ratbert's workspace is so tiny and low that he is crammed among the shoes, which suggests that call center employees are treated as the lowest of the low, with the cheerful request to hang things on his wall making the grim conditions even funnier.
summary: A tiny rodent is given a workstation so cramped and low that it looks like a hole amid a sea of footwear, yet he politely asks about decorating it.

file: 1999/1999-03-03_people fear public speaking_fear death_kill a guy_scheduled to speak_sleep_threats_dogcart threatens dilbert_hints at death_health.gif
title: Killing Speakers Is Doing Them Favors

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: They say people fear public speaking more than they fear death.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: So technically, if you kill a guy who's scheduled to speak, you're doing him a favor.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: When are you going to sleep?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Never.

setting: Dilbert's home, at a table with his laptop
situation: Dogbert sits across from Dilbert at a table and cites the statistic that people fear public speaking more than death. He reasons that killing someone who is scheduled to speak would be doing him a favor, then asks Dilbert when he is going to sleep. Dilbert, now alarmed, answers that he never will.
punchline: Dogbert's twisted logic implies he might murder Dilbert in his sleep as a kindness, so Dilbert decides to stay awake forever.
summary: A pet dog's grim reasoning about stage fright convinces his owner that sleeping is no longer safe.

file: 1999/1999-03-06_god hates pople_coffee tastes better_stir with finger_lonely religion.gif
title: Coffee Finger-Stirring Starts a Religion

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I believe God created the Earth because he hates people.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: And I believe coffee tastes better if you stir it with your finger.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It sounds like a lonely religion.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: They all start that way.

setting: Office break area by the coffee maker
situation: Wally stands at the coffee machine and shares his personal beliefs with Dilbert, starting with a cynical view of why God made the Earth. He then adds that coffee tastes better when stirred with a finger, which he demonstrates. Dilbert remarks that this sounds like a lonely religion, and Wally replies that all religions start that way.
punchline: Wally treats his bizarre, gross personal quirk as the seed of a new religion, deadpanning that every faith begins with one lone believer.
summary: While fixing his coffee, a cynical coworker lays out his odd personal creed, and when told it sounds lonely, he calmly notes that every belief system starts with a single follower.

title: Dan Will Prevent Our Success

transcript.speaker: Unseen speaker
transcript.text: You've all been chosen for this team because of your talent and professionalism.

transcript.speaker: Unseen speaker
transcript.text: Except for Dan, who is a big stubborn guy who will prevent our success.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Shall we commence failing?

transcript.speaker: Dan
transcript.text: I can't do work without a vision statement.

setting: Conference room during a new team meeting
situation: A team leader opens a kickoff meeting by praising everyone's talent and professionalism, then singles out Dan as a big stubborn guy who will prevent the team's success. Alice sarcastically asks if they should start failing, and Dan immediately proves the prediction right by refusing to work without a vision statement.
punchline: The leader's blunt prediction that Dan will sabotage the project is confirmed within seconds, as Dan demands a vision statement before doing any work.
summary: A team lead warns that one obstinate colleague will doom the project, and that colleague instantly lives up to the billing.

title: Sabotaging Her Own Project Deliberately

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: I just realized that if my project is a success, my job will be eliminated.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: The smartest thing I could do is fail miserably and blame it all on your indecisiveness.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: I'm happy because I have a clear strategy!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I haven't nodded in a while.

situation: Tina stands before The Boss's desk and explains that finishing her project successfully would cost her her job. She announces that her smartest move is to fail on purpose and blame him for being indecisive. The Boss, reclining in his chair, only thinks that he hasn't nodded in a while, so he misses that he is being insulted and set up as the scapegoat.
punchline: The Boss is so oblivious that he hears only a cheerful employee with a 'clear strategy' and thinks about nodding, not noticing that he is being told to his face she plans to fail and blame him.
summary: A programmer cheerfully reveals her plan to tank her own project and pin the blame on her clueless manager, who is too distracted to notice.

file: 1999/1999-07-29_juan delegator_requires deciosn_work on_more assignments_learned lesson_give work to alice.gif
title: Delegator Learns To Dump On Alice

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Juan Delegator

transcript.speaker: Juan Delegator
transcript.text: ... And this one also requires your decision before I can work on it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do you have any more assignments for me that I can turn into work for you?

transcript.speaker: Juan Delegator
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And have you learned your lesson?

transcript.speaker: Juan Delegator
transcript.text: Yes: give all work to Alice.

situation: Juan Delegator, a devil-horned manager, hands a stack of papers to the Boss and says each item needs the Boss's decision before he can work on it. The Boss asks whether he has any more assignments to turn into work for him, and then whether he has learned his lesson. Juan says the lesson is to give all work to Alice.
punchline: Instead of learning to stop offloading work onto others, Juan concludes that the way to avoid the Boss's counter-delegation is to dump everything on Alice, who is a convenient scapegoat.
summary: A manager who keeps passing his tasks upward is turned around by his superior, and the only lesson he takes away is to pick a different victim.

title: Imaginary Numbers Support Strategic Plan

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I found some numbers that support your strategic plan.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I had to take the square root of a negative number to do it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The timeline is on this Mobius strip.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Good work.

situation: Dilbert reports to the Boss that he found numbers backing the Boss's strategic plan. He admits he had to take the square root of a negative number to get them, and then hands over a twisted Mobius strip as the project timeline. The Boss, understanding none of it, praises him.
punchline: The supporting data is mathematically impossible and the timeline is an endless loop, yet the clueless Boss approves, showing that management accepts nonsense as long as it backs his plan.
summary: An employee props up his manager's plan with impossible math and a never-ending timeline, and the oblivious manager is delighted.

title: Catbert Mandates Identical Wallpaper, Plans Helium

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: In order to eliminate all traces of individuality...

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: All computer wallpaper must be the same.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What next?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: In theory, with enough helium, the employees would all sound alike.

setting: Office, at Catbert's and Dilbert's computer desks
situation: Catbert, the evil H.R. director, types at his computer and announces a policy that all computer wallpaper must be identical, as part of eliminating individuality. Dilbert reads the mandate at his own computer and wonders what could possibly come next. Catbert then muses that enough helium would make all employees sound alike.
punchline: Catbert's drive for corporate conformity escalates from a petty wallpaper rule to the absurd idea of making everyone's voices identical with helium.
summary: An H.R. tyrant in cat form enforces uniform desktop backgrounds and then daydreams about gassing the staff into matching voices.

title: Alice's Disguise Job Interview Scheme

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'll wear a clever disguise then interview for the engineering job here.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: If he offers me more money than I make now, I'll take the job.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Heh-heh.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're suspiciously fashionable for an engineer.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I store tools up there.

setting: Office lunch table, then the Boss's office during an interview
situation: Alice tells Wally and Dilbert over lunch that she will disguise herself and interview for an engineering job at her own company, taking it if the pay is higher than her current salary. In the interview she wears an enormous teased wig, sunglasses and a bright pink outfit, and the Boss remarks that she is too fashionable for an engineer. She claims she stores tools in her towering hat.
punchline: Alice's 'clever disguise' is so outlandish that it draws attention, and the Boss somehow fails to recognize her, accepting her absurd explanation instead.
summary: A worker plots to secretly interview for a better-paying job in her own company, but her flamboyant costume makes her stand out rather than blend in.

title: Dogbert Ruins Third-Person Speech

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Bob, from now on, I will refer to myself in the third person.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Dogbert does this to emphasize his special brand of greatness.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: Bob thinks that is a good idea.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Hey! You're ruining it!

setting: A conference table in an office, with a coffee mug on it
situation: Dogbert, wearing a crown and holding a scepter, announces to Bob the dinosaur that he will now speak about himself in the third person. He explains that it showcases his special greatness. Bob then copies the style, which annoys Dogbert.
punchline: Dogbert's supposedly unique mark of greatness is immediately cheapened when Bob imitates it, showing that his pretentious affectation isn't special at all.
summary: A self-important crowned dog's pompous new speech habit loses its shine the moment his listener starts doing it too.

title: Boss's Eating Habits Made Him Fat

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Asok, when I was your age I'd eat a huge breakfast, so I wouldn't have to stop working for lunch.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Then I'd eat a huge lunch, so I could work all night, or until dinner, whichever came first.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's how I got to be the man I am today.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Fat?

situation: The Boss tells Asok about his youthful work habits, claiming he ate enormous meals so he could keep working without breaks. He proudly says this made him the man he is today. Asok bluntly replies with a one-word guess.
punchline: Asok sarcastically suggests that the Boss's gluttonous 'work ethic' only resulted in him becoming fat, deflating his self-congratulatory story.
summary: A boastful manager credits his gargantuan meals and endless work hours for his success, only for a young employee to name the obvious result.

title: Compliance Means Falsifying Documents

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: In addition to ISO 9000, we will strive to be QS-9000 compliant.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That means falsifying the following documents: QSR, APQP, FMEA, MSA, SPC, PPAP and QSA.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Remember, you can't spell compliance without "liance".

situation: The Boss, holding a sheet of paper at a conference table, announces the company will pursue QS-9000 certification on top of ISO 9000. He then explains that this requires falsifying a long list of quality documents. He closes with a mangled wordplay about the spelling of the word compliance, while Dilbert and a coworker listen.
punchline: The Boss treats quality certification as a paperwork-faking exercise and cheerfully admits it, then caps it with a nonsensical spelling tip that actually points to the word 'lie' hidden in 'compliance'.
summary: A manager casually orders his team to forge a stack of quality-certification paperwork and jokes about the word hiding a lie.

file: 1999/1999-03-17_transfer sales dept_scapegoat_make useless pordcuts_low sales_good prodcuts_perfect wrld.gif
title: Scapegoat Transferred to Blame Sales

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm transferring you to the sales department, Scapegoat.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Then we can make useless products and blame you for our low sales.

transcript.speaker: Scapegoat
transcript.text: Wouldn't it be better to make good products?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: In a perfect world.

situation: The Boss tells Scapegoat, a goat employee, that he is being transferred to the sales department. The Boss explains the plan is to make useless products and then blame Scapegoat for the poor sales. Scapegoat suggests simply making good products, and the Boss dismisses the idea as only possible in a perfect world.
punchline: The Boss treats making good products as an unrealistic fantasy, preferring to engineer a scapegoat for failure rather than avoid the failure itself.
summary: A manager reassigns his designated fall guy to sales so that the company can ship junk and pin the weak results on him.

file: 1999/1999-04-11_information promised_ignored request_squadron_military squirrels_plausible lie_giant military squirrels_secret lair.gif
title: Demanding a Plausible Lie

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There's Ted. He never sent me the information he promised.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Why have you ignored my request, Ted?

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: I was killed by a squadron of giant military squirrels.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He doesn't respect you enough to tell a plausible lie.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I demand a plausible lie!

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Okay, maybe I wasn't killed by giant military squirrels.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: But I was imprisoned in their secret lair at the center of the earth.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You can't prove that one either way.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He did say it was a "secret" lair.

situation: Wally complains that Ted never sent him promised information and confronts him about it. Ted claims he was killed by giant military squirrels, and when Wally demands a more plausible lie, Ted offers an equally absurd story about being imprisoned in their secret lair at the center of the earth. Wally, grudgingly satisfied, admits it can't be disproved.
punchline: Ted's second excuse is just as ridiculous as the first, but because it can't be disproven (it's a "secret" lair), Wally accepts it as a valid excuse.
summary: A coworker who skipped a promised task offers a wildly absurd alibi, then barely upgrades it, and his unfalsifiable excuse is accepted anyway.

file: 1999/1999-01-26_carol on phone_yell kids_key to cabinet_supply cabinet_cheetah_panda_jungle_office.gif
title: Waiting Like a Cheetah, or Panda

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: As usual, Carol is on the phone yelling at her kids.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I wait, like a cheetah, for a chance to ask her for the key to the supply cabinet.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Are you waiting like a cheetah?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm more of a panda.

setting: Office cubicle area, with Dilbert and a coworker peeking over cubicle walls
situation: Dilbert peers over his cubicle wall, thinking about how Carol is on the phone yelling at her kids again. He wants to ask her for the supply cabinet key and imagines himself lying in wait like a cheetah. A coworker peeking over a nearby wall asks if he is waiting like a cheetah, and Dilbert corrects him.
punchline: Dilbert's grand predator metaphor is deflated when he admits he is really more of a panda, meaning slow and unthreatening, which fits how timidly he waits to ask for a mundane supply key.
summary: A cubicle dweller imagines himself as a stalking predator while hesitating to interrupt a coworker, then confesses he is really a docile bear.

file: 1999/1999-04-04_peggy pr dircetor_press release_technical accuracy_trained squirrel_run on sentences_transparent lies_spelling grammar_errors_criticism stronger.gif
title: Brutal Review of Press Release

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, this is Peggy the P.R. Director.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I want you to review her press release for technical accuracy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Who wrote this? A trained squirrel?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't know where to begin.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll cross out the run-on sentences and transparent lies first.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then the failed attempts at cuteness ... the spelling errors ... grammar.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There you go. Remember, criticism makes you stronger.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It was a mistake to make her stronger.

setting: Office, Dilbert's cubicle and the Boss's office
situation: The Boss introduces Peggy, the P.R. director, and asks Dilbert to check her press release for technical accuracy. Dilbert viciously tears the document apart, insulting its writing and crossing out everything wrong with it while Peggy grows angrier. He tells her criticism makes you stronger, and in the last panel he appears bandaged and in a cast after she beats him up.
punchline: Dilbert's cheerful claim that criticism makes you stronger backfires when the stronger Peggy physically assaults him, leaving him injured.
summary: A harsh edit of a colleague's press release turns out to be a painful lesson when the person he critiqued retaliates with newfound strength.

file: 1999/1999-05-19_recovered memory_ritual abuse_annual performance review_memories fade_takes 12 months.gif
title: Performance Review Trauma Lasts a Year

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Aaagh! I'm having a recovered memory of ritual abuse!

transcript.speaker: Balding Coworker
transcript.text: You had your annual performance review this morning.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Do the memories ever fade?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It takes about twelve months.

setting: Office lunch table or break room
situation: Three coworkers sit eating lunch at a table when one suddenly cries out that he is having a recovered memory of ritual abuse. A balding colleague points out that he just had his annual performance review that morning. The traumatized coworker asks if such memories fade, and Dilbert says it takes about a year.
punchline: Annual performance reviews are so unpleasant that they feel like traumatic abuse, and the pain only fades just in time for the next review twelve months later.
summary: A shaken employee mistakes his morning appraisal for repressed trauma, and a colleague dryly notes the sting wears off just as the next one arrives.

file: 1999/1999-04-26_lost two pounds_less of you_happy_scrap of encouragemnet_tapped out.gif
title: Dogbert Withholds Weight-Loss Encouragement

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I lost two pounds!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm happy. Guess why.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Because you're supportive?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Because there's less of you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I was hoping for a scrap of encouragement.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm all tapped out. Try back tomorrow.

situation: Dilbert, in a bathrobe, proudly announces to Dogbert that he lost two pounds. Dogbert, reading a newspaper, says he is happy but gives a selfish reason rather than support. When Dilbert asks for a little encouragement, Dogbert says he has none left and tells him to come back tomorrow.
punchline: Dogbert's happiness comes from there being less of Dilbert to put up with, and he sarcastically claims to have used up all his encouragement for the day.
summary: A man seeking praise for a small diet victory gets a dry, self-serving brush-off from his dog.

file: 1999/1999-02-12_dogberts tech support_serial number_inside unit_warranty void_open case_anything changes.gif
title: Serial Number Inside Warranty-Voiding Case

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert's Tech Support

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll need your serial number, which is conveniently located inside the unit.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: The sticker says my warranty will be void if I open the case.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Well, call me if anything changes.

setting: Dogbert's tech support call center desk, with the customer at his own desk
situation: Dogbert works a tech support line and asks a customer for the computer's serial number, which is printed inside the case. The customer explains that opening the case will void the warranty. Dogbert calmly tells him to call back if the situation changes, offering no help at all.
punchline: Tech support makes the customer's problem impossible to solve, and Dogbert blithely dismisses him rather than helping, since the policy leaves no way to get support.
summary: A tech support rep demands a serial number hidden behind a warranty-voiding seal, then shrugs the caller off when he points out the catch.

file: 1999/1999-01-10_how to book_teach people_winning lottery numbers_find free real estate_lose weight_tubs of ice cream_strong abs_see angels_near death experience_get rid witnesses.gif
title: Dogbert's Scam-Filled How-To Book

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm writing a comprehensive "how to" book.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: In Chapter One, I teach people how to pick winning lottery numbers.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Chapter Two: How to find free real estate in very nice neighborhoods.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Chapter Three: How to lose weight by eating huge tubs of ice cream.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Chapter Four: How to build strong abs by joining a gym and never going.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Finally, how to see angels by giving yourself a near death experience.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That last one is just to get rid of all the witnesses.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: (thought) On the plus side, I don't feel so bad about not recycling.

setting: Dilbert's home, at the computer desk
situation: Dogbert types at a computer while describing the chapters of his how-to book to Dilbert, who stands by in a red robe holding a coffee mug. Each chapter promises something impossible or absurd, such as picking lottery numbers or losing weight on ice cream. The last chapter, about near death experiences, is revealed to be a way to eliminate everyone who could expose the scam.
punchline: Dogbert's book is a series of fraudulent self-help promises, and the final chapter kills off the readers who could testify that the book doesn't work, leaving Dilbert to think only of how it excuses his own bad habits.
summary: A scheming dog outlines a self-help guide full of impossible promises and admits the finale exists to silence anyone who could complain.

title: Power Supply Made of Nail

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I didn't know how to design a power supply, so I put a nail in a piece of wood.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'm on vacation tomorrow, so I'll give you my files in case you need to make changes.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Once I had the idea, it all came together pretty quickly.

situation: A coworker hands Dilbert a piece of wood with a nail in it, claiming it is his power supply design because he didn't know how to design a real one. He casually offers his files in case changes are needed, since he is going on vacation. Dilbert glares at the useless block while the coworker brags about how quickly it came together.
punchline: The coworker passes off a nail in a board as a finished engineering deliverable, dumping the problem on Dilbert and then leaving for vacation.
summary: A colleague who couldn't engineer a power supply hands over a nailed block of wood as his finished work and heads off on holiday.

file: 1999/1999-11-09_can't control_based on perfromance_not a team player.gif
title: Bonus Tied to Another Company

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: ...And since our bonuses depend on things we can't control...

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: ...Can mine be based on the performance of some other company?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You ask one question and suddenly you're not a team player.

setting: Office conference room during a meeting
situation: Wally sits at a meeting table and notes that employee bonuses depend on factors outside their control. He then sarcastically asks if his bonus could be based on some other company's performance. Dilbert listens, and in the last panel Wally complains that asking one question gets him labeled as not a team player.
punchline: Wally sarcastically points out that bonuses tied to uncontrollable factors are arbitrary, and the complaint that follows shows that questioning management gets you branded as not a team player.
summary: A sarcastic employee mocks a bonus plan built on random outside factors and then grumbles that merely asking about it gets him accused of disloyalty.

title: Dilbert Insults Date's Storytelling Skills

transcript.speaker: Blonde woman
transcript.text: And then I said, "How am I supposed to do all that?" Then I glared at her.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you have that woman's phone number? She sounds nicer than you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert (thought)
transcript.text: I don't see why it's MY fault she can't tell a decent story.

setting: A social gathering or party where people are holding wine glasses
situation: A woman at a party tells Dilbert a long story about a workplace argument in which she glared at a coworker. Dilbert, bored by the story, bluntly asks for the other woman's phone number because she sounds nicer than the storyteller. In the last panel he privately thinks it isn't his fault she tells such a poor story.
punchline: Dilbert tactlessly insults the woman by saying the person she's complaining about sounds nicer than she does, then blames her for being a bad storyteller instead of recognizing his own rudeness.
summary: While a woman recounts a petty work confrontation at a party, Dilbert rudely says her adversary sounds more pleasant and then blames her poor storytelling for his reaction.

file: 1999/1999-10-03_mordac_preventer of information services_exceeded disk sapce_one week_no email_engineer_survive_modem taped ankle_engineering.gif
title: Mordac Bans Email, Dilbert Hides Modem

Dilbert calmly says it's no problem, which makes Mordac suspicious. Mordac frisks him against the wall and finds a modem taped to his ankle, but Dilbert reveals he still has a hidden wireless pen modem.
punchline: Dilbert had prepared for the e-mail ban with a hidden backup modem, so Mordac's punishment was ineffective and Dilbert outsmarted him.
summary: A power-tripping IT enforcer cuts off an engineer's e-mail, only to discover the engineer has already smuggled in a secret way to stay connected.

file: 1999/1999-05-02_take six months_time line_leadership_made me unmotivated_foreseen or unforseen_wally is dysfunctional_schedule is random_looks mad.gif
title: Unforeseen Problems Include Unmotivated Employees

transcript.text: The project will take six months...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Unless there are unforeseen problems.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Question.
