transcript.text: Your leadership has made me unmotivated.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is that considered foreseen or unforeseen?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And Wally is dysfunctional on many levels.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I really am.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Was that foreseen? Or are you saying the schedule is random?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: He looks mad.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I didn't see that coming.

setting: Conference room during a project planning meeting
situation: The Boss presents a six-month project timeline with a caveat for unforeseen problems. Dilbert asks whether the team's demotivation from the Boss's own leadership counts as foreseen or unforeseen, and adds that Wally is dysfunctional. The Boss gets angry and asks if Dilbert is calling the schedule random.
punchline: Dilbert's sarcastic question exposes that the Boss's poor leadership is a predictable problem, so the 'unforeseen problems' escape clause in the schedule is meaningless, and the Boss's anger proves the point.
summary: A manager hedges his project estimate, and an employee cheekily asks whether bad management counts as a surprise.

title: Pre-Meeting Moved After the Meeting

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I rescheduled the pre-meeting.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Now the pre-meeting is after the meeting.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll schedule some time for me to pre-care.

situation: Alice hands Dilbert a paper and tells him she has rescheduled the pre-meeting. She explains that it now takes place after the actual meeting, which defeats its purpose. Dilbert responds that he will schedule time to 'pre-care' about it.
punchline: Since the pre-meeting now happens after the meeting, Dilbert sarcastically says he'll need to schedule time to 'pre-care', showing how pointless and absurd the scheduling has become.
summary: A meeting meant to prepare for another meeting gets moved to follow it, and Dilbert deadpans that he'll make time to care in advance.

file: 1999/1999-08-30_catbert_evil director_promote_from within_yanking your chain_hiring from outside_you're so smart.gif
title: Promoting From Within, Then Not

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: We like to promote from within the company, Asok.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: But what we like even more is yanking your chain and then hiring from the outside!

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Explain why you work here if you're so smart.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I'm timid.

situation: Catbert, the evil H.R. director, tells Asok the company likes to promote from within. He then reveals he enjoys even more stringing employees along before hiring an outsider. He taunts Asok to explain why he works there if he's so smart, and Asok timidly admits he's too timid to leave.
punchline: Asok's only reason for staying at an abusive company is his own timidity, which Catbert's cruel promotion games exploit.
summary: An H.R. cat gleefully admits to dangling promotions before filling the job externally, and his smart but meek victim confesses he stays out of fear.

title: Spoofing the Boss's Email Account

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: The boss is away.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: An unscrupulous employee could send e-mail from his account.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: The following employees have odd-looking nostrils.

situation: A bald, bespectacled employee notices the boss is away and thinks about how an unscrupulous person could misuse the boss's email account. He then sits at the boss's computer and sends out a message insulting his coworkers.
punchline: Given the chance to abuse the boss's email access, the employee uses it for petty, childish insults about coworkers' nostrils rather than anything of real consequence.
summary: Left alone in the absent manager's office, a worker hijacks the computer to email silly insults about colleagues.

title: Boss Boosts Morale By Insulting Staff

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We have the best employees in the world...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: ...not counting the people who refuse to work here because the pay is so low.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Improve morale... done.

situation: The Boss sits at the head of a meeting table addressing Dilbert and a bald coworker. He praises his employees as the best in the world, then adds that this excludes everyone who won't work there because the pay is so low. In the last panel he thinks to himself that he has improved morale and ticked it off his list.
punchline: The Boss believes a backhanded compliment that highlights the company's poor pay counts as a morale boost, showing how out of touch he is with how his words land.
summary: A manager thinks he has lifted team spirits with a speech whose praise is undercut by a jab about the pitiful salaries.

file: 1999/1999-05-22_work all night_finish prodcut_random act_management_seem less random.gif
title: Random Act of Management

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, I expect you to work all night to finish that project. It's vital!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Aagh!! I'm a victim of a random act of management!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I was sure the arm-pumping would make it seem less random.

setting: Office, Alice's cubicle area and the Boss's desk
situation: The Boss orders Alice to work all night to finish a project he calls vital. Alice complains that she is a victim of a random act of management. In the last panel the Boss, sitting at his desk, thinks that his arm-pumping gesture should have made the demand seem less random.
punchline: The Boss realizes his demand really was arbitrary and only worries that his emphatic gesture failed to disguise that, not that the demand itself is unreasonable.
summary: A boss springs an overnight work order on Alice and then privately frets that his gestures did not make the whim look planned.

title: Perfect Crime: Resume Sent to Boss

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Heh-heh... I'm using company resources to e-mail my résumé to a headhunter.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: It's the perfect crime.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've got mail!

setting: Office cubicle and the boss's office
situation: Alice smugly thinks to herself that she is using company equipment to email her résumé to a headhunter and believes no one will find out. In the final panel the Boss, sitting at his own computer, announces that he has received new mail, implying her résumé reached him instead.
punchline: Alice's supposedly perfect crime falls apart because her résumé was evidently delivered to her boss rather than the headhunter.
summary: A worker gloats about secretly job hunting on the company's dime, only for her boss to cheerfully announce that he has received an email.

file: 1999/1999-02-27_catbert_evil dircetor_new policy_reimbursement_travel_bring back fork_ten percent meals.gif
title: Catbert's Fork Reimbursement Policy

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Computer
transcript.text: ...New policy on reimbursement for travel...

transcript.speaker: Computer
transcript.text: Do not tip more than ten percent for meals...

transcript.speaker: Computer
transcript.text: If the meal costs more than six dollars, bring back a fork.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Purrr

setting: Office, Catbert's desk and Dilbert's cubicle
situation: Catbert, the evil H.R. director, types a new travel reimbursement policy that Dilbert reads on his computer screen. The rules start out ordinary, with a cap on tipping, then turn absurd when employees are told to bring back a fork as proof of an expensive meal. Catbert purrs happily as he writes it.
punchline: The policy is deliberately ridiculous and petty, showing that the evil H.R. director enjoys inventing humiliating, nonsensical rules for employees' expense claims.
summary: A malicious HR cat drafts a travel expense memo whose rules grow steadily sillier, ending with an order to steal cutlery as proof of pricey dining.

title: Coworker's Baby: Hoping It's Not Moronic

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: My wife had a baby!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I hope it's not a moron.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Have you looked into foster care?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe we shouldn't have gone with our first instinct.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: We meant well.

setting: Office hallway near the coffee area
situation: A coworker excitedly announces that his wife has had a baby. Wally and Dilbert, holding coffee mugs, respond with insulting remarks, first hoping the baby isn't a moron and then suggesting foster care. After the coworker leaves, they privately wonder whether their first instinct was wrong, but justify it by saying they meant well.
punchline: Instead of congratulating the new father, Dilbert and Wally say tactless, insulting things and then excuse their rudeness as good intentions.
summary: Two cynical coworkers respond to happy parenting news with rude, tactless remarks, then lamely defend themselves afterward.

title: Lawyer's Brutal Testimony Practice Session

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The Corporate Lawyer

transcript.speaker: Corporate Lawyer
transcript.text: Let's prepare for your court testimony. I'll pretend to be the other side.

transcript.speaker: Corporate Lawyer
transcript.text: Liar! Why is your attorney so handsome?

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Whap!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: They can hit me?

transcript.speaker: Corporate Lawyer
transcript.text: I don't see why not.

setting: Office, during a mock courtroom preparation session
situation: A corporate lawyer prepares Dilbert for court testimony by role-playing the opposing attorney. He shouts an absurd accusation and smacks Dilbert with a rolled-up document. Dilbert, dazed, asks whether the other side is allowed to hit him, and the lawyer casually says he sees no reason why not.
punchline: The lawyer's deadpan, unhelpful answer suggests that being physically assaulted is simply part of testifying, and he is not bothered by it.
summary: A lawyer rehearses courtroom questioning by swatting his client with rolled-up papers, then shrugs off the idea that opposing counsel might do the same in court.

file: 1999/1999-09-22_never been summoned_intern_respect_great honor_air from outdoors_air duct_building.gif
title: Intern Sent Into Air Duct

transcript.speaker: Intern
transcript.text: I have never been summoned to your office before. It is a great honor for an intern.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need you to crawl through this air duct and find out where air comes from.

transcript.speaker: Intern
transcript.text: Air comes from outdoors.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, I think it's coming from our building.

situation: A cheerful young intern, thrilled to be called into the boss's office for the first time, is told to crawl through an air duct to discover where air comes from. When the intern correctly says air comes from outdoors, the boss dismisses this and insists it originates in the building.
punchline: The boss is so confident in his wrong idea that he rejects basic common sense from the intern, who was sent on a pointless errand anyway.
summary: An eager intern is handed a ridiculous assignment to trace the source of air, then is contradicted by his manager when he gives the obvious answer.

title: Boss Blames Employees for Electricity Hogging

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It seems a bit dark in my office today.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I think you employees are hogging all the electricity.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You just double-clicked! I heard it!

situation: The Boss stands behind Dilbert, who is working at his computer, and complains that his own office seems dark. He concludes that employees are using up all the electricity. He then accuses Dilbert of double-clicking his mouse, claiming he heard it, as if each click drains power.
punchline: The Boss's technical ignorance leads him to believe that computer use physically siphons electricity from his office lights, and that he can hear a double-click consuming power.
summary: A clueless manager decides his dim office is caused by staff computers stealing power and blames a mouse click for it.

file: 1999/1999-01-24_red white shirt_spilled_women_party_drink in face_salt_lighter fluid_set on fire_burned_not happy_not popular.gif
title: Party Guests Escalate Stain Removal

transcript.speaker: Woman 1
transcript.text: You spilled red wine on your shirt.

transcript.speaker: Woman 1
transcript.text: You should dilute it with white wine.

transcript.speaker: Woman 1
transcript.text: You'll thank me for this later.

transcript.speaker: Woman 1
transcript.text: I think that helped.

transcript.speaker: Woman 2
transcript.text: You need salt to absorb it.

transcript.speaker: Woman 2
transcript.text: Try my margarita.

transcript.speaker: Woman 1
transcript.text: Salt didn't work. Let's try pepper spray.

transcript.speaker: Woman 2
transcript.text: Perhaps lighter fluid...

transcript.speaker: Woman 1
transcript.text: No harm in trying.

transcript.speaker: Woman 2
transcript.text: I have one more idea.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Just once, I'd like to go to a party and not be set on fire.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: There's a stain on your rag.

characters: Woman at party (dark red hair, pink outfit)
setting: A cocktail party, then Dilbert's home
situation: At a party, two well-meaning women try to remove a red wine stain from Dilbert's shirt. Their remedies escalate from white wine to salt, a margarita, pepper spray and finally lighter fluid and fire. Dilbert ends up at home in tattered, burned clothing, while Dogbert comments on the stain.
punchline: After being doused, sprayed and set on fire in the name of helping, Dilbert is left with a burned rag, and Dogbert callously points out it is still stained.
summary: Overeager party guests turn a small wine spill into a series of increasingly dangerous cleaning attempts that leave Dilbert singed and shirtless.

title: Boss Pretends To Like Dilbert

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do you mind if I pretend to like you? I hear it increases productivity.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I need to go back to my cubicle now.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's working!

situation: The Boss carries his lunch tray over to Dilbert's table and asks permission to pretend to like him because he heard it boosts productivity. He sits and smiles awkwardly while Dilbert eats, then Dilbert says he needs to go back to his cubicle. The Boss, in a thought bubble, believes his plan is working.
punchline: The Boss's fake friendliness is so uncomfortable that Dilbert flees back to work, which the oblivious Boss mistakes as proof that the productivity trick is succeeding.
summary: A manager tries a productivity tip by faking friendship over lunch, and his employee's hasty retreat to work convinces him it succeeded.

title: Dilbert Finds Defects in Mom's House

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your wall is warm, Mom.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mom
transcript.text: Is that bad?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There's no way to be sure unless you remove the sheetrock and look.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mom
transcript.text: Please stop finding defects in my house.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I smell propane.

situation: Dilbert feels his mother's wall and announces it is warm, then says the only way to know if that is a problem is to tear out the sheetrock. His mom, sitting with a cup of tea, begs him to stop finding defects in her house. He responds by saying he smells propane.
punchline: Dilbert, a compulsive problem-finder, ignores his mother's plea and immediately raises an even scarier defect, showing he can't stop inspecting and worrying.
summary: A son's relentless home inspection keeps turning up alarming problems no matter how much his mother asks him to quit.

title: Secret Lair Is a Dumpster

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Asok, come to my secret lair and I will teach you about reality.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Your secret lair is a dumpster?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Get in.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: It's like my cubicle, but with much better lumbar support!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: French fry?

situation: Wally, dressed in a red hooded costume and holding a giant wooden spoon, tugs Asok by the tie and promises to teach him about reality at his secret lair. The lair turns out to be a dumpster, and Wally tells Asok to climb in. Sitting among the trash, Asok observes that it beats his cubicle for comfort while Wally offers him a french fry.
punchline: The dumpster is more comfortable than Asok's cubicle, which is a bleak comment on office working conditions, and Wally's casual offer of a french fry from the trash makes the 'reality' lesson both grim and funny.
summary: A costumed Wally lures a naive coworker into a garbage bin, where the young man decides it's actually an upgrade over his workspace.

title: Requirements Document Destroyed by Bees

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The huge product requirements document was destroyed in a freak accident.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll ask Marketing to send you a new copy.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I told you we can't stop them one-bee-at-a-time. We have to go for the queen.

situation: Dilbert and Wally, their clothes tattered and torn, tell The Boss that the huge product requirements document was destroyed in a freak accident. The Boss calmly offers to get a new copy from Marketing, oblivious to their battered state. Wally then remarks to Dilbert that they can't fight the attackers one bee at a time and must go after the queen.
punchline: The tattered state of the engineers and Wally's bee remark reveal they were attacked by a swarm of bees, which the Boss completely ignores while focusing only on replacing the document.
summary: Two ragged engineers blame a mysterious mishap for a lost document while hinting they are really under siege by bees, and their boss only cares about getting a replacement copy.

file: 1999/1999-04-18_process manager_process_poorly manged_intern_no process_voted out of meeting_annoying.gif

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: She only knows how to do things BETTER!

transcript.speaker: Patty
transcript.text: Process!

transcript.speaker: Patty
transcript.text: For example, this meeting is poorly managed because you have no process.

transcript.speaker: Patty
transcript.text: And this intern obviously had no process for deciding whether to attend.

transcript.text: Okay, Patty is annoying.

transcript.speaker: The Boss

Patty then criticizes the meeting for lacking process and the intern for attending without one. The annoyed attendees promptly vote to get rid of her, and she is ejected from the room.
punchline: Patty's process-obsessed criticism is so annoying that the group instantly votes her out, and Dilbert notes she outlasted the last facilitator, implying such consultants are routinely run off.
summary: A newly hired process expert nitpicks everyone's meeting habits until the group democratically boots her out, just like her predecessor.

file: 1999/1999-05-30_change contract_signed months ago_hurt to ask_discount_clueless_primary vendors_acts of god_poltergeists_steal best.gif

transcript.text: No one said it would be easy.

Alice objects that she would look foolish in front of the vendor, but he piles on a silly request to add poltergeists to the 'acts of God' clause. punchline: The Boss believes vendors never poach his best employees because of how he treats them, when in fact the reason is obviously his own absurd demands, which make working for him unattractive.

title: Wally's Astral Projection Meeting Plan

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm gonna try this during our meeting.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Does anyone want to switch chairs?

In the meeting, Wally sits rigid and grimacing at the table, apparently attempting it, while Alice and another coworker watch uneasily. Alice asks if anyone wants to switch chairs, wanting to get away from him.
punchline: Wally's attempt to project his spirit out of his body makes him so creepy and unsettling that his colleagues want to move away from him.
summary: A coworker's plan to leave his body during a meeting leaves his colleagues desperate to sit somewhere else.

title: Tina Proves Writers Bleed Too

transcript.text: If you prick us, do we not bleed like engineers?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What kind of experiment?

setting: The Boss's office, then a hallway
situation: Tina confronts the Boss at his desk, asking why the tech writers must be laid off after the merger. She then paraphrases Shylock's 'if you prick us, do we not bleed' speech to argue writers are as human as engineers. In the last panel she has a bandage on her hand and the Boss is beside her while Dilbert asks what kind of experiment this is.
punchline: Tina's 'if you prick us' argument was apparently carried out literally, with the Boss pricking her finger as an experiment to see whether tech writers bleed like engineers.
summary: A laid-off-threatened writer quotes Shakespeare to defend her colleagues, and a bandaged finger suggests the proof was gathered the painful way.

title: Turnaround CEO Is Literally a Demon

transcript.text: The Turnaround CEO

transcript.speaker: Training Manager
transcript.text: ...From a value-based management perspective it's clear...

transcript.speaker: Training Manager
transcript.text: ...that the training department's return exceeds the cost of capital...

transcript.speaker: Training Manager
transcript.text: So please don't kill me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay, you're next...and begging doesn't work.

setting: Corporate office, the CEO's desk and a hallway
situation: A nervous employee presents a financial case for keeping the training department to a red, horned, demonic turnaround CEO, then pleads for his life. In the last panel Dilbert, apparently acting as the CEO's enforcer, tells the next victim that begging doesn't work as the Boss is shown being flung out of the room with his legs in the air.
punchline: The turnaround CEO's downsizing is portrayed as literal murder, with employees begging for their lives and the victims being violently disposed of, so corporate layoffs are shown to be brutal and merciless despite the polite financial arguments.
summary: A devilish cost-cutting executive dispatches department after department while terrified staff justify their existence in finance jargon.

title: Turnaround CEO Takes Employee's Head

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Everyone says you're a great turnaround CEO.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: What does it take to turn around a company like this one?

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I guess it's better to not be noticed the first month.

situation: An employee in a yellow-spotted tie nervously compliments a snarling red demon-like CEO and asks how he turns companies around. The CEO apparently responds by literally turning the employee's head around. In the last panel the employee walks away with his head twisted backwards, thinking he should have stayed unnoticed.
punchline: The CEO's 'turnaround' expertise is taken literally when he twists the employee's head around, and the employee concludes that new executives are best avoided early on.
summary: A worker flatters a monstrous new CEO about his turnaround skills and ends up with his head literally screwed on backwards.

file: 1999/1999-03-26_wear jeans_work pants_sworn secrecy_butt looks good_comfratble_jeans under work pants.gif

title: Boss Buys Obsolete Osborne Laptops

punchline: The Boss is buying laptops from an ancient, long-defunct computer line and marvelling at floppy drives, showing the company is hopelessly behind the times despite the dot-com boom's talk of "Internet time."
summary: Management proudly standardizes on antique computers, prompting a wry observation that the company is far from cutting-edge.

file: 1999/1999-11-25_the turnaround ceo_work of 10 people_strategic planning_traitorous mole.gif

punchline: Dilbert's attempt to save his job by trashing his colleagues gets him recruited as a backstabbing spy, rewarding disloyalty rather than competence.

transcript.text: Aaagh!! We can't do all of this!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Couldn't we just change the names of all our departments?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Those imbeciles! How dare they ignore my advice!

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: You're supposed to say that behind our backs later.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm in a hurry.

situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, hands management his final report recommending radical changes and admits he expects them to be too cowardly to act. The managers read it, panic, and the Boss proposes merely renaming the departments. Dogbert immediately complains about being ignored, skipping the usual step of doing it behind their backs.
punchline: Dogbert knows management will ignore any real advice, so he sarcastically blames them on the spot instead of waiting, because he's in a hurry to get paid and leave.
summary: A consultant delivers a bold report, predicts the executives will chicken out, and angrily denounces them the moment they do.

title: Well-Engineered Project Meets Marketing

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This completes my portion of the project.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This project is so well-engineered it would take a squadron of idiots to ruin it.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Meanwhile in Marketing

transcript.speaker: Marketing Manager
transcript.text: And when I'm napping, it is NOT okay to use my ears as coasters.

setting: Dilbert's cubicle, then the marketing department
situation: Dilbert finishes his part of a project and thinks to himself that it is so well designed that only a squadron of idiots could ruin it. The scene then cuts to the marketing department, where a manager is scolding his staff for using his ears as coasters while he naps.
punchline: The marketing department, which will take the project next, is staffed by exactly the kind of idiots Dilbert fears, as shown by their absurd behavior.
summary: An engineer's confidence in his flawless work is undercut by a glimpse of the silly people who will inherit it next.

file: 1999/1999-10-17_dumb boss_tape measure_postage on email_my boss is so dumb.gif
title: Dumb Boss Jokes Backfire

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: My boss is so dumb, he brought a tape measure to a distance learning class.

transcript.speaker: Group
transcript.text: HA HA HA HA HA!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: My boss is so dumb...

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: He puts postage stamps on his e-mail.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Now he can't see his PC screen.

transcript.speaker: Group
transcript.text: HA HA HA HA HA HA

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: How about you, Dilbert? Do you have any dumb boss jokes?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, my PC is warm. I think our fire wall is acting up.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: We're sorry.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: We didn't know.

situation: Dilbert's coworkers sit around a meeting table trading jokes about how dumb their bosses are, laughing hysterically. When they ask Dilbert for his own dumb boss joke, he stays silent, and The Boss walks in and says his PC is warm and the fire wall must be acting up. The coworkers realize Dilbert's boss is the dumbest of all and apologize.
punchline: Dilbert doesn't need to tell a joke because his boss's real-life stupidity (thinking a warm PC means the firewall is literally on fire) tops every dumb boss joke, leaving the others embarrassed.
summary: A round of boss-bashing humor ends when Dilbert's own clueless manager wanders in and proves he's the real punchline.

file: 1999/1999-04-01_answer phone_trick question_meeting_better get this_phone rings_ignores boss call_business.gif
title: Wally Answers Phone Only Now

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, I've been calling you for two hours! Why don't you answer your phone?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Is that a trick question?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, unless you're in a meeting...

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Hold on. I'd better get this.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Ring ring ring

situation: The Boss complains to Wally that he has been calling him for two hours without an answer. Wally asks if it's a trick question, and as the Boss offers meetings as the only acceptable excuse, Wally's phone finally rings and he reaches to pick it up.
punchline: Wally has been deliberately ignoring his boss's calls, and he answers the phone only when it rings after the boss has finished talking, seemingly as if the excuse of a meeting were a convenient out, or just to dodge the question.
summary: A manager scolds his lazy employee for ignoring the phone, and the employee deflects the accusation by treating it as a riddle and then conveniently answering a call.

title: Whistle-Blower Bores Clueless Jury

transcript.speaker: Lawyer
transcript.text: Okay, whistle-blower, explain to the jury the alleged crimes of your employer.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ... Then our applets were designed to corrupt cookie data from all competing portals.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Nice jury selection.

transcript.speaker: Lawyer
transcript.text: So far you've made them hungry.

situation: Dilbert is testifying as a whistle-blower, and his lawyer asks him to explain his employer's alleged crimes to the jury. Dilbert launches into technical jargon about applets and cookie data while the jurors look blank, bored or one sticks out his tongue. Dilbert complains about the jury, and the lawyer replies that the testimony has only made them hungry.
punchline: The jury doesn't understand the technical testimony and only hears 'cookie', so the lawyer says Dilbert has merely made them hungry.
summary: A whistle-blower's tech-heavy courtroom testimony leaves jurors baffled, with the word 'cookie' being the only thing that registers with them.

file: 1999/1999-03-01_dense planets_more garvity_more dense planets_no loose ends_dogbert.gif
title: Circular Reasoning About Planetary Gravity

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...And we know mass creates gravity because dense planets have more gravity.

transcript.speaker: Small egg-shaped character
transcript.text: How do we know which planets are more dense?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: They have more gravity.

transcript.speaker: Small egg-shaped character
transcript.text: That's circular reasoning.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I prefer to think of it as having no loose ends.

setting: Outdoors on a grassy hill with a tree and rocks
situation: Dilbert lectures a small egg-shaped companion about gravity, claiming mass creates gravity because dense planets have more gravity. When asked how we know which planets are denser, he answers that they have more gravity. Called out for circular reasoning, he spins it as a virtue.
punchline: Dilbert defends his circular logic by recasting it as a tidy argument with no loose ends, rationalizing a flaw as a strength.
summary: A self-assured explanation of physics collapses into a loop, and the explainer cheerfully reframes the flaw as a feature.

title: Moth Coworker Drawn to Meetings

transcript.speaker: Moth Coworker
transcript.text: My moth sense has detected a meeting.

transcript.speaker: Moth Coworker
transcript.text: Hi, guys! What are you talking about? Is this a meeting? I can't resist joining in.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Run for it! I'll hold him off with this cedar-flavored donut!!!

situation: Two coworkers are talking when a colleague dressed as a moth, peeking around a doorway, announces that he has sensed a meeting. He cheerfully approaches and invites himself in. One coworker tells the other to run and distracts the moth by waving a cedar-flavored donut at him.
punchline: The moth coworker is compulsively attracted to meetings the way moths are drawn to light, and the only way to escape him is to distract him with a cedar-flavored donut, like repelling a moth with cedar.
summary: A moth-winged coworker is helplessly drawn to any gathering, forcing his colleagues to flee using bait that plays on the insect's weakness.

title: Capturing the Marketing Queen Bee

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm going to capture the Queen Bee of Marketing.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No matter what she says, don't be seduced by her marketing buzz.

transcript.speaker: Assistant
transcript.text: A man with a rope is here to see you. I wasn't loyal enough to stop him.

setting: Marketing department office, in the Queen Bee's lair
situation: Dilbert, carrying a coil of rope, announces he will capture the Queen Bee of Marketing and warns Ratbert not to be swayed by her marketing buzz. In the final panel the Queen Bee, dressed in a bee costume and seated in an armchair, is told by her assistant that a man with a rope is here. The assistant admits he wasn't loyal enough to stop him.
punchline: The queen bee's own underling readily admits he lacks the loyalty to protect her from the person coming to capture her, showing her power rests on hollow allegiance.
summary: A rope-toting engineer sets out to snare the bee-costumed head of marketing, only to find her own staffer gladly waves him through.

title: Hiding Documents Before the ISO Audit

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our annual ISO 9000 audit is next week.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We can pass the audit if we put all of our non-conforming documents in the trunks of our cars.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Doesn't that defeat the purpose of a voluntary audit?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And then torch the cars.

situation: At a meeting, the Boss announces the annual ISO 9000 audit is next week and proposes passing it by stashing all non-conforming documents in the trunks of employees' cars. Dilbert points out this defeats the purpose of a voluntary audit, and the Boss responds by adding that they should then burn the cars to destroy the evidence.
punchline: The Boss treats the audit as something to be gamed rather than a genuine quality check, and escalates from concealing evidence to casually suggesting arson.
summary: A manager's plan to cheat a quality audit by hiding bad paperwork in car trunks escalates into destroying the evidence by fire.

situation: The Boss announces a CEO policy banning coffee from cubicles because it distracts and messes up desks. Alice launches into an angry tirade questioning how the CEO got his job, while Wally and Dilbert treat her outbursts as turn-based entertainment and applaud. When the Boss mentions the CEO also discussed unnecessary expenses, Wally says 'Lucky!' and Dilbert clears his throat, signaling it's his turn to rant.
punchline: Alice's rants are so predictable that her coworkers take turns provoking them like a sport, and they are thrilled at the chance for the next one.
summary: Coworkers treat Alice's furious reactions to dumb management edicts as a rotating spectator sport.

title: Dogbert Autographs Book on Boy

transcript.speaker: Dogbert

transcript.speaker: Dogbert

situation: A young boy runs up to Dogbert asking for an autograph in his book. Dogbert agrees but has the boy lie face down so he can sit on his back and use it as a writing surface. When Dilbert points out the boy has parents, Dogbert keeps writing and decides to personalize the dedication with a different name because the boy's real name is too long.
punchline: Dogbert casually abuses the fan as a desk and ignores the concern about his parents, caring only that the boy's name is too long to write, so he renames him "Allen".
summary: A dog celebrity treats an adoring child as furniture while signing his book, then swaps the kid's name for a shorter one out of sheer convenience.

title: Hammerhead Bob Joins Lunch Uninvited

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Hammerhead Bob

transcript.speaker: Hammerhead Bob
transcript.text: I'll speak louder in case the other tables want in on this.

setting: Office hallway and a restaurant lunch table
situation: Hammerhead Bob, a coworker with a hammerhead-shaped head, invites himself along to lunch with two female colleagues. At the table he lectures them about clean rooms, leaving them slumped and miserable. When they appear uninterested, he responds by raising his voice so nearby tables can hear too.
punchline: Bob is so oblivious to his colleagues' boredom that he interprets their discomfort as a reason to broadcast his tedious lecture to even more unwilling listeners.
summary: A relentlessly dull coworker crashes a lunch outing and responds to his tablemates' glazed expressions by projecting his lecture across the whole restaurant.

file: 1999/1999-07-16_buy island nation_sell a kit_conquermoppress_indigent people_buy rhode island_evil tyrant.gif

In the last panel Dogbert phones in an order for Rhode Island and an Evil Tyrant conquest kit, and the salesperson cheerfully asks if he wants a flag too.
punchline: Buying a country and a tyrant starter kit is treated as a routine retail transaction, complete with a upsell offer for a flag.
summary: Dogbert browses a magazine, discovers that nations and dictator supplies are for sale, and orders both over the phone like an ordinary shopper.

title: Budget Forecast Earns Tiny Guts Insult

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Asok, I've chosen you to put our budget forecast together.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's a hard job, but you'll get the satisfaction of making everyone hate your tiny guts.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: My guts are not tiny.

situation: The Boss assigns Asok, the intern, the task of assembling the department's budget forecast. He cheerfully tells Asok the reward is that everyone will hate him, and adds an insult about his 'tiny guts'. In the last panel Asok silently thinks that his guts are not tiny, offended by the insult rather than the burden.
punchline: Handed a thankless job that will make him widely hated, Asok fixates on the insult about his 'tiny guts' instead of the real problem.
summary: A manager dumps the unpopular budget forecast on a young employee and sneers at his courage, which the employee privately resents.

file: 1999/1999-03-13_all that i can be_exact oposite_holding accountable_vague feeling_dilbert_boss.gif
title: Boss Contradicts Himself, Calls It Accountability

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yesterday you told me to do the exact opposite of what you told me today.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's my way of holding you accountable.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have a vague feeling that I am not being all that I can be.

situation: Dilbert confronts the Boss about giving him instructions that are the exact opposite of what he demanded the day before. The Boss casually claims this is his method of holding Dilbert accountable. Back in his cubicle, Dilbert sits in resigned frustration, pondering his lack of fulfillment.
punchline: The Boss twists his own inconsistent, contradictory orders into a management virtue called accountability, leaving Dilbert with a sardonic sense that he's being wasted.
summary: A manager justifies flip-flopping directives as a deliberate accountability technique, leaving his employee feeling unfulfilled.
keywords: be all that you can be

title: Venture Capitalists Fund Nonexistent Business

transcript.speaker: Venture Capitalist
transcript.text: Wally, we're venture capitalists. We want to invest in your web-based business.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I don't own a web-based business. I'm just an engineer with a cool ponytail.

transcript.speaker: Venture Capitalist
transcript.text: That's good enough for us.

transcript.speaker: Venture Capitalist
transcript.text: We like to get in early.

situation: Two suited venture capitalists approach Wally, holding coffee at his cubicle, and offer to invest in his web-based business. Wally explains he has no business and is merely an engineer with a cool ponytail. The investors happily open a briefcase full of cash anyway, saying that is good enough for them.
punchline: During the dot-com bubble, investors were so eager to fund anything internet-related that they would throw money at someone with no business at all, just because he looked the part.
summary: Eager investors pour cash on an employee who admits he has no company, mocking the reckless funding frenzy of the dot-com boom.

title: Too Late For Internet Idea

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I like your Internet business idea. Let's do it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I sent you that idea a year ago. Since then, five companies have gone IPO in that space.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Can we buy one of them?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If by "one" you mean one share of stock, yes.

situation: The Boss, speaking from off-panel, says he likes Dilbert's Internet business idea and wants to pursue it. Dilbert points out he submitted the idea a year ago and that five companies have since gone public in that market. The Boss asks if the company can simply buy one of them, and Dilbert sarcastically says it can afford a single share.
punchline: The Boss's year-late enthusiasm leaves the company so far behind that the only thing it could realistically buy is one share of stock in a competitor.
summary: After sitting on a staffer's web startup proposal for a year, a manager suddenly wants in, only to discover the market has already been claimed by public companies.

file: 1999/1999-06-26_catbert_evil_director_use the science_determine potential_riding proudly_mighty thoroughbred horse_jockey_saddle.gif

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Saddle.

situation: Catbert, the evil H.R. director, announces he will use face-reading to determine an employee's potential. He shines a flashlight at the man and describes a vision of the man's face riding a thoroughbred horse. The employee hopefully guesses he might be a jockey, but Catbert says his face is the saddle.
punchline: Catbert insults the employee by saying his face is the saddle, meaning his face will be sat on, rather than predicting any glorious future.
summary: A malicious H.R. cat pretends to read an employee's future from his face, then reveals his prospects are to be literally sat upon.

title: Austria or Australia, Who Cares

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Prepare a presentation for our foreign visitors.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: On what topic?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It doesn't matter. I'm told they're from Austria and they only understand their own language.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Or was it Australia?

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle, then a hallway
situation: The Boss orders Dilbert to prepare a presentation for foreign visitors without caring what it is about. He says the visitors are from Austria and only understand their own language. As he walks away, he muses that they might actually be from Australia.
punchline: The Boss is so careless and ignorant that he cannot tell Austria from Australia, and the second-guessing exposes the absurdity of his claim that the visitors speak only their own language.
summary: A manager vaguely assigns a pointless presentation for visitors from a country he cannot even identify correctly.

file: 1999/1999-01-30_biggest customer_missed deadline_overnight mail_evil and lazy_bonus effort_second guess.gif

Alice points out that the Boss himself ordered all overnight mail to go through his evil and lazy secretary, and then sarcastically predicts he will apologize and give her a bonus. summary: A manager pins a lost client on his employee, who traces the failure back to his own mail rule and mockingly predicts a reward that never comes.

title: Attendance Award For Most Absences

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The attendance award goes to Judy for missing the most days.

transcript.speaker: Unidentified coworker
transcript.text: I think we all agree that morale is higher when Judy isn't here.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We took turns coughing on the certificate.

situation: The Boss announces that the attendance award is going to Judy for missing the most days. A coworker says morale is higher when Judy is absent while the others clap, and the Boss then hands her the certificate, admitting the team coughed on it.
punchline: The award is really a passive-aggressive insult, and the coworkers are spreading their germs onto Judy's certificate to show how little they want her around.
summary: A workplace prize for the biggest absentee turns out to be a spiteful gift the staff deliberately contaminated.

title: Boss Hibernation Demands a Number

transcript.text: I need your budget estimate today.

Dilbert explains that the boss goes into a trance until someone states a number, then demonstrates by saying three million dollars and receiving praise. He admits that when he first saw this, he panicked and blurted out a ridiculously low figure.
punchline: Managers don't care whether a budget figure is justified, only that someone says one, so Dilbert's panicked first guess of $911 shows how arbitrary the whole exercise is.
summary: A veteran engineer teaches a newcomer that a frozen manager can be reactivated by any number at all, however made up.

Dilbert points out that he recommended the opposite and accuses the Boss of only hearing what he wants to hear. The Boss, proving the point, responds as if Dilbert had complimented him on looking thinner.
punchline: The Boss's reply about looking thinner shows he misheard Dilbert yet again, hearing a compliment instead of criticism and confirming that he only hears what he wants to hear.
summary: A manager who has done the reverse of his employee's advice then misinterprets the employee's complaint as flattery about his weight.

transcript.text: I'm a step ahead of him - the analysis itself is unnecessary.

situation: The Boss asks Wally whether the analysis due tomorrow is finished, and Wally bluntly says no. He explains he is deliberately waiting until the last minute so the Boss has no time to request changes. The Boss, in a thought bubble, smugly believes he is ahead of Wally because the analysis isn't needed at all.
punchline: Wally's scheme to avoid pointless revisions is trumped by the Boss's realization that the whole analysis is pointless, exposing the needless work Wally is dodging.
summary: An employee admits he is stalling a report to dodge his manager's meddling, only to have the manager privately conclude the report was never needed.

file: 1999/1999-08-18_ten billion dollars_no decorations_walls_cubicle_important today_we both_money for company.gif
title: Billion-Dollar Invention, No Wall Decorations

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your invention will earn ten billion dollars for this company.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: By the way, you're not allowed to have decorations above the walls of your cubicle.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We both did something important today. Give me five.

situation: The Boss examines Dilbert's invention, a small gray electronic device, and tells him it will earn the company ten billion dollars. He then casually reminds Dilbert that cubicle decorations are forbidden, and finishes by claiming they both accomplished something important and asking for a high five. Dilbert stays silent throughout.
punchline: The Boss takes equal credit for Dilbert's multibillion-dollar invention while enforcing a petty cubicle rule, showing how management rewards innovation with nothing but trivial restrictions and a hollow high five.
summary: A manager praises an employee's lucrative invention, lectures him on cubicle decor rules, then treats the day's work as a shared triumph.

file: 1999/1999-10-13_tina tech writer_inventing stories_bizarre workplace crimes_media_kick start_entertainment.gif
title: Tina Invents Workplace Crime Stories

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Tina the Tech Writer

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: I grew tired of writing the same old stories for the newsletter.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: So I started inventing stories of bizarre workplace crimes.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Sometimes we in the media have to give the copycat criminals a little kick-start.

situation: Tina, the tech writer, tells the Boss she got bored writing routine newsletter stories, so she began making up bizarre workplace crimes. The Boss reads a newspaper while she explains. She then adds that the media sometimes need to give copycat criminals a little kick-start.
punchline: Tina cheerfully admits to fabricating crime stories on purpose to inspire real copycat crimes, treating it as a normal part of journalism and showing she is bored and amoral.
summary: A bored newsletter writer confesses she fabricates outlandish office crime stories so that real imitators will follow.

file: 1999/1999-02-08_meeting moth_attracted to meetings_resist the urge_beat myself_senseless_sense off purpose.gif
title: The Meeting Moth's Fatal Attraction

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The "meeting moth" is attracted to all meetings.

transcript.speaker: Meeting Moth
transcript.text: Excuse me. I can't resist the urge to beat myself senseless on your table.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You have to envy his sense of purpose.

situation: A man in moth wings and antennae, the 'meeting moth', walks toward a conference room where a meeting is underway. He politely interrupts the attendees, announces he cannot resist the urge to beat himself senseless on their table, and then slams himself onto it. Wally, watching the spectacle, remarks that you have to envy the moth's sense of purpose.
punchline: Wally sarcastically envies a self-destructive moth for at least having a clear purpose, implying that his own work and meetings have none.
summary: A costumed insect-man is irresistibly drawn to meetings, compelled to bang himself unconscious on the table, while a bystander admires his clarity of mission.

title: Dilbert's Opinion Hits the Boss

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's my opinion.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's my opinion.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Nice try, but I can wipe it off with a damp sponge!!

situation: Dilbert states his opinion, and the speech balloon literally flies across the room and splats onto the Boss's face as he sits behind his desk. The words are plastered across his features, but the Boss calmly claims he can simply wipe it off with a damp sponge.
punchline: The Boss dismisses Dilbert's opinion as something trivial and easily erased, showing he has no intention of taking employee feedback seriously.
summary: A spoken opinion is rendered as a physical object thrown at the boss, who shrugs it off as easily cleaned away.

title: Doctor Prescribes Assisted Suicide Brochure

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Are you saying my job makes me sick?

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: Don't worry. There's a cure.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: Here's a brochure on assisted suicide.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: How do you assist?

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: I gave you the brochure.

situation: Alice, sitting on an exam table, asks her doctor whether her job is making her sick. The doctor says there is a cure and hands her a brochure on assisted suicide. When Alice asks how he would assist, he deadpans that handing her the brochure was his help.
punchline: The doctor's idea of a cure for a job-induced illness is death, and his 'assistance' is nothing more than handing over a pamphlet, mocking both the hopelessness of work and unhelpful professionals.
summary: A patient who suspects her workplace is making her ill is offered a morbid pamphlet as treatment, and the doctor insists that was all the help she'd get.

title: Employee Treated Like Furniture Seeks Help

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: My boss treats me like furniture!

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I'd help you, but it might set a dangerous precedent.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I need a new position.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Have you tried crouching?

situation: An employee, with a lamp strapped to his back like furniture, complains to Catbert, the H.R. director, that his boss treats him like furniture. Catbert refuses to help, citing a dangerous precedent, and then answers the employee's request for a new position with a crude joke about crouching.
punchline: Catbert takes the employee's request for a new job position literally, mocking him by suggesting he try a different physical posture while also showing H.R.'s total indifference to employee complaints.
summary: A man dressed up as a piece of furniture asks the cat running personnel for relief and gets only a pun and a bureaucratic brush-off.

title: Optimism Versus Thirty Failed Attempts

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Here's what I don't understand...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You just asked me to follow a process that has failed thirty times in a row

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And you know it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: At what point can this no longer be called "optimism"?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: When it succeeds?

situation: Dilbert stands before the desk of the horned, pointy-haired manager and complains that he has been told to follow a process that has already failed thirty times, which the manager knows. Dilbert asks when such hopefulness stops being optimism, and the manager calmly replies that it stops when the process finally succeeds.
punchline: The manager redefines optimism so that it only ceases to be optimism if the doomed process works, which dodges the question and shows he has no intention of changing anything.
summary: A frustrated engineer challenges his boss over a repeatedly failing procedure and gets a glib non-answer that keeps the bad process alive.

title: Morale Survey Dismisses Her Complaint

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Tell me what morale issues you have. I'll summarize them under the appropriate categories.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: My managers are incompetent, arrogant, micro-managing misogynists.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's one under "time of month."

situation: The Boss, typing on a laptop, asks Alice to list her morale problems so he can sort them into categories. Alice says her managers are incompetent, arrogant, micromanaging misogynists. The Boss tallies it as a single entry under "time of month," dismissing her complaint with a sexist assumption.
punchline: The Boss proves her point about misogynistic managers by filing her legitimate complaint under "time of month," attributing it to her menstrual cycle.
summary: A manager collecting employee grievances for a morale report responds to a woman's complaint about sexist bosses with a sexist remark, illustrating exactly what she described.

file: 1999/1999-06-03_catbert_evil director_training classes_skilled_better job_secret untraining method_hammer_head_hit on head.gif
title: Catbert Untrains Overskilled Asok

transcript.text: Catbert: Evil H.R. Director

transcript.text: Asok, you have taken too many training classes.

transcript.text: Too many?

transcript.text: You're too skilled now. There's a risk you'll leave for a better job.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Does the "secret untraining method" work every time?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I've never tried it before.

situation: Catbert, acting as the evil H.R. director, tells Asok he has taken too many training classes and is now at risk of leaving for a better job. To prevent this, Catbert prepares to use a 'secret untraining method', which turns out to be hitting a blindfolded Asok on the head with a large mallet. Catbert admits he has never tried it before.
punchline: Rather than rewarding or retaining a skilled employee, the company literally tries to knock the skills out of him, and the 'method' is an untested experiment on Asok.
summary: A malicious personnel chief decides an employee has learned too much to be safe and prepares to bludgeon the knowledge out of him.

file: 1999/1999-09-17_leave so soon_sidewalk is cracking_drainage trench_sump pumps_powder keg_weird yelp.gif
title: Dilbert Warns Mom About Her House

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mom
transcript.text: Thanks for dropping in. Too bad you have to leave so soon.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your sidewalk is cracking. You need to build a drainage trench, with sump pumps.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: When I told her she was living in a powder keg she made a weird yelping sound.

setting: Dilbert's mother's house, at the front door and inside the home
situation: Dilbert's mother pushes him toward the door, thanking him for visiting while clearly eager to get him out. On the way out, Dilbert lectures her that her sidewalk is cracking and she needs a drainage trench with sump pumps. Back home, he tells Dogbert that she yelped when he said she was living in a powder keg.
punchline: Dilbert is oblivious that his catastrophizing, unsolicited home-inspection warnings upset his mother and are why she is rushing him out the door.
summary: A son's visit ends with his mother shoving him out after he frightens her with alarming warnings about her house, and he cannot understand why she was upset.
keywords: too bad you have to leave

title: Boss's Photography Hobby Insult

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Photography is my new hobby.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Click

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you want a picture of me?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, I like to look at them later.

situation: The Boss stands over Dilbert's desk and announces that photography is his new hobby. He snaps a flash photo of Dilbert, who then politely offers to have a picture taken of the Boss. The Boss declines, explaining that he prefers to look at photographs later.
punchline: The Boss's reply implies he doesn't want to look at Dilbert's face in the photo now, so he prefers viewing the prints later, which is an unintentional (or oblivious) insult.
summary: A boss with a new camera snaps a flash photo of an employee, then brushes off the offer of a return portrait with a backhanded remark about viewing pictures afterward.

file: 1999/1999-03-21_big dumb guy_disagree_lazy_habitual liar_excellent track record_excellent work.gif
title: Boss Assigns Alice a Dumb Coworker

transcript.speaker: The Boss

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He's also lazy and a habitual liar.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Then why do you let him work here?!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He has an excellent track record.

transcript.speaker: Big Dumb Guy

transcript.text: Look what I just did.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Excellent work.

transcript.speaker: The Boss

situation: The Boss introduces Alice to a new coworker and cheerfully lists his flaws: he is dumb, lazy, a habitual liar, and will badmouth her if she disagrees. When Alice asks why he's employed, the Boss cites his excellent track record, which even the coworker can't explain. The coworker then shows off a trivial accomplishment and the Boss praises it, while Alice fumes.
punchline: The Boss rewards a clearly incompetent employee with praise for nothing and then smugly tells Alice she can learn from him, mocking her competence and frustration.
summary: A manager pairs a capable engineer with a lazy, lying incompetent whose success nobody can explain, then holds him up as a role model.

file: 1999/1999-12-23_free medical advice_some exercose_lazy hog_wait for ipo.gif
title: Free Medical Website, Instant IPO

situation: Dogbert, seated at a computer, announces he is building a website of free medical advice. He types a single piece of advice, telling the reader to exercise and calling them a lazy hog. Dilbert asks if that's all there is, and Dogbert says the only thing left is to wait for the IPO.
punchline: During the dot-com bubble, a website with almost no content could supposedly become hugely valuable, so Dogbert's one-line site is treated as enough to cash in on an IPO.
summary: A dog posts one insulting sentence as a health website and expects to get rich when the company goes public.

file: 1999/1999-08-27_save money_cut used papaer_little squares_note pads_less than hour_print blank pages.gif
title: Saving Money With Homemade Notepads

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We can save money by cutting used paper into little squares to use as note pads.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I made these in less than one hour.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Not counting the time it took me to print the blank pages.

situation: At a meeting, the Boss proudly proposes cutting used paper into small squares to make free note pads and shows off the stack he made in under an hour. He then admits he did not count the time spent printing blank pages to cut up. Dilbert and a bald coworker sit beside him looking on.
punchline: The Boss's cost-saving idea is self-defeating because he wasted paper, printer resources and his own time printing blank pages, so he saved nothing.
summary: A manager brags about his frugal homemade notepads, then accidentally reveals he created them by printing fresh blank sheets.

title: Denied Raise, Then Told Be Empowered

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I can't give you a raise because you came to work on one of your vacation days.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Employees are not allowed to change vacation days without permission.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: On an unrelated note, try to be more empowered.

situation: Alice stands before the boss's desk asking about a raise. He refuses because she worked on one of her scheduled vacation days, citing a rule that employees can't change vacation days without permission. He then tells her to be more empowered.
punchline: The boss punishes Alice for acting on her own initiative, then immediately demands empowerment, which reveals that his talk of empowerment is hollow and contradicts his own rules.
summary: A manager rejects a raise over an unapproved schedule change and then, with no sense of irony, urges the same employee to show more empowerment.

file: 1999/1999-03-12_astrologer_plotting_rip off_astrologer charging_plotting rip off_hourly billing_prefer to call.gif
title: Astrologer Admits Hourly Billing Rip-Off

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How much is your astrologer charging you?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Are you plotting to rip me off?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I prefer to call it hourly billing.

situation: During a meeting, the Boss announces that his astrologer has warned him someone present is plotting to rip him off. Dilbert asks how much the astrologer charges, and the Boss turns to Dogbert, who is wearing a tall blue astrologer's hat. Dogbert, evidently the astrologer, cheerfully admits to it by calling it hourly billing.
punchline: The astrologer is Dogbert himself, and he is the one ripping the Boss off, which he casually reframes as normal hourly billing.
summary: A gullible manager consults a fortune-telling dog who warns of a swindler and turns out to be the one doing the swindling.

title: Leader Laughing Inside While Listening

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: A good leader listens to his employees...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No matter how much he is laughing on the inside.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe this isn't a good time.

situation: The Boss leans back in his chair and lectures Dilbert, who stands in front of his desk, about what makes a good leader. He adds that a leader keeps listening even when secretly laughing at his employees. In the last panel the Boss looks wide-eyed and tense, and Dilbert decides to leave.
punchline: The Boss unintentionally admits he privately finds his employees' concerns laughable, so Dilbert concludes there's no point raising his issue now.
summary: A manager boasts about listening to staff while mocking them inwardly, which convinces the employee to back off.

file: 1999/1999-03-31_dogberts tech support_hard reboot_listen carefully_rent a van_dynamite_stolen dynamite_main relay station_talk_aim bazooka_van.gif

His instructions escalate into renting a van, filling it with stolen dynamite and parking it near the power company's relay station. Dilbert walks up wanting to talk while Dogbert continues instructing the caller to aim a bazooka at the van.
punchline: Dogbert's idea of a hard reboot is literally cutting power by blowing up the electrical grid, a ridiculous and criminal overreaction to a simple computer problem.
summary: A tech support dog answers a computer problem by walking a customer through a plan to blow up the local power infrastructure.

punchline: The Boss confidently insists he knows engineering better than Dilbert, yet he cannot tell a project timeline chart from a circuit design, proving his authority is based on rank rather than knowledge.
summary: A manager who cannot even identify what is on the screen claims his job title makes him the superior technical expert.

file: 1999/1999-01-06_celebrate service reps_exceptional customer service_emplyees_extra pay_smart employees_someday.gif

situation: The Boss announces that employees who provide exceptional customer service will now be celebrated. Dilbert raises his hand and asks why the company would celebrate people who do extra work without extra pay. The Boss says it will make them happy, and an off-panel voice asks if the smart employees can be celebrated some day.
punchline: The smart employees are the ones who refuse to do unpaid extra work, so they are the ones who never get celebrated, implying that management rewards gullibility with praise instead of money.
summary: A manager promises recognition for staff who go above and beyond, and the sharper workers point out that applause is a poor substitute for a raise.

punchline: Wally normally has to fake working whenever someone approaches, so being ordered to do nothing is a dream come true for him.
summary: A manager's order to hold off on work lets the perpetually lazy Wally stop pretending to be busy.

file: 1999/1999-02-18_unprofessional_thirty minutes_six minutes_too professional_death to those who eat.gif

summary: A manager's lunch-length rule gets one-upped by an overzealous employee until even the manager thinks it's too much.

file: 1999/1999-12-30_concludes one hour course_pick up diploma_laser printer_fill in name_prestigious_dont discuss.gif

situation: Dogbert, acting as an instructor, wraps up a one-hour executive MBA course. The chalkboard behind him lists lessons like 'Be boring,' 'Money equals good,' and 'Remember to embezzle!' summary: A scheming dog ends a ridiculously brief business-school class by letting students print their own diplomas and swearing them to secrecy.

situation: Wally eats lunch with Dilbert and Asok and announces that his long-term career plan is to drift into a job where he has no impact on anything. punchline: Wally's cheerful lack of ambition was so dispiriting that Asok lost the will to even swallow his food and choked on it.
summary: A coworker's cheerfully hopeless career outlook leaves a nearby colleague so drained of motivation that he nearly dies at lunch.

summary: A notoriously lazy employee complains to his manager about being pressured to work, then cites the manager's own reminder of his duties as proof.

title: Forgotten in Org-Limbo
