transcript.text: Forgotten in the reorganization plan, I exist in org-limbo.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: The normal people can't see me or hear me.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Sometimes the unassigned have unfinished business. I can see them.

setting: Office hallway and the Boss's office
situation: Tina, with arms outstretched, narrates in thought bubbles that she was left out of the reorganization plan and now exists in 'org-limbo', invisible to coworkers who walk right past her. In the last panel, Dogbert, wearing a bandage-like wrap on his head, stands on the Boss's desk and claims he can see the unassigned, as if they were ghosts.
punchline: Employees left off the reorg chart are treated like ghosts, and Dogbert plays a medium who can see them, mocking how reorganizations erase people from the company.
summary: An employee overlooked in a corporate restructuring becomes a ghost-like presence nobody notices, until Dogbert claims he can see her.

title: Dogbert Diagnoses Elbow Injury Absurdly

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Doctor Dogbert

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I hurt my elbow, doctor.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Let me see it.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I recommend a career in marketing.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And it's not a good idea to vote.

situation: Dogbert, wearing a crown and a stethoscope as Doctor Dogbert, is told by a patient that he hurt his elbow. Dogbert asks to see it, and the patient bends over and pulls his pants down, mistaking the request or presenting the wrong body part. Dogbert then reads from a clipboard and recommends a career in marketing and advises against voting.
punchline: After examining the patient's bare backside, Dogbert's verdict is that the man should go into marketing and shouldn't vote, implying he is a complete ass.
summary: A man shows his bare rear to a doctor who was only asked to inspect an injured arm, and the doctor's diagnosis amounts to calling him a jerk.

file: 1999/1999-06-07_talk now wally_meet deadline_poor planning_nicknames for cofee_java wave_bean brew.gif
title: Wally Mocks Alice's Deadline Panic

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I can't talk now, Wally. I'm rushing to meet my deadline.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Sounds like poor planning. Why must I suffer?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Do you mind if I stay here and think up new nicknames for coffee?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Java-wava... Bean brew...

situation: Alice is typing frantically at her computer and tells Wally she has no time to chat because of a deadline. Wally, holding his coffee mug, responds that her rush is the result of poor planning and complains that her problem is somehow making him suffer. He then asks to loiter at her desk while he invents silly nicknames for coffee, as Alice glares in anger.
punchline: Wally turns Alice's deadline crisis into his own inconvenience, then adds insult to injury by idly hanging around her desk making up coffee nicknames while she works.
summary: A stressed coworker racing to finish her work is lectured and then loitered over by a lazy colleague who cares only about his own annoyance.

title: Wally Angrily Identifies Problems, Fixes Nothing

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Someone should take care of that problem!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You could take care of it.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I can't do everything.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You don't do anything.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Not a single thing.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It's my job to angrily identify problems.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That is not your job!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Everything is so ambiguous here!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Someone should take care of that problem!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Is it just me, or is this meeting taking forever?

situation: In a meeting, Wally complains that someone should fix a problem, and Dilbert suggests he do it himself. Wally insists his job is to angrily identify problems, and the Boss tries to correct him. The Boss then complains about the ambiguity and the slow meeting, doing the very thing he just criticized.
punchline: The Boss tells Wally that angrily identifying problems isn't his job, then immediately does exactly that himself, complaining about ambiguity and a slow meeting without fixing anything.
summary: A lazy employee claims his role is merely to rage about issues, and the manager who scolds him promptly does the same thing.

file: 1999/1999-12-26_totally correct_time under budget_give up features_shoebox falloff yarn_yarn is free_open door policy_serious threat_new design.gif
title: Shoebox Full of Yarn Design

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You were totally correct.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We can develop the product on time and under budget.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: All we have to do is give up some features.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: For example, the original design called for a scalable wide area network switch...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...with multi-protocol support and full network diagnostics.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The new design calls for a shoebox full of yarn.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So we're in good shape.. Assuming yarn is free.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're a serious threat to my open door policy.

situation: Dilbert visits the Boss and tells him he was right that the product can ship on time and under budget, as long as some features are dropped. Dilbert explains that the sophisticated network switch has been replaced by a shoebox full of yarn, and the Boss only worries about whether yarn is free. The Boss then complains that Dilbert's visits threaten his open door policy.
punchline: The Boss accepts an absurdly gutted design as long as the budget works, and then blames Dilbert for making him regret keeping his door open.
summary: An engineer cheerfully reports that a sophisticated networking product can meet its deadline by swapping the hardware for craft supplies, and his manager only cares about the cost.

file: 1999/1999-02-23_salary budget_shouldn't have hired_furniture budget_credenza_lamp_operates as credenza.gif
title: Hired Yesterday, Now a Credenza

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Allen, I have to cut the salary budget. I probably shouldn't have hired you yesterday.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Luckily, I have extra money in the furniture budget.

transcript.speaker: Allen
transcript.text: As God is my witness, someday I will be a credenza.

situation: The Boss tells Allen, a new employee hired just yesterday, that the salary budget has to be cut and he probably shouldn't have hired him. He then notes that there is spare money in the furniture budget. In the last panel Allen is on all fours with a lamp on his back, serving as a piece of office furniture, and thinks he will someday be a credenza.
punchline: Because furniture money is available while salary money is not, the employee is effectively kept on as office furniture, and his dream is to be promoted to an actual credenza.
summary: A freshly hired worker is told there's no payroll money for him but plenty for furniture, so he ends up serving as a lamp table and aspires to rise to credenza status.

title: The Boss Thinks in French

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I speak English but I think in French.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Someday I'll take French lessons to find out what the heck I'm thinking.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Croissant.

situation: The Boss sits at his desk and tells his assistant Carol that he speaks English but thinks in French. He adds that he will take French lessons someday to learn what he is actually thinking. In the last panel Carol walks away and thinks the only French word she can come up with.
punchline: Carol's silent thought, 'Croissant', shows she finds the Boss's claim absurd and reduces his supposed French thinking to the one French word everybody knows.
summary: A manager boasts about a bilingual mind he doesn't really have, and his assistant privately mocks him with a pastry.

title: Farmer Tends the Cube Farm

transcript.speaker: Farmer
transcript.text: My cube farm has an excellent crop this year.

transcript.speaker: Farmer
transcript.text: Here you go, fella. This will fatten you up.

transcript.speaker: Farmer
transcript.text: If you ever need salt, just lick this pretzel stick.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Mmm... ooh!

situation: A farmer in overalls and a pitchfork walks through the cubicles as if they were a literal farm, talking about his 'crop' of cubicle workers. He tosses food to Dilbert with the pitchfork to fatten him up and then holds up a pretzel stick for Dilbert to lick for salt, treating him like livestock.
punchline: The joke takes the 'cube farm' nickname literally, with office workers being tended like livestock, and Dilbert goes along with it by enjoying the feed.
summary: A pitchfork-wielding farmer tends his field of cubicles and feeds the employee inside like a farm animal.

title: Tech Support Superior Religious Debate

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Finally!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've been in the tech support queue for an hour!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Loser.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can I speak to your superior?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: There's some religious debate on that question.

setting: Dilbert's cubicle and Dogbert's tech support desk, connected by phone
situation: Dilbert finally reaches tech support after an hour in the queue. The support agent, Dogbert wearing a headset, insults him as a loser. When Dilbert asks to speak to a superior, Dogbert replies that there is religious debate over whether anyone is superior to him.
punchline: Dogbert, as an arrogant tech support agent, implies that no one is truly his superior, framing the question as a theological controversy.
summary: After a long wait for help, a caller is insulted by the support agent and then told that the existence of any higher authority is a matter of faith.

file: 1999/1999-09-12_relocatating_better cubicle_team of movers_boxed possessions_undisclosed location_laminate company id.gif
title: Fired Coworker Misreads His Dismissal

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'm relocating to a better cubicle.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Tonight a team of movers will take my boxed possessions to an undisclosed location.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: They're also going to laminate my company I.D.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'm supposed to leave it with the guard on the way out.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: And I got paid two days early!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: It's all because management appreciated the constructive criticism I posted on the message board.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: As I hoped, my condescending tone helped them to see their folly.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you mind if I rifle through your boxes and take office supplies?

situation: A cheerful coworker tells Dilbert he is being moved to a better cubicle, listing signs like movers taking his boxes to an undisclosed location, handing his ID to the guard on the way out, and getting paid early. He believes management loved his critical message board post. Dilbert recognizes he has been fired and asks to take his office supplies.
punchline: The coworker is obliviously describing his own termination as a reward, while Dilbert opportunistically asks to loot his desk supplies.
summary: A man proudly narrates what are clearly the standard steps of being laid off, convinced it is a promotion, while Dilbert quietly eyes his stationery.

title: Dilbert Calls Dogbert's Bathrobe Bluff

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll give you a million dollars if you go to work like that.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll call your bluff. I'm doing it. I'm going right now!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Go ahead!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Tonight I expect a long debate over the exact definition of "go to work like that."

setting: Dilbert's kitchen table at home, morning
situation: Dogbert sits on the kitchen table and bets Dilbert a million dollars that he won't go to work dressed as he is, in a bathrobe over breakfast. Dilbert accepts the challenge and announces he is leaving right now. Dogbert, unbothered, thinks ahead to the argument that will follow over what the bet actually meant.
punchline: Dogbert never intended to pay up; he is already planning to weasel out of the bet by quibbling over the wording of the terms.
summary: A wager over wearing a robe to the office is met with confidence from one side and a cynical plan to dispute the rules from the other.

file: 1999/1999-02-22_sacrificial lamb_head count vacancy_budget cut_shake hands_get attached.gif
title: Hiring a Sacrificial Lamb Employee

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, meet our new sacrificial lamb.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I filled our headcount vacancy so we have someone to dump after the next budget cut.

transcript.speaker: New Employee
transcript.text: Should we shake hands?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't want to get attached.

situation: The Boss introduces Dilbert to a smiling new hire, openly calling him the sacrificial lamb. He explains the position was filled only so there would be someone to lay off at the next budget cut. The naive new employee asks whether they should shake hands, and Dilbert declines to avoid getting emotionally attached.
punchline: Dilbert coldly refuses to befriend the new hire because he is already doomed to be laid off, highlighting how disposable employees are to management.
summary: A manager cheerfully presents a fresh recruit hired purely to be fired later, and Dilbert keeps his distance so he won't mourn the loss.

file: 1999/1999-03-14_dogcart wrecking company_special_srushing_new car_parking lot_cost_monthly plan_free model of car_crush little one_crush boss car.gif
title: Dogbert Wrecks the Boss's Car

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm from the Dogbert Wrecking Company.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm running a special on crushing your boss's new car in the parking lot.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: What does it cost?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The first one is free.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: If you're satisfied, I hope you'll consider my monthly plan.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: It's the red one. He brags about it every day.

transcript.speaker: Car Dealer
transcript.text: And when you spend that much, the dealer gives you a free model of your car!

transcript.speaker: Unknown
transcript.text: Beep beep beep

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: And next month can you crush the little one on his desk too?

setting: Office cubicle and parking lot view
situation: Dogbert, wearing a hard hat, visits an office worker offering to crush the boss's new car in the parking lot, with the first crushing free. The worker eagerly points out the boss's red car, which he brags about daily. Dogbert then upsells a monthly plan, and the worker pays and asks him to crush the boss's model car on his desk next.
punchline: Dogbert parodies the drug-dealer 'first one is free' hook and monthly-subscription upselling, while the employee's revenge on the bragging boss escalates into an addictive habit, even extending to the toy model car.
summary: A demolition-minded dog hooks a resentful worker on a subscription service for destroying his braggart boss's prized possessions.

file: 1999/1999-07-06_strategic plan_everyone supports_a way to copy_images_piece of paper.gif
title: Strategic Plan, No Copier Available

transcript.speaker: Old Bearded Employee
transcript.text: I did it!

transcript.speaker: Old Bearded Employee
transcript.text: It's a strategic technology plan that everyone supports.

transcript.speaker: Old Bearded Employee
transcript.text: If only there were a way to copy images from one piece of paper onto many.

situation: A long-bearded old employee triumphantly announces he has finished a strategic technology plan that everyone supports, while a big-haired coworker listens. He then laments that he has no way to distribute it, wishing for a way to copy images from one paper onto many.
punchline: The company's strategic technology plan is a single sheet of paper that cannot be shared because nobody has a photocopier, mocking how out of touch the organization's technology really is.
summary: A man who has just completed his company's technology strategy realizes it exists on one sheet of paper and wistfully wishes copying machines existed.

file: 1999/1999-06-09_lawsuit_against company_truth_usual engineering_no one understands_whistleblower_sound the same.gif
title: Testify Truthfully, But Incomprehensibly

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, I'd like you to testify in the lawsuit against our company.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Tell the truth, but do it in your usual engineering way so that no one understands you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Actually, I've decided to be a whistleblower.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Whatever. It'll all sound the same!

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert to testify in a lawsuit against the company, instructing him to tell the truth but in his usual confusing engineering manner so nobody can follow it. Dilbert responds that he has decided to become a whistleblower, and the Boss shrugs it off, confident it will all sound the same.
punchline: The Boss is so sure engineers are incomprehensible that he believes even whistleblowing testimony will be harmless, since no one will understand what Dilbert says.
summary: A manager sends his engineer to court counting on technobabble to hide the truth, and even a threatened whistleblowing doesn't worry him.

title: Strategic Planning: Illusion of Knowledge

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our executives have started their annual strategic planning sessions.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This involves sitting in a room with inadequate data until an illusion of knowledge is attained.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Then we'll reorganize, because that's all we know how to do!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Have you tried it with a magazine?

situation: The Boss explains to Wally and Dilbert how the executives conduct their annual strategic planning sessions. He describes it as sitting in a room with too little data until they feel they understand things, after which they reorganize. Wally responds by asking whether he has tried doing it with a magazine.
punchline: Wally sarcastically suggests that the executives could just read a magazine for their strategy, implying that their planning is no better than skimming a trendy publication and that reorganizing is their only real skill.
summary: A manager cheerfully admits that executive planning means guessing with poor information and then shuffling the org chart, and a coworker quips that a magazine would work just as well.

file: 1999/1999-12-19_laptop computer_order for me_tech seminar_hawaii_sign up_four day weekend_eat catepillar_recognize pattern_copies everything_boss.gif
title: Boss Answers No But Delegates

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: May I get a laptop computer?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, but you can order one for me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: May I go to this technical seminar in Hawaii?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, but you can sign me up for it.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: May I take this Friday off so I have a four day weekend?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, but you can sit in for me while I take that Friday off.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: May I eat this caterpillar?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Give me that.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hope they never recognize the pattern.

situation: Employees take turns asking the Boss for a perk: a laptop, a trip to a Hawaii seminar, a Friday off. Each time he refuses but then redirects the benefit to himself, making them order the laptop, sign him up, and cover his shift. When Wally asks to eat a caterpillar, the Boss grabs it too, then privately hopes nobody spots the pattern.
punchline: The Boss denies every request only to claim the benefit for himself, and even takes a caterpillar, while hoping his staff never notices his selfish pattern.
summary: A manager turns down each worker's perk request but shamelessly appropriates every one of them for his own use.

title: Boss's Brain Pops Over Bad Numbers

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If your numbers are correct, my strategic plan is irrational.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Cognitive dissonance takes over

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Spoink

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You sure are bad with numbers.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What was that noise?

situation: The Boss reads Dilbert's numbers and realizes that if they are accurate, his own strategic plan makes no sense. His mind briefly snaps with a 'spoink' sound, and he then concludes that Dilbert must simply be bad with numbers. Dilbert is left puzzled by the strange noise.
punchline: Rather than accept that his plan is flawed, the Boss's brain literally short-circuits and blames the person who supplied the facts.
summary: Confronted with data that contradicts his grand plan, a manager's mind pops and he decides the messenger must be wrong.

title: Delegator Trades Work for Haircut

transcript.speaker: Juan Delegator
transcript.text: My name is Juan Delegator. I bring you an assignment.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This is YOUR assignment. You're trying to get me to do your work.

transcript.speaker: Juan Delegator
transcript.text: Teamwork!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well, I guess I could do you a favor.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And I wouldn't say no to a haircut.

situation: A coworker introduces himself as Juan Delegator and hands Dilbert an assignment. Dilbert points out it is really the coworker's own work being dumped on him, and the coworker defends it as teamwork. Dilbert then agrees to do the favor, and the coworker pulls out scissors, implying he will cut Dilbert's hair in return.
punchline: The coworker's 'teamwork' pitch is a thin excuse for offloading his job, and the strip ends with an odd, mismatched trade of a haircut for work that exposes the absurdity of the arrangement.
summary: A man with a conveniently descriptive name tries to pass off his own task as collaboration, then offers a grooming service as payment.

file: 1999/1999-10-16_two more people_enough direct reports_vice president title_strategy.gif
title: Boss Cuts Training for Title

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If I eliminate the training budget, I can afford to hire two more people.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Then I'll have enough direct reports to get a vice president title.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Shouldn't we have a strategy?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I have one. Thanks for asking.

situation: The Boss sits at his desk in thought bubbles, planning to scrap the training budget so he can hire two more people. More direct reports will qualify him for a vice president title. Dilbert asks whether the company shouldn't have a strategy, and the Boss cheerfully says he already has one.
punchline: The Boss's only 'strategy' is a self-serving plan to inflate his headcount and win a promotion, at the expense of employee training and any real company direction.
summary: A manager secretly schemes to trade away staff development for a bigger team and a loftier title, then claims that's his strategy.

title: Employee Names Make Hat Comfortable

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Write on a scrap of paper the names of employees who do great work and put them in the hat in my office.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: And then do you select one name each week to receive valuable rewards?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, the scraps of paper make my hat more comfortable.

situation: The Boss tells employees to write the names of high performers on scraps of paper and put them in the hat in his office. Asok eagerly asks whether a name is drawn weekly to win a valuable reward. The Boss reveals the paper is only there to pad his hat.
punchline: The employee recognition program is a sham, since the scraps of paper exist only to cushion the boss's hat and no rewards are ever given.
summary: A manager dreams up a suggestion-box style scheme that turns out to be pure stuffing for his headwear rather than any real incentive.

file: 1999/1999-05-06_reliable computer_use software_poing a spoon_hole in back_doing it worng.gif
title: Spoon-Restart Computer Sales Pitch

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: This is our most reliable computer, unless you try to use software.

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: It'll freeze several times a day. But you can restart it by poking a spoon into a hole in the back.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Has that ever worked?

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: We think people are doing it wrong.

situation: A computer salesman pitches a machine to an older female customer holding a purse. He admits it only works if you avoid using software, freezes several times a day, and must be restarted by poking a spoon into a hole in the back. When she asks if that has ever worked, he says they think people are doing it wrong.
punchline: The salesman blames users rather than the obviously defective product, and the absurd spoon-restart remedy has never actually worked.
summary: A shopper learns a store's flagship computer is flaky and needs utensil-based rebooting, and the clerk blames customers when the fix fails.

file: 1999/1999-11-19_dilbert and mother_watching_web cam_not working hard_fire wall_using mail server.gif
title: Mom Hacks Dilbert's Firewall for Mahjongg

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: RRRING

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mother
transcript.text: I've been watching you through your web cam and I don't think you're working hard enough.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mother
transcript.text: Well, it wasn't much of a fire wall. I'm using your mail server to spam my mah-jongg club.

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle, and his mother's living room
situation: Dilbert's phone rings at his desk and his mother, sitting in an armchair with a laptop, tells him she has been spying on him through his web cam and thinks he isn't working hard enough. When he apparently objects that his computer is protected, she casually replies that his firewall was weak and she is now using his mail server to spam her mah-jongg club.
punchline: A sweet elderly mother has casually broken through the corporate firewall, is spying on her son at work, and is misusing his company's mail server for trivial spam, showing how weak the security is.
summary: A nagging mom spies on her son through his webcam, then cheerfully admits she cracked his security to send junk mail to her game club.

title: Skills Database Is Step Two

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I'm starting an employee skills database.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Question: Is this the first step in moving everyone to jobs they don't want?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: No, no, no...

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: The first step was when I laughed myself fuzzy thinking about it.

situation: Catbert, the evil H.R. director, announces to a meeting that he is starting an employee skills database. Dilbert raises his hand and suspects it is the first step in reassigning everyone to jobs they don't want. Catbert corrects him, saying the real first step was laughing gleefully at the idea.
punchline: Catbert gleefully confirms Dilbert's suspicion by saying the first step of his malicious plan was laughing himself fuzzy at the thought of it.
summary: A sinister HR cat unveils a skills database, and when challenged about his motives, he cheerfully admits the scheme began with cackling over the misery it would cause.

file: 1999/1999-12-16_blood pressure screening_below company average_get away with.gif
title: Low Blood Pressure Earns More Work

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Free blood pressure screening today

transcript.speaker: Nurse

transcript.speaker: The Boss

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How long did you think you could get away with that?

setting: Company blood pressure screening station in an office
situation: A nurse takes Dilbert's blood pressure at a free workplace screening while the Boss waits behind him. The Boss, who has been watching the reading, announces that Dilbert is below the company average and hands him a stack of extra work. As they walk away, the Boss asks how long Dilbert thought he could get away with it.
punchline: The Boss treats a healthy, low blood pressure reading as proof that Dilbert isn't working hard or stressed enough, so he punishes him with more work.
summary: A routine health check becomes a pretext for management to pile extra tasks on an employee whose stress level is deemed too low.

title: Free Tissues for Ungrateful Engineers

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: May I have a tissue?

transcript.speaker: Secretary
transcript.text: No!

transcript.speaker: Secretary
transcript.text: Why should the low-paid secretary provide free tissues to engineers?

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: Hey, free tissues!

transcript.speaker: Secretary
transcript.text: Gaaa!

situation: Dilbert asks the secretary at her desk for a tissue and she angrily refuses, ranting about being low-paid while supplying free tissues to engineers. As she complains, another engineer walks up, points at the box and cheerfully takes advantage of the free tissues, leaving her fuming.
punchline: The secretary's tirade about being underpaid and exploited is completely ignored by an engineer who only hears the words 'free tissues'.
summary: A resentful secretary protests handing out supplies to engineers, only for a clueless colleague to latch onto the freebie and ignore her complaint.

title: Boss Hides Meeting Flaws Until Review

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Meet with our vendor and come up with a plan. I'll do the same with their executives.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can you see any reason why my meeting might be a complete waste of time?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Sure, lots of them, but I'm planning to spring those on you during your performance review.

situation: The Boss instructs Dilbert to meet with a vendor and develop a plan while the Boss meets with the vendor's executives. Dilbert asks whether the Boss sees any reason his meeting might be a waste of time. The Boss cheerfully admits there are many but is saving them for Dilbert's performance review.
punchline: The Boss knows Dilbert's assignment is likely pointless but withholds that candor so he can use the flaws against Dilbert in his performance review instead of helping him now.
summary: A manager assigns a vendor meeting, then admits he foresees plenty of problems but is holding them back to criticize his employee later.

file: 1999/1999-01-12_middle aged guy_bad hair_hair in pnytail_coolest guy_office_raising bar.gif
title: Wally's Ponytail Makes Him Cool

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Watch this, Asok. I start out looking like a middle-aged guy with bad hair ...

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: But simply by putting my hair in a ponytail, I transform into...

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: The coolest guy in the office.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Curse you for raising the bar for us all!

situation: Wally, lounging in his chair, tells Asok to watch while he demonstrates a transformation. He gathers his thinning hair into a ponytail and declares himself the coolest guy in the office. Asok, rather than mocking him, grudgingly accepts it and complains that Wally has raised the standard.
punchline: Wally's pathetic little ponytail is treated as genuine coolness, and Asok's bitter reaction implies that the office's standard for cool is so low that even Wally clears it.
summary: A balding, slouching coworker ties up his sparse hair and proudly crowns himself the office's coolest man, leaving a younger colleague resentful.

file: 1999/1999-05-14_enable intergration_okay to do nothing_redesign processes_resources and tools_wally and boss.gif
title: Is It Okay To Do Nothing?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We'll redesign our processes to enable enterprise integration of knowledge resources and tools.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Question: Is it okay if I do nothing?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Well, excuse me for making a suggestion.

setting: Conference room during a team meeting
situation: The Boss announces a grand initiative to redesign processes for enterprise integration of knowledge resources and tools. Wally raises his hand and asks whether he is allowed to do nothing. The Boss flatly says no, and Wally sarcastically replies as though he had been offering a helpful idea.
punchline: Wally treats his habitual laziness as a constructive suggestion and acts offended when the Boss rejects it, while the Boss's buzzword-laden plan is met with the only reaction it deserves.
summary: Faced with a jargon-heavy corporate overhaul, Wally asks permission to do nothing, gets refused, and feigns hurt feelings.
keywords: excuse me for making a suggestion

file: 1999/1999-07-04_finish project_on time_geta better boss_better project_weeks of confsuion_no work_less work_morale up.gif
title: Boss Threatens Job Loss, Team Cheers

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If you don't finish the project on time, I'll probably lose my job.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What would happen to us?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: We would get a better boss.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: We might get a better project too!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: There could be weeks of confusion with no work at all!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: YAY!!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: It's all ours if we simply do less work!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Whoo! I've never felt my morale go up before.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm dizzy.

setting: Conference room during a project meeting
situation: The Boss warns his team that missing the project deadline could cost him his job, hoping to motivate them. Instead, the employees realize his firing would mean a better boss, a better project, and weeks of chaos with no work. They cheer and decide to deliberately do less work, while the Boss grows dizzy and swears.
punchline: The Boss's threat to motivate the team backfires because his employees would be happy to see him fired and see missing the deadline as a reward rather than a risk.
summary: A manager's attempt to guilt his staff into hitting a deadline backfires when they celebrate the prospect of his dismissal and decide to slack off.

title: Diagnosis: Bad Case of Job

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I feel sick every morning.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: All day long, I feel like either crying or punching people.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: You've got a bad case of mahjobis crappus.

situation: Alice sits on an exam table and tells a doctor she feels sick every morning and spends the day wanting to either cry or punch people. The doctor listens with a stethoscope, then writes on a clipboard and announces a made-up Latin-sounding diagnosis.
punchline: The fake Latin diagnosis "mahjobis crappus" is a pun meaning "my job is crap," implying that her illness is simply caused by her miserable workplace.
summary: A distressed woman describes her daily misery to a doctor, who diagnoses it with a pseudo-Latin name that really just blames her lousy job.

file: 1999/1999-06-20_catbert_evil director_new engineer_cheap_huge raise_under budget_static electricity_fuzzy cute_dead now.gif
title: Catbert's Cheap Engineer Gets Zapped

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil Director of Human Resources

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I hired a new engineer for your project.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: He's never been an engineer before.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: But you're an engineer, so how hard could it be?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: And he's cheap! I'll get a huge raise for being under budget.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: And your project will fail! Ha ha ha ha!

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Uh-oh. I laughed myself full of static electricity.

transcript.speaker: New Engineer
transcript.text: Fuzzy. Cute.

transcript.speaker: Sound Effect
transcript.text: ZAP!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He's dead. Now what?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I guess you'll have to drag him to meetings.

situation: Catbert tells Dilbert he hired a cheap new engineer with no engineering experience for Dilbert's project, so Catbert can earn a raise for coming in under budget and watch the project fail. Catbert laughs so hard he builds up static electricity, and when the naive engineer reaches out to pet him, he is electrocuted. Dilbert notes the engineer is dead, and Catbert suggests dragging the corpse to meetings.
punchline: The unqualified hire is killed by Catbert's static shock, but the callous Catbert suggests the corpse can still be useful by attending meetings, implying meeting attendance requires no actual life or contribution.
summary: A scheming HR cat saddles an engineering team with an unqualified bargain hire, then accidentally zaps the poor guy dead and shrugs it off.

file: 1999/1999-07-24_new software_gently warm_key board_easier_laptop lighter_market driven_create diversion.gif
title: Market Driven Absurd Product Pitch

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our new software will gently warm your keyboard so the keys are easier to press.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We'll bundle it with our software that makes your laptop lighter.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: In a word, we have become "market driven."

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Create a diversion. I'll run for help.

setting: Conference room during a product presentation
situation: The Boss presents ridiculous new software features, claiming a program can warm a keyboard so the keys are easier to press and another can make a laptop lighter. He declares the company has become market driven. A bald coworker at the table, scared by the nonsense, asks Dilbert to create a diversion so he can escape and get help.
punchline: The product ideas are so physically impossible and absurd that a coworker treats the boss's 'market driven' pitch as a crisis requiring rescue.
summary: A manager unveils impossible software that heats keyboards and lightens laptops, leaving a listener desperate to flee for help.

title: Catbert Mauls Mordac, Dilbert Gloats

transcript.speaker: Mordac
transcript.text: I am Mordac, the Preventer of Information Services!

transcript.speaker: Mordac
transcript.text: I'll take your computer and your little P.D.A. too!

transcript.speaker: Mordac
transcript.text: Do you recognize this?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Aaagh! That's my network cable!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What do you want from me?!

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Mordac, it is I, Catbert, the evil Director of Human Resources!

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: You made my personal printer a shared device!

transcript.speaker: Mordac
transcript.text: Grrrr!! Aaagh!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Two wrongs made a right.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Welcome to my reality.

situation: Mordac, the head of Information Services, barges into Dilbert's cubicle to confiscate his computer and PDA, and cuts his network cable while Dilbert pleads for mercy. Catbert, the evil HR director, then leaps onto Mordac and mauls him in revenge for turning his personal printer into a shared device. Dilbert calmly watches the carnage.
punchline: Dilbert is delighted that two tyrannical bullies destroy each other, and the line 'two wrongs made a right' sums up his satisfaction at seeing the usual oppressors get a taste of their own medicine.
summary: Two petty corporate tyrants settle their own grudge in a savage fight, sparing the hapless engineer who was their target.

file: 1999/1999-07-03_dogberts tech support_upgrade software_old software_back up data_delete it yourself.gif
title: Dogbert's No-Win Tech Support

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert's Tech Support

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: If you upgrade your software, all of your data will be lost.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: But if you don't upgrade, the old software will corrupt your data one bit at a time.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And if you try to back up your data, our software will hunt you down and bit-slap you until you delete it yourself!

setting: Dogbert's tech support call desk, with a headset, monitor and keyboard
situation: Dogbert, working a tech support line with a headset on, advises a caller about their software options. Every choice he lists leads to data loss: upgrading wipes the data, not upgrading slowly corrupts it, and attempting a backup triggers a violent software response.
punchline: Tech support offers a series of lose-lose options, ending with backup software that attacks users until they destroy their own data, mocking buggy software and unhelpful support.
summary: A smug tech support dog explains that every possible way of handling your files ends with your data destroyed.

title: Designing an Inhumane Call Center

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Designing a call center

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If the employees get this volume of calls per day they will wish they were dead.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But they won't be dead, just too beaten-down to look for better jobs.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't know how to make it any more inhumane.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We can punish them for not being cheerful.

situation: Dilbert and the Boss are planning the design of a call center. Dilbert calmly explains that the call volume will be so high employees will wish they were dead, but will be too worn down to seek other jobs. When Dilbert runs out of ideas to make it crueler, the Boss suggests punishing workers who aren't cheerful.
punchline: Even after designing a deliberately soul-crushing workload, management finds a way to be crueler by demanding employees stay cheerful or be punished.
summary: Two men plotting a call center openly engineer misery for the staff, and the boss tops it off with a penalty for unhappiness.

file: 1999/1999-04-25_managing by analogies_dogbert presents_distribution problem_eskimos_gather ice_lean summer months_eat penguins_hibachi_ban for life.gif
title: Managing by Flawed Eskimo Analogies

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert presents

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Managing by analogies

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's easy!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We'll solve our distribution problem the Eskimo way.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Huh?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The Eskimos gather ice all winter long.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Later, during the lean summer months, the Eskimos eat the ice they stored.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We'll do the same thing!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But... the Eskimos would starve if they only ate ice.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe they eat penguins too.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: They're delicious.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Did you know that the zoo can ban you for life if they catch you using a hibachi?

setting: Office meeting at a desk, with a Dogbert-presented title panel
situation: Under the banner of Dogbert's 'Managing by Analogies', the Boss proposes solving a distribution problem by copying how Eskimos stockpile ice in winter and eat it in summer. Dilbert points out that Eskimos would starve on ice alone. The Boss tries to patch the analogy with penguins, then drifts into an anecdote about being banned from the zoo for cooking with a hibachi.
punchline: The Boss's analogy collapses under the slightest scrutiny, and rather than admit it he rambles about eating penguins and a zoo ban, implying he has personally tried cooking zoo animals.
summary: A manager's folksy ice-hoarding analogy for a business problem falls apart when questioned, ending in an unhinged confession about barbecuing zoo penguins.

title: Demonizing Call Center Employees Before Mistreating

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've been ordered to build a company call center with inhumane working conditions for the employees.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But I don't feel guilty because I'm only acting under orders.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And maybe they did something to deserve it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I might need your help to demonize them.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm all over it.

setting: Dilbert's kitchen table at breakfast, both in robes with cereal and mugs
situation: Dilbert tells Dogbert over breakfast that he has been ordered to build a call center with inhumane working conditions. He tries to ease his conscience by claiming he is only following orders, and Dogbert suggests the employees may have deserved it. Dilbert then asks Dogbert to help him demonize the future workers, and Dogbert eagerly agrees.
punchline: Dilbert wants to avoid guilt over mistreating employees, so he plans to justify it by inventing reasons to villainize them, and Dogbert cheerfully volunteers to help rationalize the cruelty.
summary: A man seeking to dodge guilt over a cruel workplace assignment recruits his dog to smear the people he is about to mistreat.

title: Cube Farmer Promotes Tall Employee

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Cube farming

transcript.speaker: Cube Farmer
transcript.text: He outgrew his container.

transcript.speaker: Cube Farmer
transcript.text: I'll replant him in a big container with a door.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Why do tall guys always get picked?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm sure there's a good reason.

setting: Office cubicle area and a manager's office
situation: A gardener-like cube farmer notices a tall employee has outgrown his cubicle, then drags him away by the necktie to 'replant' him in an office with a door. Wally, holding a coffee mug, complains to Dilbert that tall people always get promoted. Dilbert sarcastically replies that there must be a good reason.
punchline: Tall employees get promoted to offices simply because they are physically too big for their cubicles, which Dilbert sarcastically passes off as a 'good reason'.
summary: Office space is treated like horticulture as a tall worker is uprooted from his cubicle and moved into a private office, prompting grumbling about height-based promotions.

title: Wally Ignores Dilbert's Dramatic Farewell

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: They're transferring me to "Quality Assurance," Wally.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But I'll be back, no matter how long it takes, or how hard! Just stay alive!!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Wow. There must be a million web sites about wiener dogs.

situation: Dilbert tells Wally he is being transferred to Quality Assurance, and he is physically dragged away by two coworkers while making a dramatic vow to return and urging Wally to stay alive. Wally, unmoved, sits at his computer browsing the web and muses about the number of wiener dog websites.
punchline: Wally is so self-absorbed and lazy that he shows no concern for Dilbert's dramatic departure, instead wasting time surfing the internet.
summary: As a colleague is hauled off to a feared department with a heroic farewell, the unbothered cubicle neighbor just goofs off online.

file: 1999/1999-12-29_dogcart one hour course_executive mba_took money_nothing in retrurn_case study.gif
title: Dogbert's One-Hour Executive MBA

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Welcome to the Dogbert one-hour executive MBA course.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Notice that I took your money and I'm giving you almost nothing in return.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That was a case study.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: We have time for one more.

setting: Classroom for an executive training course
situation: Dogbert, acting as an instructor, opens his one-hour executive MBA course in front of a small audience that includes The Boss. He points out that he took the students' money and is giving almost nothing back. He then declares that this was a case study and offers to do another.
punchline: Dogbert presents his own scam as a legitimate teaching example, mocking MBA programs and business advice that charge a lot while delivering little of value.
summary: A scheming dog sells a rushed business course, then passes off his own rip-off of the students as the first lesson.

file: 1999/1999-11-30_day care is closed_tess is yeller_smokey is biter_towns people torched.gif
title: Coworker's Kids Torched the Day Care

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I brought my kids to work because day care is closed.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Tess is a yeller and Smokey is a biter.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why is day care closed?

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: The townspeople torched it.

situation: Carol, a coworker, brings her two children to the office because day care is closed and warns Dilbert that one yells and the other bites. As the kids cling to Dilbert and the daughter screams, he asks why day care is closed. Carol casually reveals that the townspeople burned it down.
punchline: The day care was closed because an angry mob burned it down, implying her kids are so monstrous that the whole town turned against them.
summary: A mother parks her unruly children on a coworker, then calmly admits that an angry mob destroyed the day care.

title: Astrology Beats the Boss's Judgment

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You must use the stars as your management guide.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Does that work?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: If you believe it works, then you're not bright enough to make your own decisions anyway.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So randomness is probably an improvement.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Q.E.D.

setting: Office, across a desk during a consulting session
situation: Dogbert, dressed as a consultant in a tall blue astrologer's hat decorated with a moon, advises the Boss to use the stars as his management guide. When the Boss asks if it works, Dogbert says anyone who believes in it can't make good decisions anyway. The Boss concludes that random choices would be better than his own judgment.
punchline: The Boss's own decision-making is so poor that consulting astrology, which is basically randomness, would be an upgrade, and Dogbert cheerfully confirms the logic.
summary: A horoscope-peddling consultant gets the boss to admit that blind chance would manage the company better than he does.

title: Always Right Initially, Says Boss

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I have to disagree with you, Alice.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Have you noticed that every time we disagree, I'm eventually proved correct?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Every single time!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Yes, but I'M always right initially.

situation: The Boss tells Alice he disagrees with her. Alice points out that whenever they disagree, she is eventually proved correct, every single time. The Boss concedes this but claims that he is always right initially.
punchline: The Boss twists the facts to protect his ego, claiming he is right at the start of every dispute even though Alice is always the one proved correct in the end.
summary: An exasperated employee notes she always wins their arguments in the end, and her boss defends himself with a meaningless claim of initial rightness.

file: 1999/1999-10-11_twenty percent over budget_two months late_bungledm_allocation resources_bungled.gif
title: Never Say Bungled To Bosses

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your project is twenty percent over budget and two months late.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's because you bungled the allocation of resources.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Bosses hate the word "bungled."

setting: The Boss's office, then Dilbert's home
situation: The Boss sits at his desk and scolds Dilbert because his project is over budget and behind schedule. Dilbert retorts that the Boss himself bungled the allocation of resources. Back at home, Dogbert dryly observes that bosses react badly to that particular word.
punchline: Dilbert blames his boss for the failure in blunt terms, and Dogbert's deadpan remark implies he has just made a career-damaging mistake by being honest.
summary: An employee blames his manager for a failing project using an unwelcome word, and his dog notes how badly that tends to go over.

file: 1999/1999-05-23_quick question_innocent work realted_question_try to impress_knowledge of engineering_pathetic hope_value_intelligence_physical appearence_red bmw_lights on.gif
title: Dilbert Misreads Coworker's Dating Rejection

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can I ask a quick question?

transcript.speaker: Woman coworker
transcript.text: I doubt it.

transcript.speaker: Woman coworker
transcript.text: Oh, sure, it'll start as an innocent, work-related question.

transcript.speaker: Woman coworker
transcript.text: Then you'll try to impress me with your knowledge of engineering...

transcript.speaker: Woman coworker
transcript.text: ...in the pathetic hope that I value intelligence over physical appearance.

transcript.speaker: Woman coworker
transcript.text: Well, I don't!! I only care about looks!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you drive a red BMW?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The lights are on.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And you still tried to ask her out?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: She's hard to read.

setting: Office cubicles, then Dilbert's home living room
situation: Dilbert approaches a female coworker with a quick question, and she preemptively lays out how he will try to impress her with engineering knowledge and then bluntly declares she only cares about looks. Dilbert's response is an unrelated question about her car's headlights being on. Later at home he tells Dogbert about it and is chided for still trying to ask her out.
punchline: Dilbert, after being brutally and explicitly rejected in advance, ignores it completely and claims the woman is 'hard to read'.
summary: A coworker predicts and shuts down a man's clumsy romantic approach before he even asks, yet he insists her feelings were ambiguous.

title: Dinosaur's Typewriter Evolution Regret

transcript.speaker: Dinosaur
transcript.text: Computers aren't for everyone. I love my trusty manual typewriter.

transcript.speaker: Dinosaur
transcript.text: Oops.

transcript.speaker: Dinosaur
transcript.text: I hope I can correct that before all my friends evolve into birds.

setting: A dinosaur's office desk, in a prehistoric-era version of the workplace
situation: A green dinosaur sitting at a desk declares that computers aren't for everyone and that he loves his manual typewriter. He then realizes something is wrong, and in the last panel worries he needs to fix his mistake before the other dinosaurs evolve into birds.
punchline: The dinosaur's thought reveals that his typewriter-typed claim about computers contained a typo, a typo that matters only if it can be corrected before his friends evolve into birds, which undercuts his boast about a manual typewriter and implies he is stuck with the machine's limitations while evolution proceeds.
summary: A smug dinosaur praises his old-fashioned typewriter, then frets over an irreversible mistake as time runs out for his species.

file: 1999/1999-01-15_venture capitalists_cool ponytail_squandered_investment_no more funding_mutter words_e commerce_gurgle_swoon.gif
title: E-Commerce Makes Investors Swoon

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Venture capitalists

transcript.speaker: Venture Capitalist
transcript.text: Despite your cool ponytail, you seem to have squandered our investment.

transcript.speaker: Venture Capitalist
transcript.text: You'll get no more funding unless you mutter empty Internet words that make us swoon!

transcript.speaker: Ponytail Man
transcript.text: E-commerce.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Gurgle

setting: Conference room at a venture capital meeting
situation: Two venture capitalists scold a ponytailed startup founder for squandering their investment. They say he will get more funding only if he utters empty Internet buzzwords that make them swoon. He says 'e-commerce' and both investors collapse in ecstasy with their tongues hanging out.
punchline: Investors in the dot-com bubble were so enamored of buzzwords that a single meaningless term like 'e-commerce' could win funding, no matter how badly the money had been wasted.
summary: Two dot-com financiers threaten to cut off a founder, then melt into delirium the instant he says the magic word.

title: Withholding Top Rating, Alice Fetches Harpoon

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, your performance exceeded all expectations this year.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But I'm not giving you the top rating because I want you to have something to shoot for.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's always good to have something to shoot for.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Stay here while I get my harpoon.

setting: The Boss's office during a performance review
situation: The Boss tells Alice her performance exceeded all expectations, but explains he won't give her the top rating so she has a goal to aim for next year. Alice, angered by the logic, tells him to stay put while she fetches a harpoon.
punchline: Alice takes the boss's 'something to shoot for' cliche literally and threatens him with a harpoon, showing how infuriating it is to be denied a deserved rating.
summary: A manager praises an employee's outstanding year yet denies her the best review score, prompting her to go arm herself.

title: Conspiracy to Hire Incompetent Employees

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Your compensation is related to the number of people you manage.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Likewise, my career as Director of Human Resources depends on the quantity of employees.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: It's as if there were a conspiracy to hire hordes of incompetent employees.

setting: Office, in the Boss's office and then a cubicle area
situation: Catbert, the Director of Human Resources, explains to the Boss that the Boss's pay depends on how many people he manages. Catbert adds that his own career depends on headcount as well. Overhearing from the cubicles, Alice remarks that it seems like a conspiracy to hire masses of incompetent people.
punchline: Alice's sarcastic remark reveals that managers and HR are financially motivated to inflate headcount, which explains why so many incompetent people get hired.
summary: Two managers admit their pay depends on staff numbers, and an overhearing coworker connects the dots to the flood of unqualified hires.

file: 1999/1999-04-24_blame others_catbert_evil hr director_oversized head_problem_tight pantyhose_low morale.gif
title: Catbert Blames Alice's Pantyhose

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Alice, you blame others for your low morale.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: But the real problem is your tight pantyhose!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I don't think so.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Then how do you explain your oversized head?

situation: Catbert, acting as the evil H.R. director, tells Alice that she blames others for her low morale. He then claims her real problem is tight pantyhose. When Alice rejects that, he fires back by mocking her oversized head.
punchline: Catbert dishes out absurd, insulting pseudo-diagnoses and, when challenged, simply makes another insult, showing that H.R. has no interest in actually addressing morale.
summary: An uncaring H.R. cat pins an employee's unhappiness on her own failings, then on her clothing, and finally on her head size.

title: Exhausted Employee's RFQ Lost in Stack

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I stayed awake for two days straight to finish this R.F.Q. by the deadline.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: But it will all be for nothing if you don't send it out today.

transcript.speaker: Secretary
transcript.text: I'll put it in the middle of this stack so I won't forget it.

situation: A frazzled, sleep-deprived employee with wild hair tells a seated secretary that she stayed awake two days to finish an RFQ and that it must be sent out today. The secretary calmly says she will put it in the middle of a large stack of papers so she won't forget it, and the employee reacts with a clenched-teeth grimace.
punchline: Filing something important in the middle of a huge pile is the surest way to lose it, so the secretary's plan to avoid forgetting guarantees the opposite, making the employee's two-day effort worthless.
summary: After pulling a two-day all-nighter on a vital proposal, a worker watches the unbothered secretary bury it in the middle of an overflowing pile.

file: 1999/1999-01-29_urgent document_overnight drop_nine minutes_spare_eight minutes_coffee fisrt_truck pulling away_box_wedge_back bumper.gif
title: Urgent Document, Coffee Stop First

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I'm taking your urgent document to the overnight drop box, with nine minutes to spare.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: The box is only eight minutes away. I'll stop for coffee first.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Don't worry. If the truck is pulling away from the box, I'll wedge this in the back bumper.

situation: Carol tells a coworker she will take their urgent document to the overnight drop box with nine minutes to spare. She then reveals the box is eight minutes away and she plans to stop for coffee first. When the anxious coworker reacts with alarm, Carol casually offers to wedge the package into the delivery truck's bumper if it is leaving.
punchline: Carol's wildly casual attitude toward a time-critical delivery, including a ridiculous backup plan, shows she isn't taking the deadline seriously while her coworker panics.
summary: A relaxed assistant plans a coffee break before delivering a time-sensitive package, leaving the coworker horrified at her improvised backup plan.

title: Secretary Laughs at Room Request

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Carol, I'd like to reserve the conference room.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Ha ha ha ha! I laugh at your request without even explaining why.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Someday I will be so powerful that secretaries will HAVE to explain why they laugh at me.

setting: Office cubicle area outside Carol's desk
situation: Dilbert politely asks Carol, the administrative assistant, to reserve the conference room. She bursts into laughter and refuses to explain why she finds the request funny. Dilbert walks away fuming and thinks about a future where he has enough power to demand explanations.
punchline: Carol holds all the real power over scarce resources like conference rooms, and Dilbert can only fantasize about the status it would take to make a secretary justify her mockery.
summary: A gatekeeping office assistant cackles at a simple booking request, leaving the humiliated engineer to daydream about someday wielding enough clout to demand an explanation.

title: Scapegoat Shot Instead of Messenger

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Who are you?

transcript.speaker: Scapegoat
transcript.text: I'm a scapegoat.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Bang!

transcript.speaker: Man with gun
transcript.text: Oops. I was aiming for the messenger.

transcript.speaker: Man with gun
transcript.text: It's his own fault for being here.

situation: Dilbert sits at a meeting table and asks a goat-headed stranger in a suit who he is. The goat explains he is a scapegoat, and a gunshot goes off. A man holding a gun says he was actually aiming at the messenger, and blames the scapegoat for being in the way.
punchline: The scapegoat gets shot in place of the messenger, and the shooter blames the victim, mocking how blame in organizations lands on whoever happens to be nearby.
summary: A man hunting for someone to blame accidentally shoots the designated scapegoat and then faults him for standing in the wrong spot.

title: Strategy Slide Defended After Criticism

transcript.speaker: Presenter
transcript.text: Our strategy is to detect any trends and react accordingly.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Isn't that exactly the same as not having a strategy?

transcript.speaker: Presenter
transcript.text: Hey, this slide didn't make itself.

situation: A presenter in a meeting uses a slide to announce that the company's strategy is to detect trends and react to them. Dilbert points out that this is the same as having no strategy at all. The presenter, offended, responds by defending the effort he put into making the slide.
punchline: Instead of addressing the valid criticism that reacting to trends is not a strategy, the presenter defensively complains about the work spent on the slide, showing the slide has no real content.
summary: A presenter's vacuous strategy slide gets called out as no strategy at all, and he protests that producing the slide took effort.

title: Wally Takes Credit for Teamwork

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Will you please go hang around in someone else's cubicle? I need to finish my project.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Hey, I see Wally is helping on the project. Good teamwork, Wally!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I hope you do good work. I have a reputation to maintain.

situation: Alice is trying to finish her project and tells Wally, who is loitering in her cubicle with a coffee mug, to go bother someone else. The Boss passes by, sees Wally standing there, and praises him for helping on the project. Wally lets the credit stand and tells Alice he hopes her work is good because he has a reputation to maintain, while Alice glares in anger.
punchline: Wally, who did nothing, gets praised for teamwork and then pressures the person doing all the actual work to make sure it reflects well on him.
summary: A lazy coworker who was merely loitering gets mistaken for a helpful team player and then lectures the real worker about protecting his image.

file: 1999/1999-11-22_new ceo_turnaround expert_pleasure to meet_business process_value based_management method.gif
title: Devil Introduced as Turnaround CEO

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This is our new CEO. He has a reputation as a turnaround expert.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: It is a pleasure to meet you. Do you favor TQM or more of a business process approach?

transcript.speaker: New CEO
transcript.text: I'm partial to the value-based management method.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I'm not familiar with that one.

setting: Conference room at a meeting table
situation: The Boss introduces a snarling red devil as the company's new CEO, praised as a turnaround expert. An employee politely asks whether he prefers TQM or a business process approach. The devil-CEO replies that he favors value-based management, which the employee admits he doesn't know.
punchline: The new CEO is literally a devil, and the employee earnestly discusses management methodologies with him, ignoring the obvious sign that this leader is bad news for the company.
summary: A monstrous red demon takes over as chief executive and gets treated to routine small talk about management fads.

title: Wally Pages Boss's Ear Clip

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, are you sure this kind of pager is supposed to clip on my ear?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It hurts. Maybe you can call someone to double-check.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Good idea.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Beep beep beep

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Bzzz Bzzz Bzzz

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Is there anything else I can do for you?

situation: The Boss complains that his new pager, clipped to his ear, hurts and asks Wally to call someone to verify it is worn correctly. Wally agrees, dials the pager's number, and the vibrating pager sends the Boss convulsing in his chair while Wally calmly offers further help.
punchline: Wally exploits the Boss's vague request by literally 'calling someone' - the pager itself - so the Boss gets shaken by the vibration, and Wally feigns innocent helpfulness.
summary: A boss with a pager clipped to his ear asks his lazy employee to phone someone for advice, and the employee ends up buzzing the device right against his head.

title: Palm Pilot Trips Instead of PDAs

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The company will not buy PDA's for employees.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Question: Will you still pay for business trips of no discernable value?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Of course.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: A lot of people are traveling to Palm Pilot California lately.

setting: Conference room meeting, then the Boss's office
situation: At a staff meeting, the Boss announces that the company won't buy PDAs for employees. Dilbert asks whether the company will still pay for pointless business trips, and the Boss readily agrees. The Boss then thinks to himself that lots of people are traveling to 'Palm Pilot, California' lately, implying employees will be expensing trips rather than getting the cheap gadgets.
punchline: The Boss refuses to spend a little on PDAs but will happily fund wasteful business trips, so he is only fooling himself about saving money, since the trips cost far more.
summary: A manager rejects buying cheap gadgets for staff while cheerfully approving costly, pointless travel, revealing how misplaced his cost-cutting priorities are.

file: 1999/1999-08-31_most common metal errors_hot day_heel_add anew category.gif
title: Checklist of Dilbert's Mental Errors

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: In order to save time, I made a checklist of your most common mental errors.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It'll be a hot day in Hell before you need that, my friend.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I need to add a new category.

setting: Dilbert's cubicle, at his desk and computer
situation: Dogbert walks up holding a clipboard and announces he has prepared a checklist of Dilbert's most common mental errors to save time. Dilbert scoffs that he will never need it. Dogbert responds by noting he must add a new category to the list.
punchline: Dilbert's confident dismissal of the checklist is itself a mental error, proving Dogbert right and giving him something new to record.
summary: A smug claim that an error-tracking list is unnecessary instantly becomes the first entry in a brand-new section of that list.

file: 1999/1999-05-31_story ever end_purchase silence_fist of death_two warning system.gif
title: Alice's Fist of Death Silences Colleague

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: But then I...

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Excuse me.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Does your story ever end? Or must I purchase your silence with my fist of death?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I might have to go to a two-warning system.

situation: A coworker keeps rambling on during a meeting until Alice interrupts him. She asks whether his story will ever end or whether she must silence him with her fist of death. She then knocks him out and drags him from the room, remarking that she may need to give two warnings in future.
punchline: Alice's single polite warning before violence is so inadequate that she realizes she should perhaps give two warnings before knocking someone out.
summary: Fed up with a droning colleague at a meeting, Alice knocks him unconscious and hauls him away while reflecting that her warning policy could be more generous.

title: Scapegoat Crashes the NRA Chili Cook-Off

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm sorry you got shot, Scapegoat.

transcript.speaker: Scapegoat
transcript.text: I'm used to it.

transcript.speaker: Scapegoat
transcript.text: The worst was the day I blundered across the National Rifle Association's chili cook-off.

transcript.speaker: Scapegoat
transcript.text: At first, everyone wanted to stand near me. Then the accusations started...

situation: Dilbert walks alongside Scapegoat, a goat with his arm in a sling, and sympathizes that he was shot. Scapegoat shrugs it off and recalls an even worse day when he wandered into the National Rifle Association's chili cook-off. People initially crowded around him, until the accusations began.
punchline: Because a scapegoat is the one who gets blamed, a goat wandering into a chili cook-off is first admired as an ingredient, then accused of being the source of the meat, with an implied threat of being shot.
summary: A wounded goat with a habit of getting blamed recalls how a gathering of gun enthusiasts turned on him after an initial burst of popularity.

title: Phil's Huge Spoon Needs Waxing

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Phil, you have taught me so much about life. How can I repay you?

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: You can wax my huge spoon.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Why do you have a huge spoon?

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: I'm just lucky, I guess.

situation: A junior employee thanks Phil, the red-hooded devil-costumed Prince of Insufficient Light, for teaching him about life and offers to repay him. Phil asks him to wax his huge wooden spoon. When asked why he owns such a spoon, Phil just says he's lucky.
punchline: Phil's deadpan, nonsensical answer about his huge spoon shows he has no real wisdom or explanation, making his supposed life lessons and the repayment request absurd.
summary: A grateful young coworker offers to repay his mentor, who absurdly requests that he polish an oversized spoon and then brushes off any explanation.

title: Tech Support Transfers Destroy Hope

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert's Tech Support

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: First, I need to ask you many questions.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Then I will transfer you to someone who will ask the same questions again.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: We do this to remove any hope you might have had that we understand technology.

setting: Dogbert's tech support call desk, wearing a phone headset at a computer
situation: Dogbert, working as a tech support agent with a headset, explains his support process to a caller. He will first ask many questions, then transfer the caller to someone who asks the same questions again. He then reveals the real reason for the routine.
punchline: The pointless repeated questioning and transferring is deliberately designed to convince customers that the support staff are clueless about technology, so they give up hoping for help.
summary: A tech support dog cheerfully admits that bouncing callers between agents who repeat the same questions is meant to crush their confidence in his team's competence.

file: 1999/1999-04-08_budget calculated_double check numbers_mentally adjust_huge mistake_upside down nine.gif
title: Boss Mentally Adjusts for Wrong Budget

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do you have the budget calculated yet, Asok?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I need to double-check the numbers.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Give me a copy now. I'll mentally adjust for the possibility the numbers are wrong.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Am I making a huge mistake?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This six is probably an upside-down nine.

setting: Office, Asok's cubicle and a desk with a printer
situation: The Boss asks Asok for the budget, and Asok says he wants to double-check the numbers first. The Boss demands an unchecked copy immediately, claiming he will mentally correct for any errors. He then squints at the printout and guesses that a figure is an upside-down digit, while Asok nervously wonders if he has made a huge mistake.
punchline: The Boss's claim that he can mentally compensate for errors is absurd, as his 'adjustment' is just a wild guess about misread digits, making the unchecked budget even less reliable.
summary: Rather than wait for verified figures, a manager grabs an unchecked budget and cheerfully speculates about which digits might be upside down.
