file: 1999/1999-09-23_mother_phone call_get joke_realizations_actual life_no joke_office_life as intern_engineers_smart kid_inidan kid_educated_smart_family.gif
title: Mother's Joke Was His Life

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Hello, Mother. I called to tell you I get your joke.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: You don't know what I'm talking about? Ha ha! You're really playing this one all the way.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: It turns out that this is my actual life.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's the good part.

situation: Asok phones his mother, saying he finally understands her joke about his work life, and assumes she is feigning ignorance when she doesn't follow. In the last panel he is seated at a conference table with Dilbert and Wally, who are eating snacks, and Asok realizes it wasn't a joke at all. Dilbert chimes in that the meeting is the good part.
punchline: Asok thought his mother was joking about the grim reality of office work, but she was sincerely describing his actual life, and his coworker deadpans that the dismal meeting is the good part.
summary: A young employee calls home to praise what he thinks is a clever gag, only to discover that the bleak picture of his job is simply his real life.

file: 1999/1999-05-12_personal goal_self actaulization_outdated binders_alpahbetical_reqiuested_feel unfulfilled_phase two_project_find meaning_ship binders_dump.gif
title: Alphabetizing Binders Destined for Dump

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I fear I am not meeting my personal goal of self-actualization.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I put all of our outdated binders in alphabetical order as you requested, yet I feel unfulfilled.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I assume that in phase two of this project I will find meaning.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Now ship the binders to the dump.

situation: Asok, a young employee, tells his boss he isn't achieving self-actualization. He explains that he alphabetized all of the company's outdated binders as requested and still feels unfulfilled. He hopes phase two of the project will give him meaning, and the boss replies that the next step is to ship the binders to the dump.
punchline: The boss's reply reveals that the tedious task was utterly pointless, since the binders were being thrown away, so Asok's hoped-for meaning in phase two will not come.
summary: A young worker hopes his next task will bring meaning after sorting obsolete binders, only to be told to haul them to the trash.

file: 1999/1999-02-02_no engineers_product planning_art history majors_party_cloak of invisibility_students_education.gif
title: Art History Majors Plan Products

transcript.speaker: Marketing Man
transcript.text: We didn't include engineers in the product planning sessions because... um... because...

transcript.speaker: Marketing Woman
transcript.text: Because we were art history majors in college.

transcript.speaker: Marketing Man
transcript.text: Pa-r-r-rty!

transcript.speaker: Marketing Woman
transcript.text: How soon can you build the cloak of invisibility?

transcript.speaker: Marketing Man
transcript.text: Let the man think, Clover.

setting: Conference room during a product planning meeting
situation: Two marketing people try to explain to Dilbert why engineers were left out of product planning, but the man can't come up with a reason. His colleague supplies the real one: they were art history majors, so they have no technical grounding. She then asks Dilbert how soon he can build a cloak of invisibility, an impossible product they have planned.
punchline: Marketing planned an absurdly impossible product without engineers because their art history backgrounds left them unable to tell what is feasible, and the exclusion of the people who could have said so is the whole problem.
summary: Marketing staff with humanities degrees admit why they shut out engineers, then casually request a fantasy gadget as if it were routine.

file: 1999/1999-06-18_hiding nametag_fake babies_see name_start fliting_babies_third fake baby_still hides name.gif
title: Juggling Fake Babies to Read Nametag

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: She's hiding her name tag so I won't get friendly with her.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll toss these fake babies in the air. When she catches them, I'll see her name and start flirting.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Dang! I knew I should have brought a third fake baby.

situation: Dilbert stands at a store counter where a female clerk is holding her hand over her name tag. Believing she is hiding it to avoid his friendliness, he tosses fake babies at her so she must use her hands to catch them and reveal her name. She catches both babies, but her hands still cover the tag, so he laments not having a third baby.
punchline: Dilbert's elaborate and absurd scheme to learn a woman's name fails because he didn't bring enough fake babies to free up all of her hands, and he never considers simply asking her.
summary: A lovelorn Dilbert hurls dolls at a cashier in a bizarre bid to expose her hidden name badge, only to find that the plan falls one prop short.

title: Prenup He Never Read

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I sold my internet business and married Roxie.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Don't worry about my money. Roxie insisted that we sign prenuptial agreements.

transcript.speaker: Roxie
transcript.text: Now for our honeymoon.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Whoa! That's not in our agreement.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: He didn't read it.

situation: At a cafeteria table, Wally announces to Alice and Dilbert that he sold his internet business and married Roxie. He assures them his money is safe because of the prenuptial agreements they signed. When Roxie announces their honeymoon, Wally protests that it isn't in the agreement, and Alice points out he never read it.
punchline: Wally confidently relies on a prenup he never read, so he is blindsided by a clause (or lack of one) about the honeymoon, which fits his habit of signing things without reading them.
summary: A newly married Wally brags that his fortune is protected by a prenup, only to discover he signed it without reading what it actually said.

file: 1999/1999-04-12_new bonus plan_peak perfromance_bonus_goods mine_car won't start.gif
title: Asok's Naive Bonus Optimism

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Introducing the new bonus plan.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Yes!!! I'm already working at peak performance, so that bonus is as good as mine!

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Asok, Mr. Reality wanted to visit you, but his car won't start. I'm Phil.

situation: The Boss announces a new bonus plan to the team at a conference table. Asok eagerly cheers, convinced that because he already works at peak performance he is guaranteed a bonus. Phil, dressed in a red devil costume and holding a big wooden spoon, tells him that Mr. Reality couldn't come in person and he is here instead.
punchline: Asok's naive belief that hard work guarantees a bonus is so detached from how corporate bonus plans actually work that even the personification of reality can't be bothered to correct him, so Phil does it in a devil costume.
summary: A cheerful young employee assumes a new bonus plan will reward his efforts until a devil-costumed coworker delivers a sarcastic reality check.
keywords: bonus is as good as mine

file: 1999/1999-09-21_air duct_award for good work_been summoned_intern_boss office.gif
title: Intern Expects Award, Boss Wants Air Duct

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I have been summoned to the Boss's office.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: He probably wants to give me some sort of award for my good work as an intern.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Why do you need to know where that air duct ends?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's been bugging me.

setting: Office cubicle area and the Boss's office
situation: Asok, the intern, tells Dilbert he has been summoned to the Boss's office and proudly assumes it is to receive an award for his work. In the last panel, the Boss is shown talking with Alice and revealing the real reason: he wants to know where an air duct ends, apparently so he can send the intern into it.
punchline: Asok's hopeful expectation of recognition is undercut when the Boss's real motive is to use the intern as expendable labor to explore an air duct, with the Boss's "bugging me" line adding a pun on the bugs in the duct.
summary: A hopeful intern heads to the boss's office expecting praise, but the boss actually just wants someone to crawl through a duct and solve his curiosity.

title: Cartoon Without a Punchline Presentation

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'd like to start with a cartoon.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's about a guy who shows a cartoon before giving a boring presentation.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But it doesn't work because the cartoon has no punchline.

setting: Conference room with an overhead projector
situation: Dilbert begins a presentation at an overhead projector while a coworker watches. He announces he will start with a cartoon, then describes a cartoon about a presenter who opens with a cartoon before a boring talk. He explains that the cartoon fails because it has no punchline.
punchline: The cartoon Dilbert describes is the very strip we are reading, and he admits it has no punchline, which is itself the self-referential joke, and it implies his presentation will be boring too.
summary: A presenter opens his talk by describing a cartoon that is secretly the strip itself, a joke that falls flat on purpose.

file: 1999/1999-07-22_mordac_preventer of information_cios office_delete meail_server_message_insulting email_regeret sending.gif
title: Shooting the CIO to Delete Email

transcript.speaker: Mordac
transcript.text: Why do you seek Mordac - the Preventer of Information Services?

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: I regret sending an insulting e-mail message to our CIO. I need to delete it from the server.

transcript.speaker: Mordac
transcript.text: The server was in that closet, right?

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: That's the CIO's office.

setting: Office hallway outside a closet door
situation: A woman approaches Mordac, the Preventer of Information Services, and explains she sent an insulting email to the CIO and wants it deleted from the server. She reaches into her purse and Mordac recalls the server was in a closet. She corrects him that it is the CIO's office, and she is now holding a smoking gun.
punchline: The woman has apparently just shot up the CIO's office, treating a gun as a way to destroy the evidence of her insulting email, implying she may have shot the CIO and the server.
summary: An employee desperate to erase a rude email to the CIO turns up with a smoking pistol, having apparently taken drastic measures in the executive's office.

file: 1999/1999-11-26_the turnaround ceo_mole_fire_affect revenue_outsource everything_one smart employee_risk_rude.gif
title: Outsource Everything, Keep One Smart Employee

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The Turnaround CEO

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Tell me, Mole, who can I fire without affecting revenue?

transcript.speaker: Mole
transcript.text: In theory, you could outsource everything and run the company with one smart employee.

transcript.speaker: Mole
transcript.text: And at the risk of sounding rude, only one of us knew that.

situation: Dilbert, cast as a turnaround CEO, asks a red devilish advisor called Mole who can be fired without hurting revenue. Mole answers that the company could outsource everything and keep a single smart employee. He then adds that only one person in the room understood that, which implies Dilbert didn't.
punchline: Mole's polite warning about being rude is a setup for an insult: he is implying that the CEO is not the smart one who understood this obvious cost-cutting idea.
summary: A new chief executive asks his devilish advisor where to cut staff and gets a blunt answer plus a backhanded dig at his own intelligence.

file: 1999/1999-03-29_bill agtes_bill gates_competition keeper_infrared_linus rules_linux box_missiles_sent email_visit mom_dilberts mother.gif
title: Mom's Linux Email Triggers Missiles

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mom
transcript.text: ...I'm going infrared from the keyboard to my "Linux" box.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Nice, Mom.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mom
transcript.text: I just sent a flaming e-mail to Bill Gates, saying, "Linux rules!"

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You what?

transcript.speaker: Bill Gates
transcript.text: Launch the CompetitionKeeper missiles.

setting: Mom's living room, then a high-tech control room
situation: Dilbert sits on the couch with his mom while she proudly shows off her technical skills, using an infrared keyboard to control her Linux computer. She casually mentions sending a flaming email to Bill Gates saying Linux rules, and Dilbert reacts with alarm. The final panel cuts to a sci-fi command center where a Gates-like leader orders missiles launched in response.
punchline: A harmless fan email from a Linux-loving mom is treated by Microsoft as an act of war, implying the company retaliates ruthlessly against any competitor.
summary: An elderly woman's cheerful pro-Linux message to the software mogul supposedly prompts a missile-armed response from his command center.

title: Boss Condescends, Dilbert Takes Pat

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So, that's my idea. What do you think?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, you are so naive.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: There are many things you don't understand.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's because you never tell me anything!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, Dilbert, Dilbert...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Like now, for example!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Jeepers cripes! Just tell me what's wrong with my idea!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Lean over here so I can pat your head in a condescending way.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: So you took the pat?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I didn't want to leave empty-handed.

setting: The Boss's office, then Dilbert's home living room
situation: Dilbert pitches an idea to the Boss, who dismisses him as naive without explaining what is wrong. Dilbert gets frustrated and demands feedback, so the Boss offers to pat his head condescendingly instead. At home, Dogbert asks if he really accepted the pat.
punchline: Having received no useful feedback, Dilbert accepted the patronizing head pat just so he'd get something from the meeting.
summary: A frustrated engineer seeks real feedback on his idea but is offered only a patronizing head pat, which he accepts anyway so the visit isn't a total loss.

title: Faking Care To Reduce Turnover

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll reduce turnover by showing I care about you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Tell me about your kids, Asok.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I don't have any.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let's say you do for the sake of this exercise.

situation: The Boss announces at a meeting that he will reduce employee turnover by showing he cares about his staff. He asks Asok about his kids, and when Asok says he has none, the Boss tells him to pretend he does so the exercise can continue.
punchline: The Boss's attempt at sincere concern is just a mechanical exercise, so he can't even adapt when the facts don't fit and simply asks Asok to invent kids.
summary: A manager rehearses caring about his employees as a retention tactic, then insists a childless worker pretend to have children so the script still works.
keywords: for the sake of this exercise

file: 1999/1999-07-12_management book_obvious advice_quotes from dead people_ganghi_assert cart_dogbert.gif
title: Management Book Full of Dead Quotes

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What's your new management book about?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's a bunch of obvious advice packaged with quotes from famous dead people.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did Gandhi really say "Get that #!%@ dessert cart off of my foot!"?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: He might have.

setting: Office, at a desk with a computer
situation: Dilbert asks Dogbert what his new management book is about. Dogbert explains it is obvious advice dressed up with quotes from famous dead people. Dilbert then asks whether Gandhi really said an angry, profanity-laced line about a dessert cart on his foot, and Dogbert shrugs that he might have.
punchline: Since the dead can't dispute what they supposedly said, management book authors can attribute any quote to anyone, and Dogbert cheerfully admits the quotes may be fabricated.
summary: A dog's business book recycles platitudes and borrows credibility from historical figures who can't object to being misquoted.

title: Catbert Mocks The Boss's Perks

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Being a manager means never having to be less condescending just because you're wrong.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: HA HA HA HA HA

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did he finish my performance evaluation?

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: I heard him working on it.

setting: The boss's office, then the office cubicle area
situation: Catbert sits on the boss's desk and explains that managers can be condescending even when they are wrong, while the boss reclines in his chair. Both burst into laughter. Afterward Dilbert asks a coworker whether his performance evaluation is done and is told that the laughing he heard was the boss working on it.
punchline: The boss's evaluation of Dilbert is apparently being written as a big joke, with the manager and Catbert laughing at the employee's expense.
summary: A cat and a manager howl with mirth behind a closed door, and the employee waiting on his review learns that is what the writing process sounds like.

title: Ratbert Hides in Coffee Can

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Bob, have you ever noticed that the people with the most experience are the ones who die?

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: My plan is to spend the rest of my life in an old coffee can, experiencing nothing. Hence, immortality.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How was your first week of immortality?

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: So far, it's overrated.

situation: Ratbert tells Bob, the dinosaur, that the most experienced people are the ones who die, and announces a plan to live forever by hiding in an old coffee can and experiencing nothing. A week later Dilbert asks how his first week of immortality went. Ratbert, sitting in the coffee can on a desk, admits it is overrated.
punchline: Ratbert's plan to cheat death by experiencing nothing produces a life so dull that immortality isn't worth it.
summary: A small rodent tries to dodge death by sealing himself in a can, only to find that a life without experiences is a miserable one.

file: 1999/1999-11-14_salesman_questions_best running shoe_sneakers are sneakers_far superior_expensive ones.gif
title: Salesman Upsells After Manager Intervenes

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: SALE

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: Do you have any questions?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What's your best running shoe?

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: They're all the same. Sneakers are sneakers.

transcript.speaker: Store Manager
transcript.text: Alan, may I have a word with you?

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: The expensive sneakers are far superior.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll take them!

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: I feel like I'm clubbing a baby seal.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Will these work with my old socks?

setting: A shoe store during a sale
situation: Dilbert asks a shoe salesman for his best running shoe and gets an honest answer that all sneakers are basically the same. The store manager takes the salesman aside for a word, after which the salesman suddenly claims the expensive sneakers are far superior. Dilbert happily buys them while the salesman feels guilty about it.
punchline: After being scolded by his manager for honesty, the salesman switches to a dishonest upsell, and the gullible customer eagerly buys the pricey shoes while the salesman feels like he is clubbing a baby seal.
summary: A candid shoe clerk is pressured by his boss into pushing costly footwear, and his trusting customer falls for it without a second thought.

file: 1999/1999-12-25_hyper inflated stock_real value_hype triumphs substance_moral compass_spinning.gif
title: Hype Beats Substance, Compass Spins

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Now I'll use my hype-inflated stock to buy companies that have real value.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The lesson is that hype always triumphs over substance.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: How's your moral compass doing?

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Spinning, just like you said it would!

setting: A therapist-style office with a red ottoman and a brown armchair
situation: Dogbert, sitting on an ottoman, explains that he will use his hype-inflated stock to acquire companies with real value. He draws the lesson that hype always triumphs over substance, then asks Ratbert, sitting in the armchair, how his moral compass is doing. Ratbert replies that it is spinning, as Dogbert predicted.
punchline: Dogbert's plan to profit from overvalued stock is so unethical that it leaves Ratbert's moral compass spinning, which Dogbert had predicted all along.
summary: After boasting about turning overvalued shares into real assets, a smug dog checks on his companion's ethics and learns they are in a tailspin.

title: Hammerhead Bob Corners Asok

transcript.speaker: Hammerhead Bob
transcript.text: You can't escape the relentless conversation of Hammerhead Bob.

transcript.speaker: Hammerhead Bob
transcript.text: Buwhaha! Your body language can't stop me!

transcript.speaker: Hammerhead Bob
transcript.text: Where's your personal space now?!

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Sob

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Ear plugs, Asok! Ear plugs!

situation: Hammerhead Bob, a coworker with a hammer-shaped head, chases Asok through the office. He corners Asok, who is curled up in a ball in his cubicle, and gloats that body language cannot stop him. Asok sobs while Alice, in the next cubicle, shouts advice to use ear plugs.
punchline: Hammerhead Bob is an unstoppable, oblivious talker who ignores every social cue and personal boundary, leaving his victim helpless and reduced to tears.
summary: A relentlessly chatty coworker hunts down a cowering colleague, ignoring all his defensive signals until a neighbor suggests the only real defense.

file: 1999/1999-12-07_idiots_i quit_higher paying job_miles away_adios_web designer_hear your idiots_ethernet.gif
title: Quitting, Re-hired Two Miles Away

transcript.speaker: Web designer
transcript.text: You're all idiots. I quit!

transcript.speaker: Web designer
transcript.text: There... I found a higher paying job two miles away. Adios, suckers.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Click click

transcript.speaker: New web designer
transcript.text: I'm the new web designer. I hear you're idiots. Where's the ethernet jack?

situation: During a meeting, a web designer announces he is quitting because his coworkers are idiots. He then quickly uses his laptop to find a higher-paying job just two miles away. Immediately a new web designer arrives, already knowing the team's reputation, and asks for the ethernet jack.
punchline: The departing employee's job is filled instantly by a replacement who already knows the team are idiots, showing that everyone is job-hopping and nobody stays or respects the company.
summary: A web designer storms out of a meeting and lands a better job nearby on the spot, only for his replacement to arrive already warned about the staff.

file: 1999/1999-05-27_new office rebel_nice bathrobe_easily manipulated_dare you_use barnding_the fire.gif
title: Office Rebels Easily Manipulated Into Stupidity

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You must be the new office rebel we heard about.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Nice bathrobe.

transcript.speaker: Rebel
transcript.text: We're called rebels because we're easily manipulated into doing stupid things.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Give it up for us! Whoo whoo!

transcript.speaker: Rebel
transcript.text: I dare you to use branding irons on each other right now.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Start the fire!

situation: A group of coworkers greets a new employee who is known as the office rebel, noting his bathrobe. The rebel explains that rebels are called that because they are easily manipulated into doing stupid things. His coworkers promptly cheer him on and dare him to brand people with branding irons, while Dilbert and Alice look on uneasily.
punchline: The self-proclaimed rebel admits that rebels are just suckers who can be goaded into reckless stunts, then immediately proves it by escalating to a dangerous dare, showing that nonconformity is just another form of peer pressure.
summary: A so-called nonconformist admits his rebellious streak is really just gullibility, then eagerly demonstrates it by falling for a dangerous dare.

title: Dogbert Summons Employees From Org-Limbo

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I can contact employees who are in org-limbo.

transcript.speaker: Woman with big hair
transcript.text: Hello-o-o! Why doesn't anyone return my calls?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Come toward the revised org chart, Alice!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: It's so beautiful!

situation: Dogbert, dressed in a mystic's turban like a medium at a seance, claims he can contact employees stuck in org-limbo while Dilbert and the Boss look on. A big-haired employee, Alice, appears behind him complaining that no one returns her calls. Dogbert holds up a revised org chart and beckons her toward it as if guiding a spirit into the light, and she marvels at it.
punchline: Employees displaced by a reorganization are treated like dead spirits in limbo, and Dogbert coaxes Alice toward the 'light' of the new org chart the way a medium sends ghosts to the afterlife, implying the reorg has effectively killed her position.
summary: Playing a spirit medium, Dogbert lures a reorganization casualty toward the glowing new org chart like a ghost being sent into the light.

title: Obsolete Mainframe Is Under-Utilized Because Obsolete

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Move our budget system onto the under-utilized mainframe.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's under-utilized because it's obsolete.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Reality versus management; who shall be the victor?

setting: Office, in front of Dilbert's workspace
situation: The Boss orders Dilbert to move the company's budget system onto a mainframe that is barely being used. Dilbert points out that nobody uses the mainframe because it is obsolete. In the last panel, Dilbert silently wonders whether reality or management will win the standoff.
punchline: Management sees an idle mainframe as spare capacity to exploit, while Dilbert knows it sits idle because the technology is outdated, and he privately frames the clash as a contest he expects reality to lose.
summary: A manager sees an idle old computer as a bargain home for an important system, while the engineer knows why nobody uses it.

file: 1999/1999-11-21_young dilbert_mother_kitchen denied permission_skateboard_construction site_jumped off cliff_credibility_family.gif
title: Young Dilbert Out-Argues Mom's Cliff Cliché

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Young Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Young Dilbert
transcript.text: Mom, can I go skateboarding at the construction site?

transcript.speaker: Mom
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Young Dilbert
transcript.text: Why not? Everyone else does it.

transcript.speaker: Mom
transcript.text: If everyone jumped off a cliff, would you do that?

transcript.speaker: Young Dilbert
transcript.text: Well, that would depend on many factors, including height, training and equipment.

transcript.speaker: Young Dilbert
transcript.text: But if 100% of the people who jumped off cliffs said they enjoyed it, as in my skateboard example ...

transcript.speaker: Young Dilbert
transcript.text: ... then I would conclude that it was safe.

transcript.speaker: Mom
transcript.text: A better question might have been, "If everyone wore clothes, would you do that?"

transcript.speaker: Young Dilbert
transcript.text: Her credibility gets worse every day.

setting: Dilbert's childhood home kitchen, then outdoors at dusk
situation: Young Dilbert asks his mom if he can skateboard at a construction site and she refuses. When she uses the classic 'if everyone jumped off a cliff' line, he calmly answers with a logical analysis of risk factors and survey data. His mom fumbles a retort about wearing clothes, and Dilbert walks off with his skateboard, dismissing her credibility.
punchline: Dilbert treats a parental cliché as a rigorous argument to be rebutted with data, and concludes his mom's weak comeback proves she is losing credibility.
summary: A logical young boy dismantles his mother's stock parental warning with risk analysis, then leaves for the construction site unconvinced by her flustered reply.

title: Dogbert Exorcises the Possessed Boss

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm here to perform an exorcism.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your mother implements multi-vendor processes without synergy!!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Here's the problem. Someone gave you this oversized coffee mug.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Reorg!!

situation: Dogbert, wearing a crown and holding a wand, arrives in the boss's office to perform an exorcism while Dilbert, Wally and Alice peek in through the window. The boss shouts nonsensical buzzword insults as if possessed. Dogbert diagnoses the cause as an oversized coffee mug, and the boss yells 'Reorg!!'.
punchline: The boss's bizarre outbursts are just ordinary management jargon, so his 'possession' is indistinguishable from his normal behavior and is blamed on a giant coffee mug.
summary: A costumed Dogbert treats the boss's ranting buzzword gibberish as a demonic possession and blames his oversized mug.

file: 1999/1999-06-06_email two copies_fax_green paper_email_files_hard copy_internet_motivation gone_losing consciousness_lazy employees_technology.gif
title: Boss Demands Absurd Technology Requests

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: E-mail two copies to me when you're done.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Two copies? It's e-mail.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Never mind. I'll e-mail two copies.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And fax a copy on green paper for my files.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Green? It's a fax!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And bring me a hard copy of the Internet so I can do some serious surfing.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Motivation... gone... losing... consciousness...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How did I end up with all the lazy employees?

setting: The Boss's office and the hallway outside it
situation: The Boss gives Dilbert a series of increasingly nonsensical technology requests: two copies of an e-mail, a fax on green paper, and a printout of the entire Internet. Dilbert's protests are ignored until he loses the will to continue and collapses in the hallway among other fainted employees.
punchline: The Boss's own absurd demands have drained everyone's motivation and left employees unconscious, yet he blames the staff for being lazy.
summary: A manager's baffling requests about digital files and the Internet leave his staff literally collapsing, which he blames on their laziness.

title: Employee Confesses Internet Company Theft

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I used company resources to build my own internet company.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Apparently my low job satisfaction bred disloyalty, which drifted into outright theft.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Sabotage can't be far away.

situation: At a meeting table, a balding employee cheerfully admits to the boss, who is reading a note, that he used company resources to start his own internet company. He analyzes his own behavior as a chain from low job satisfaction to disloyalty to theft. The boss puts his face in his hands as the employee casually predicts sabotage will come next.
punchline: The employee calmly diagnoses his own escalating misconduct, blaming the company's poor morale, and helpfully warns that sabotage is the next step, leaving the boss in despair.
summary: A staffer matter-of-factly explains how his unhappiness turned him into a thief and then forecasts he will soon become a saboteur.

title: Overtime Not Mandatory, Just Required

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Overtime is no longer mandatory.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's required.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I manage and I manage, but nothing seems to make them happy.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Grrrr

setting: Conference room during a staff meeting
situation: The Boss sits at the head of a meeting table and announces to his staff that overtime is no longer mandatory. He then clarifies that it is now required instead. In his thought bubble he wonders why employees are never happy, while a coworker growls angrily.
punchline: The Boss swaps the word 'mandatory' for 'required' as if that changes anything, then is clueless about why his employees are unhappy.
summary: A manager pretends to relax an overtime rule by renaming it, then puzzles over his team's discontent.

file: 1999/1999-07-14_dogbert in hollywood_book into movie_keep real_normal people_watch movies.gif
title: Hollywood Exec Wants Normal Movie

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert in Hollywood

transcript.speaker: Hollywood Executive
transcript.text: I'd like to turn your book into a movie.

transcript.speaker: Hollywood Executive
transcript.text: We have to keep it real, so any normal person can relate to it.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Do you know any normal people?

transcript.speaker: Hollywood Executive
transcript.text: No, but I'm willing to watch movies to learn about them.

setting: Restaurant table during a lunch meeting in Hollywood
situation: A Hollywood executive wearing an odd blue hat meets Dogbert over lunch and says he wants to adapt Dogbert's book into a movie. He insists the film must be realistic so normal people can relate, and Dogbert asks whether he actually knows any normal people. The executive admits he doesn't, but says he'll watch movies to learn about them.
punchline: The executive is so detached from ordinary life that his only plan for understanding normal people is to watch movies, which are themselves made by people like him, a circular and absurd source of realism.
summary: A movie producer promises a relatable adaptation but has no real-world contact with ordinary folks, so he plans to study them through films.

title: Shipping Trash by FedEx Expenses

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Wally, what is the quickest way to send these old binders to the landfill?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I usually use "FedEx." Charge it to Marketing; they never look at their expense reports.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Here's one more thing I can never tell anyone about my job.

situation: Asok, carrying a box of old binders, asks Wally how to get them to the landfill quickly. Wally casually advises shipping them by FedEx and billing the cost to the Marketing department, since nobody there checks expense reports. Asok, stunned, thinks to himself that this is yet another thing he can never tell anyone about his job.
punchline: Wally's routine abuse of the expense system, sending garbage by overnight courier on someone else's budget, is so absurd and wasteful that Asok realizes his workplace is too embarrassing to describe to outsiders.
summary: A coworker learns that the office's standard method for disposing of junk is to courier it away at another department's expense.

file: 1999/1999-09-10_prospective client_touring dept_marketing department_vacant cubicle_pretending to work.gif
title: Pretending to Work for Client

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: A prospective client will be touring our marketing department in an hour.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We need you to sit in a vacant cubicle so it looks as if work is done there.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Hey! That one is only pretending to work!

setting: Office cubicles in the marketing department
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that a prospective client will tour the marketing department soon, and asks him to sit in an empty cubicle so it looks like real work happens there. During the tour, a woman visiting with a man points at Dilbert and loudly announces that he is only pretending to work.
punchline: The scheme to fake productivity for a visitor is instantly exposed because the visitor can spot someone merely pretending to work, implying real workers look different from those faking it.
summary: A manager stages a fake busy workstation to impress a visiting customer, but the visitor sees through the act immediately.

title: Boss Cuts Newspaper Subscriptions, Dilbert Unfazed

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The company will no longer pay for newspaper subscriptions.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I pay for this myself. The news is highly relevant to my job.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Is there anything I can do to make it less enjoyable?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Just keep jabbering.

situation: The Boss announces that the company will no longer pay for newspaper subscriptions while Dilbert sits reading a paper. Dilbert says he pays for his own copy and that the news is relevant to his job. The Boss then asks how he can make the reading less enjoyable, and Dilbert tells him to just keep talking.
punchline: The Boss, determined to take away any perk, is told that his own annoying chatter already ruins Dilbert's enjoyment of the paper, so he needs to do nothing more.
summary: A manager tries to stop an employee's newspaper reading and is told his own babbling already spoils it.

title: Rubber Babies Chick Magnet Backfires

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: These fake rubber babies will make me a chick magnet.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Stupid fly.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Whap!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's tough love.

setting: Outdoors in a park, beside a tree on a grassy lawn
situation: Dilbert carries several fake rubber babies around a park, believing they will make him attractive to women. A woman looks at him fondly until a fly buzzes around him and he swats it by swinging one of the rubber babies, smacking another baby into the tree. Horrified, the woman watches as Dilbert claims it is tough love.
punchline: Dilbert's scheme to look like a caring father collapses when he casually uses a baby as a fly swatter, and his lame 'tough love' excuse only makes things worse.
summary: A man hoping to charm women with a collection of toy infants ruins the impression by whacking a fly with one of them.

title: Hammerhead Bob Won't Leave You Alone

transcript.speaker: Hammerhead Bob
transcript.text: You're getting a visit from Hammerhead Bob!

transcript.speaker: Hammerhead Bob
transcript.text: I can't tell when I'm boring. I might be boring now and I don't even know it.

transcript.speaker: Hammerhead Bob
transcript.text: There's no way to end a conversation with me; I'll follow you to the bathroom.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm nailed.

situation: Hammerhead Bob, a coworker with a oddly shaped hammer-like head, announces himself and stands next to Dilbert's desk while Dilbert works at his computer. Bob cheerfully admits he cannot tell when he is being boring and warns that he will even follow Dilbert to the bathroom to keep talking. Dilbert realizes in a thought bubble that he has no escape.
punchline: Hammerhead Bob openly admits he is boring and oblivious, and by announcing he'll follow Dilbert anywhere, he removes every escape route, leaving Dilbert trapped.
summary: A self-aware but clueless bore corners a coworker and cheerfully rules out every possible way to escape the conversation.

title: Doomed Plan, Eager Boss

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're suggesting a process that will fail even if we do everything right.

transcript.speaker: Man in green tie
transcript.text: When can you start?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Listen carefully. No amount of skill or effort can make this plan work.

transcript.speaker: Man in green tie
transcript.text: No pain, no gain.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're not working with many tools here, are you?

transcript.speaker: Man in green tie
transcript.text: We need some sort of conference call.

setting: Conference room table in an office meeting
situation: Dilbert tells a manager that his proposed process is guaranteed to fail no matter how well it is executed. The manager ignores the warning, cheerfully asks when Dilbert can start, and responds with a cliche. When Dilbert mocks his limited toolkit, the manager's only idea is to hold a conference call.
punchline: The manager is utterly immune to being told his plan is impossible, answering every objection with cheerful platitudes and the one tool he knows, a conference call.
summary: A cheerful manager brushes aside Dilbert's warning that his scheme cannot possibly succeed and proposes a conference call as the fix.

title: Half Budget Means Guaranteed Failure

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This is the bare minimum budget I need for my project.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What could you do with half this amount?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Fail.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: When can you start?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think I just did.

setting: Office, in front of the Boss
situation: Dilbert hands the Boss a budget request, calling it the bare minimum his project needs. The Boss asks what Dilbert could accomplish with half the money. Dilbert answers that he would fail, and the Boss cheerfully asks when he can start, prompting Dilbert to say he already has.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically points out that the Boss's budget-cutting demand guarantees failure, and that the project is already failing the moment the Boss proposes cutting the money.
summary: A manager responds to a minimal funding request by suggesting a halved budget, and the engineer deadpans that the resulting failure has already begun.

file: 1999/1999-06-22_quality assurance group_bad for company_head count problem.gif
title: Reassigned To Solve Headcount Problem

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Asok, I'm moving you to my "Quality Assurance" group.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Gasp

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I realize this is bad for you... and bad for the company... but it solves my headcount problem.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Will that be my contribution to the world: "He solved a headcount problem"?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That tops me.

setting: The Boss's office, then a conference table
situation: The Boss tells Asok he is being transferred to the Quality Assurance group. He openly admits the move harms both Asok and the company but fixes his own staffing numbers. Asok laments that this will be his legacy while Wally, sitting at the table, remarks that it beats anything he has done.
punchline: Wally's deadpan comment implies that even a meaningless contribution like solving a headcount problem is more than he has ever accomplished, mocking both management's cynicism and his own laziness.
summary: A manager cheerfully admits that shuffling a young engineer into a bogus department helps no one but his own staffing figures.

title: Boss Offers to Eliminate Her Project

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Every department was asked how it could reduce its budget ten percent.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your project is vital to the future of the company, so I cleverly offered to eliminate it, knowing they couldn't accept.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Now this is the funny part...

situation: The Boss tells a female employee that every department was told to propose a ten percent budget cut. To show how important her project is, he proudly says he offered to eliminate it entirely, assuming management would refuse. He then ominously announces that now comes the funny part, while she looks alarmed.
punchline: The Boss's 'clever' bluff has clearly backfired, and management has apparently accepted his offer to cancel her vital project.
summary: A manager brags about a risky bluff during budget cuts, and his worried employee realizes the gamble probably failed.

file: 1999/1999-08-22_stressed alice_role model_deadlines_pride_no ambition_glory_new vp_student ready_master appear.gif
title: Calm Wally Teaches Stressed Alice

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: There's no reason to be stressed, Alice.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Allow me to be your role model.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I remain calm despite the pressure of impossible deadlines.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: That's because you have no pride and no ambition!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I've worked day and night to make this deadline!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: And when I succeed, the glory will be mine!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Our new VP just canceled the project so the last VP would look bad.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: They say that when the student is ready, the master will appear.

situation: Wally offers himself as a calm role model to a stressed Alice, who is fighting an impossible deadline. She retorts that his calm comes from having no pride or ambition, and boasts about the glory she will earn. A coworker then announces that the new VP canceled the project, and Wally smugly says the master has appeared.
punchline: Alice's hard work is made worthless by a petty management decision, proving Wally's lazy detachment was the wise approach all along.
summary: A frantic overachiever mocks a lazy colleague's serenity just before learning her project has been scrapped for office-politics reasons.

file: 1999/1999-10-07_ruin career_upstart embryo_replaces me_volunteers_give constructive criticism_human resources_don't like attitude_business.gif
title: Boss Sabotages Embryo Via Catbert

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'd better ruin the career of this upstart embryo before he replaces me.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need volunteers to give constructive criticism to Human Resources.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I don't like your attitude.

situation: The Boss sits at his desk with a small jar containing an embryo and worries that it will eventually take his job. He decides to ruin its career and asks for volunteers to give constructive criticism to Human Resources. Catbert, the HR director, takes the jar and tells the embryo he doesn't like its attitude.
punchline: The Boss is so insecure about being replaced that he preemptively sabotages a jarred embryo's career, and Catbert, the evil HR director, happily delivers the criticism.
summary: Fearing that a tiny embryo in a jar will someday take his job, a paranoid manager recruits the human resources cat to start tearing down its prospects.

title: Dogbert's Instant Management Course Scam

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'd like to enroll in Dogbert's accelerated management course.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Take out your checkbook and begin your final exam now.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Question one: What is today's date?

setting: Alice's office cubicle, with Dogbert on the other end of a phone call
situation: Alice phones Dogbert to sign up for his accelerated management course. Dogbert immediately tells her to take out her checkbook and start the final exam. The first exam question is simply the date, which is what she writes on a check.
punchline: The final exam is just filling out a check, so Dogbert's course is nothing but a way to take her money for a worthless credential.
summary: A woman calls to join a fast-track management class and discovers that the entire test consists of writing a check to the instructor.

title: Eagles, Ducks, and Unread Meeting Materials

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We must be like eagles, not ducks.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: For the eggs?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I didn't do the pre-reading.

situation: The Boss addresses a meeting with a motivational line about being like eagles rather than ducks. Wally, seated at the table, responds with a nonsensical guess about eggs, then admits he did not do the pre-reading that would have explained the context.
punchline: Wally's confused answer shows he has no idea what the Boss's vague metaphor means, and he blames it on skipping the meeting prep, which implies the metaphor is meaningless anyway.
summary: A manager's empty bird metaphor draws a baffled question from a coworker who hasn't read the meeting materials.

file: 1999/1999-05-09_few upgrades to design_realize engineer_graduate of liberal arts_college_broad exposure_modern renaissance_timing circuit_moby dick_charles dickens_engineering classes_poor engineers_work is small_education.gif
title: Boss's Liberal Arts Engineering Upgrade

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I made a few upgrades to your design, Alice.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Do you realize you're not an engineer?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm better! I'm a well-rounded graduate of a liberal arts college.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The broad exposure to diverse topics made me what I am today.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: A modern Renaissance man.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You scribbled out my timing circuit and wrote in, "Moby Dick by Charles Dickens."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Exactly. I'll bet you didn't learn THAT in your engineering classes!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Poor engineers; their world is so small.

situation: The Boss tells Alice he has upgraded her circuit design, and she points out he is not an engineer. He boasts that his liberal arts education makes him better, and Alice reveals he replaced her timing circuit with a wrong claim about Moby Dick's author. He takes this as proof of his superior breadth of knowledge.
punchline: The Boss's boasted broad education is shown to be worthless, since he ruined a circuit with a bogus book fact (Moby Dick was written by Herman Melville, not Dickens), yet he still thinks engineers are the narrow-minded ones.
summary: A boss who ruined an engineer's circuit by scribbling a literary blunder over it insists his liberal arts background makes him the more worldly one.

title: Hidden Cameras and Mister Itchy

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It has come to my attention that some of you believe there are hidden cameras in the ceiling.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: How did that come to your attention?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Hey, aren't you the one we call "Mister Itchy"?

situation: The Boss tells his staff at a meeting table that some of them suspect hidden cameras in the ceiling. An employee asks how he learned of this suspicion. The Boss responds by identifying him by a nickname that suggests he has been watched fidgeting.
punchline: The Boss's casual use of the nickname "Mister Itchy" reveals that the hidden cameras do exist and that management has been secretly watching employees.
summary: A manager dismisses rumors of secret ceiling cameras, then accidentally proves them true by recognizing a worker from his private habits.

title: Presentation So Dull Audience Suffocates

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This concludes my presentation. Are there any questions?

transcript.speaker: Audience Member
transcript.text: How do I get the boredom out of my head?!!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The funny thing is that I'll list this on my annual accomplishments.

transcript.speaker: Audience Member
transcript.text: Air! I need air!!!

situation: Dilbert finishes a presentation with an org chart on the wall and asks for questions. His three coworkers sit at the table clutching their heads in agony, one pleading to get the boredom out of his head. Dilbert, unbothered, thinks about adding the presentation to his annual accomplishments while the audience gasps for air.
punchline: Dilbert's presentation is so torturous that it physically pains the audience, yet he is only concerned with claiming it as an accomplishment on his performance review.
summary: A presenter's crushing dullness leaves his colleagues clutching their skulls, while he quietly plans to take credit for the ordeal at review time.

title: Booby-Trapped Shredder Voids Warranty

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Don't use the shredder today.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I rigged it to kill our new sadistic nut co-worker.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Whoa! Whoa!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Doesn't that void the warranty?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'll switch shredders with marketing tomorrow.

setting: Office lunch table or break room
situation: Alice, eating lunch with Dilbert and Wally, warns them not to use the shredder because she has rigged it to kill their new sadistic co-worker. Dilbert is alarmed, but then only raises the concern that tampering might void the warranty. Alice calmly says she will swap shredders with the marketing department the next day.
punchline: Alice's murder plot is treated as a minor equipment concern, and her solution is to pass the dangerous, warranty-voided shredder on to marketing, whom everyone considers expendable.
summary: A coworker confesses to booby-trapping the office shredder as a trap for a nasty newcomer, and the only objections are about paperwork and who else might get hurt.

file: 1999/1999-01-01_morale is low_managers bonuses_big changes_surevy_tenth year_employee satisfaction.gif
title: Bonuses Tied to Rigging Survey

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: For the tenth year in a row, the employee satisfaction survey says morale is low.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Managers' bonuses are linked to these results. You can be sure we'll make big changes...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: ... to the survey.

setting: Conference room during a management meeting
situation: The Boss reads aloud from a sheet of paper that the employee satisfaction survey has shown low morale for the tenth straight year. He notes that managers' bonuses depend on the results and promises big changes. Dilbert and Alice listen at the table as he reveals the changes will be to the survey itself.
punchline: Instead of fixing the causes of low morale, management will change the survey so the results look better and their bonuses are protected.
summary: Faced with another year of poor survey results that threaten their pay, managers decide to alter the questionnaire rather than improve working conditions.

title: Boss Speaks Into Wrong Gadget

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It took me three days to enter all of my appointments into this PDA.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll enter our next meeting.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Tuesday... Two o'clock.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Is it voice-controlled?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I sure hope so.

situation: At a meeting table, the Boss complains that entering his appointments into a PDA took him three days. He then announces the next meeting aloud and speaks the date and time toward the device while a bald coworker watches. The coworker asks if the PDA is voice-controlled and the Boss admits he only hopes it is.
punchline: The Boss has been talking to his PDA without knowing whether it accepts voice input, showing he doesn't understand the technology he uses and explaining why it took him three days.
summary: A manager dictates his next meeting to a handheld organizer without having any idea if it can even hear him.

file: 1999/1999-05-20_almost back_date_attach tracking device_run down alley_leaves_different opinions.gif
title: Date Ends With Secret Tracking Device

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well, we're almost back to my place.

transcript.speaker: Dark-haired woman
transcript.text: Thanks for the date. I can make it from here.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'd better attach the tracking device.

transcript.speaker: Dark-haired woman
transcript.text: I'll run down that alley and hide until he leaves.

setting: A city sidewalk beside a brick building at the end of a date
situation: Dilbert walks his date back toward his place, and she politely thanks him and says she can get home from there. In the final panel, thought bubbles reveal that Dilbert plans to secretly attach a tracking device to her while she plans to run down an alley and hide until he leaves.
punchline: Both of them are thinking about completely different outcomes of the date: Dilbert's creepy plan to track her contrasts with her plan to flee, showing the date went badly and he is clueless about it.
summary: A man and his date part ways while his thoughts reveal a stalker-ish plan and hers reveal she wants to escape him.

file: 1999/1999-10-27_job secuirty_be an engineer_takes all day_get in on scam.gif
title: Engineering: The Job Security Scam

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Alice, I need a career that has job security.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Teach me to be an engineer. I don't care if it takes all day.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: But don't tell anyone; they'll all try to get in on this scam.

situation: Carol, the Boss's assistant, approaches Alice at her cubicle and asks to be taught how to become an engineer because she wants job security. She insists she is willing to spend all day learning it. She then asks Alice to keep it secret, calling engineering a scam.
punchline: Carol sees engineering as a racket in which the engineers' special knowledge keeps them indispensable, and she wants in before everyone else catches on.
summary: An administrative assistant begs an engineer for lessons in her profession, convinced it is a secret trick for never getting fired.

title: Dilbert Delivers Bad News, Coworkers Overreact

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I heard your project got cancelled.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: No! No! Why me? I'll never love again!!

transcript.speaker: Second Coworker
transcript.text: I renounce my religion.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ouch.

situation: Dilbert, holding a coffee mug, tells a coworker that his project has been cancelled. The coworker melodramatically collapses, wailing that he will never love again. A second coworker with spiky hair then announces he renounces his religion, and Dilbert winces.
punchline: The project cancellation news sends coworkers into absurdly exaggerated despair, and Dilbert's flat 'Ouch' acknowledges the over-the-top reactions, including abandoning one's faith over a canceled work project.
summary: A man learns his project was scrapped and responds with wildly theatrical grief while another colleague dramatically gives up his faith.

file: 1999/1999-08-04_dogberts tech support_shut up_reboot_shut up and hang up_call time_improving.gif
title: Dogbert Improves Call Time Rudely

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert's Tech Support

transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: Hello, I...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Shut up and reboot.

transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: Hey, it work...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Shut up and hang up.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: My average call time is improving.

situation: Dogbert, wearing a headset at his tech support desk, cuts off a caller mid-sentence and tells him to reboot. When the caller tries to say the fix worked, Dogbert tells him to hang up. Dogbert then privately notes that his average call time is getting better.
punchline: Dogbert hits his support metric by rudely cutting off customers instead of helping them, showing how call-time targets reward bad service.
summary: A helpdesk dog silences each caller with curt commands to shorten his calls and congratulates himself on the numbers.
keywords: turn it off and on again

file: 1999/1999-10-31_seven silo teams_merge them_coherent plan_mutually exclusive_deciding startegy_losers_silo teams.gif
title: Dilbert Secretly Writes Company Strategy

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Here are the strategies from our seven silo teams.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your job is to merge them into a coherent company plan.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: These are all mutually exclusive.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'd have to totally change them to make them coherent.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: In effect, I would be deciding the strategy for the entire company.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's okay.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It is?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No one ever reads it anyway.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I feel sorry for those losers on the silo teams.

setting: The Boss's office and Dilbert's cubicle
situation: The Boss hands Dilbert strategy documents from seven silo teams and asks him to merge them into one coherent company plan. Dilbert points out that they are mutually exclusive and that he would effectively be setting the whole company's strategy, and the Boss shrugs it off. In his thought bubble the Boss reveals nobody reads the plan, and Dilbert goes back to his desk pitying the silo teams whose work will be ignored.
punchline: The company strategy that teams labor over is never actually read, so the seven silo teams' work is pointless and Dilbert's unchecked authority doesn't matter.
summary: A manager casually lets his engineer rewrite the whole company's direction because he knows the resulting plan will go unread.

file: 1999/1999-12-24_dogbertmd.com_netting billions_no profit_press release_neener_profits are for losers.gif
title: Profits Are For Losers IPO

transcript.speaker: TV Announcer
transcript.text: DogbertMD.com had a successful IPO today, netting billions for Dogbert.

transcript.speaker: TV Announcer
transcript.text: The company has no profit now and expects no profit later.

transcript.speaker: TV Announcer
transcript.text: The company issued a press release that says, "Neener neener. Profits are for losers."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Succinct.

setting: Dilbert's living room, watching TV from the couch
situation: Dilbert lounges in a bathrobe on the couch while Dogbert sits beside him, watching a TV news report. The report says Dogbert's dot-com, DogbertMD.com, made billions in its IPO despite having no profit and no expectation of ever earning one. The company's press release mockingly declares that profits are for losers.
punchline: Dot-com investors will pour billions into a company that openly admits it will never make a profit, and the company gleefully taunts them for it.
summary: A television report on a wildly lucrative stock offering for a profitless pet-doctor website leaves Dilbert dryly unimpressed by the company's brazen attitude.

title: Cube Farmer Weeds The Boss

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Cube farming

transcript.speaker: Cube Farmer
transcript.text: Weed.

transcript.speaker: Cube Farmer
transcript.text: Got it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Suddenly there's more light... and I feel more nourished.

situation: A man in a green cap and gardening gear peers over the cubicle wall like a farmer tending a field. He spots the Pointy-Haired Boss standing in Dilbert's cubicle, calls him a weed, and yanks him out with a long pole. Dilbert, now alone, thinks that the space is brighter and he feels better nourished.
punchline: The Boss is treated as a weed that was choking the cubicle crop, and Dilbert thrives once he is removed, implying the boss was a harmful drain on his productivity and well-being.
summary: A gardener tending a field of cubicles plucks the boss out of Dilbert's workspace like an unwanted weed, leaving Dilbert feeling healthier.

title: Thief Description Sounds Like The Boss

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: There's been a rash of thefts from cubicles.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The suspect is described as fat and slow-witted, with pointy hair.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The bulletin stops short of actually naming her Alice.

situation: The Boss reads a security bulletin aloud to the team about thefts from cubicles. The suspect's description (fat, slow-witted, pointy hair) matches the Boss's own appearance, yet he fails to notice. He then claims the bulletin stops short of naming Alice as the culprit, implicitly accusing her while the others look on awkwardly.
punchline: The Boss reads out a description of the thief that obviously fits himself, yet remains oblivious and instead pins the suspicion on Alice.
summary: A manager reading out a theft bulletin cluelessly describes himself as the culprit while pointing the finger at a coworker.

title: Wally's Forgotten Valuable Lesson

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I lost my fortune and my trophy wife today. But I learned a valuable lesson.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Munch munch munch

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I hope I wrote it down somewhere.

situation: Wally sits at a lunch table with Alice and Dilbert, peeling a banana, and announces he lost his fortune and his trophy wife but gained a valuable lesson. After a pause of munching, he admits he hopes he wrote the lesson down somewhere, implying he has already forgotten it.
punchline: Wally claims to have learned a valuable lesson from a huge personal loss but can't actually remember what it was, showing he's learned nothing.
summary: After suffering a double disaster, Wally boasts of newfound wisdom and then reveals he has already lost track of it.

title: Boss Cares, But Only Legally

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, I care about you...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But only enough to improve your morale, not enough to be illegal in any way.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So, tell me about your health in the least specific way possible.

situation: The Boss stands over Alice at her desk and tells her he cares about her. He then qualifies this by saying his concern only goes as far as boosting morale without breaking any laws. He asks her to describe her health as vaguely as possible, while Alice glares at him with gritted teeth.
punchline: The Boss's attempt at caring about an employee's wellbeing is so hedged by legal caution that he asks for deliberately useless information, making the gesture meaningless.
summary: A manager offers sympathy to an employee but carefully limits it to avoid any legal liability, asking for only vague details about her health.

file: 1999/1999-11-07_newly designated_fire warden_bitter_assignment_regular job_last one out_safety_fire_panic_flushing self_exit door.gif
title: Wally's Self-Serving Fire Safety Briefing

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You might expect me to be bitter about this assignment.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Granted, it tells the world I wasn't productive at my regular job.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: And if the building burns, I'm expected to be the last one out.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: But my only concern is your safety.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: In the event of a fire, don't be too proud to panic.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: If the windows won't open, try flushing yourself to safety.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: And never, ever get between me and the exit door.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Wally...

setting: Office conference area during a fire safety presentation
situation: Wally, newly appointed as the floor's fire warden, gives a safety briefing to coworkers using a flip chart labeled 'Safety'. He complains about the assignment, then offers absurd advice like panicking and flushing yourself down a toilet. He ends by warning no one to block his path to the exit.
punchline: Wally claims his only concern is everyone's safety, but his real priority is saving himself, as he threatens anyone who gets between him and the exit.
summary: A lazy employee given fire warden duty delivers a ridiculous safety talk that reveals he'd trample his coworkers to escape first.

file: 1999/1999-02-21_weekly wally report_pointy haired troll_dumped record_levels of work_moral delemma_disappoint stock holders_last ounce of happiness_one choice_reading ahead_assignments.gif
title: The Weekly Wally Report Dramatic Reading

transcript.text: By Tuesday the Pointy-Haired Troll had dumped record levels of work on poor Wally.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Wally's happiness was in extreme jeopardy.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It was a moral dilemma too.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Would Wally disappoint the stockholders to save his own skin?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Or would he fight with his last ounce of happiness to complete all the assignments?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: In the end there was only one choice.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You wrote the Wally report instead of working?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Stop reading ahead!

setting: Conference room during a weekly staff meeting
situation: Wally gives his weekly report in the style of a suspenseful dramatic narration, describing the huge workload the boss dumped on him and the moral dilemma it created. He builds up to revealing his choice, but the boss figures out the answer before he finishes.
punchline: Wally's dramatic report about his heroic struggle with his workload is itself proof that he spent his time writing the report instead of doing any of the work.
summary: A slacker builds suspense over whether he did his assignments, only to reveal he spent the time writing the dramatic account instead.

title: Astrologer Accidentally Approves Good Plan

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My astrologer told me to approve your project plan as is.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: What?! That's the correct decision. What's going on here?

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: My theory is that his ignorance clouded his poor judgment.

situation: The Boss tells a colleague that he is approving her project plan unchanged because his astrologer told him to. She is stunned because approving it is actually the right call. She then explains to Dilbert that the Boss's ignorance must have cancelled out his bad judgment.
punchline: The Boss only made the right decision by accident, because his ignorance happened to override his usual terrible judgment.
summary: A manager follows his astrologer's advice and stumbles into the right decision, leaving his baffled employee to explain it as one flaw neutralizing another.

file: 1999/1999-06-02_kill coworker_employee manual_award for cost saving_evil hr director.gif
title: Murder Earns Cost-Saving Award

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Alice, did you kill another co-worker?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: But you did not discriminate, sexually harass, steal or take drugs.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Hmm...

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: It looks like I have to give you an award for your cost-saving idea.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Thank you.

Catbert checks the employee manual and finds that murder isn't among the listed violations. Because eliminating a co-worker saves payroll costs, he reluctantly concludes he must give her an award.
punchline: The employee manual only forbids a handful of HR-style offenses, so murder is technically allowed and even rewarded as a cost-saving measure.
summary: An HR cat consults the rulebook after a coworker's murder and discovers the staff handbook has no rule against it, so the killer gets praised for cutting expenses.

file: 1999/1999-09-19_give his presentation_irrelevant comparisons_low budget_development time_computers faster_obvious insights.gif

setting: Conference room during a slide presentation
situation: Dilbert is giving a presentation on behalf of his boss and openly labels each slide as he goes. He presents budget and development-time comparisons that compare things that aren't comparable, then moves to a slide of obvious insights and declines to read it aloud, while the audience watches with blank expressions.
punchline: Dilbert bluntly narrates how useless the boss's presentation content is, culminating in an 'insight' so obvious that reading it aloud would be embarrassing.
summary: A stand-in presenter cheerfully exposes the emptiness of his boss's slides, from meaningless comparisons to a banal observation about technology.

transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Fitness Coworker

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

situation: A relentlessly athletic coworker stands by Dilbert's cubicle and invites him to join increasingly extreme physical activities. Dilbert flatly declines the fifty-mile run and the triathlons. When the coworker begins describing a leap into geosynchronous orbit, Dilbert cries out in frustration and swats at the air.
punchline: The coworker's invitations escalate from extreme to absurdly impossible, and Dilbert only loses his composure when the boasting reaches literal space travel, showing how tiresome the one-upmanship is.
summary: A fitness-obsessed colleague keeps pitching ever more outlandish athletic feats to an uninterested Dilbert until the bragging becomes cosmic.

title: Golf Day Reward Worse Than Pay Cut

transcript.text: I decided to try motivating you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: ...If you do a great job, you get to go on a golfing day with co-workers.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Question: Can I take a pay cut instead.

setting: Conference room during a staff meeting
situation: The Boss announces to his team that he has decided to try motivating them. His proposed reward for doing a great job is a golfing day with co-workers. Dilbert raises his hand and asks whether he could take a pay cut instead, while Wally dozes off beside him.
punchline: Dilbert would rather lose money than spend a day socializing with his co-workers, which shows how unappealing the boss's idea of a reward is.
summary: A manager's attempt at employee motivation backfires when his chosen prize is so unappealing that an employee would prefer a salary reduction.

file: 1999/1999-05-26_knew you were rebel_cool rebels_stop talking_threats_argue_bathrobe to work.gif
title: Cool Rebels Bet a Nail

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: When I saw you wear a bathrobe to work, I knew you were a rebel.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: From now on, when you come upon a group of us cool rebels, we won't suddenly stop talking.
